paragraphs.text: Malachi, the prophet of God, who was rightly called an angel, is shown sounding a gospel trumpet when he says of him: "For you who fear his name the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings." He foretells and announces to us in advance that the only-begotten Son of God would be seen on earth, not in the essence of some other being but in his own, and that by his own grace he would light up all things. In the same way this visible sun is regularly seen in its own essence, and by its own essence it shines on all things. So too the divine radiance, Jesus our Lord, appeared on earth and filled the whole inhabited world with everlasting light. It was fitting, then, that the prophet just mentioned proclaimed him in advance as the sun of righteousness. He rose, therefore, so that, lit by his rays, we might see clearly with the eyes of the mind the sayings of the divine Scriptures that are hidden and obscure. He rose also so that we too, singing with blessed David, might say to him: "The obscure and hidden things of your wisdom you have made known to me." This is not the wisdom of the present age. It is the wisdom hidden in the Father before the ages and revealed in the last days, not only in knowledge but also in visible form and in person [?]. It was revealed so that those who believe in him might have firm assurance through the true testimony of those who saw him both before his passion and after the resurrection. He, then, who showed himself to the world, being truly himself the sun of righteousness, has now also shone his grace on us, and by it he has guided us into the unsearchable riches of the treasures of the knowledge of his sayings. For I am full of hope, brothers, that he who revealed his own Father to us will also make known to us his ever-flowing springs of these matters. Then our winepresses may overflow with his grace, so that we can share it with those who need and desire it, and the saying may be fulfilled in us: "Whoever gives one of these little ones who believe in me a cup of cold water to drink will not lose his reward." So we take courage and are glad to share with you, from his grace, the crown woven and set with many kinds of precious stones. I mean the crown of David. The whole creation, rational and intellectual, is shown to bear this crown through the hymnody it sends up to God without ceasing. The Lord of all brought this hymnody forth on earth through his servant, to whom he himself bore witness when he said: "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart." For truly he used David as his very own heart, and through him he poured out his divine doxology, our spiritual worship.

First, then, we shall begin with the account given by the writers who came before us. After touching on their prologue we shall go on, by the grace of our Lord, to more pertinent matters, for I do not think it right to pass over their introduction. Some of them, as men who worked with great precision, saw fit to bring the Hebrew text itself into the discussion. On that basis they maintained that the book of Psalms belongs to many different prophets and not to David alone. They judged this from the titles placed over the psalms, saying that some are David's, some belong to the sons of Korah, others to Asaph, one to Ethan the Israelite, others to Solomon, and one of them to Moses, while others are untitled, others anonymous, and some are headed "Alleluia." They added something else, taken from Chronicles: David chose four men from the tribe of Levi, Asaph son of Korah, Heman, Ethan and Jeduthun, and stationed them before the sanctuary with various instruments. David himself stood in their midst as leader of the leaders of songs, holding the psaltery in his hands.

As I said, some of the writers gave this account, and it is found written in some psalters that they published. They presented it as though they had drawn it from the Hebrew, but to me they do not seem right to have introduced so long an account. For if, as they themselves said, David stood in their midst holding the psaltery in his hands, how is the book of Psalms not David's? And if they were to say that he wrote down in the psaltery what those men spoke, then he is no longer their leader. Instead they are his leaders, since they passed on to him what they themselves uttered.

Likewise their division of the psalms does not seem reasonable to me. For, as I said, they claimed that some are David's, some belong to the sons of Korah, some to Asaph, another to Ethan the Israelite, some to Solomon, others to Heman, and one to Moses. In that case, I think, the psalm of Moses should have been placed first of all in the book of Psalms. Or else it should have been included in his own books, just as his songs are placed there: one in Exodus, another in Numbers and another in Deuteronomy, and not in the book of Psalms. Yet, by the reckoning of those who arranged things this way, the one psalm said to be Moses' is not placed first of all. It comes after Solomon and before David, Solomon's father.

I will also say this about the psalms of Solomon. If they were Solomon's at all, they would have been included in Kings or Chronicles, or at least this very fact would have been made clear to us in those books. It is said of him there that he had five thousand songs, but divine Scripture nowhere mentions a psalm of his.

But someone will tell me that the titles of the psalms say this plainly. Yet the titles of the psalms do not always present to us the persons who bear those names. Instead they present the interpretation and meaning of what is said. What I mean is this. A title reads "A psalm for David," or again "of David." Sometimes "of David" is interpreted "despised," and sometimes "strong of hand." Again it is interpreted "alone," and at times "this one I desired," "the desired one," and "this one is beloved." The name of David underlies all these interpretations. All of these, then, are meant allegorically. When the title reads "A psalm for David" and the psalm speaks to a people turning back from an evil way, then we understand "of David" as "despised." For it is written: "As the eyes of a maidservant look to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. For we have been filled with contempt in full measure; our soul has been filled with it more and more." And: "You have despised all who depart from your statutes, for their thought is unjust." And elsewhere he says: "Those who despise me shall be despised."

As I said, then, if the name of David is placed over a psalm, and the psalm sings about people who have sinned and are turning back, the title signifies that this psalm is spoken about those who were despised before because of their sins but afterwards turned back. If the psalm speaks about people who do what is right, the name of David can also be interpreted in this way, as I said. For the people of God are despised by the world, as the prophet says: "I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your testimonies."

Likewise, if the psalm sings about the righteous, the name of David can be interpreted "this one I desired," that is, "my chosen people," in keeping with what is said in the Gospel: "Having loved his own, he loved them to the end." The name of David can also be interpreted in another way with reference to the righteous: I mean "of the desired one," that is, the people of God, the desired one. Or else we may give yet another interpretation of David, since it is also said to mean "desired." This too is to be taken of the people of the saints, for that people is desired by the Lord.

When the title reads "A psalm for David" and the psalm is about the Son of God, we know that the name of David is interpreted "strong of hand." For it is written of him: "The Lord, strong and mighty."

Where the title reads "of the Korahites," this title too has several meanings. There were psalm-singers from among the sons of Korah, as we find in Chronicles, where it is written: "And the Levites of the sons of Kohath and of the sons of Korah stood up to praise the Lord, the God of Israel, with a loud voice on high." These psalm-singers praised the Lord with the words of David, as it says in Chronicles: "The Levites with the instruments for the songs of the Lord, which King David had made, to give thanks before the Lord, for his mercy endures forever, with the hymns of David by their hand." So the Korahites were psalm-singers along with the Levites. Wherever a psalm has the title "of the sons of Korah," this shows that the psalm is spoken about the pure in heart, or about the helpless, or about those who contradict. For the name Korah is interpreted "bald," and under the law a bald man is clean, as it is written in Leviticus: "If anyone's hair falls from his head, he is bald; he is clean." Again, in the Prophets we find God in some places angry with Israel and saying: "And there shall be baldness on every head," meaning shame and reproach for every ruler of the people when I take away their help from them. It is also plain that Korah himself became a man of contradiction. So the psalms [titled] "of the sons of Korah" are not about the sons of Korah [?]. As I said, the psalm speaks either about the pure in heart, or about those who are outside God's shelter, or about those who contradict the gospel of God. Of these the apostle says: "Woe to them, for they perished in the contradiction of Korah." Elsewhere it says: "They contradicted what was spoken by Paul." And the author of Proverbs said: "Every evil man stirs up contradictions." So we have now made plain to you the meaning of the title "of the sons of Korah."

After the sons of Korah, they said that some psalms also belong to Asaph. But this claim of theirs too proves to be weak. The titles of the psalms in which Asaph's name appears do not read "a psalm of Asaph," which would let someone say that the psalm was composed by him. Instead, each of his titles reads "a psalm for Asaph." When this name is interpreted from Hebrew into Greek, as with the others, it shows why it is placed over the psalm in this way. For Asaph is interpreted "one who collects and gathers" or "assembly." Wherever it is written over a psalm, then, the psalm speaks either about God, who gathers all people both in this age and in the age to come, some to salvation and others to judgment, or else about those who turn back and are gathered together, from Gentiles and Jews alike, into the one assembly.

After Asaph, they said there is also a psalm of Ethan the Israelite. Was Ethan, then, the only Israelite? What about David, the sons of Korah, Asaph, Solomon and Moses, who according to them are named in the Hebrew as the ones who spoke the psalms? Clearly they too are Israelites. And was Ethan the only Israelite in all the tribes? I do not think so. If you look at the genealogy of the twelve tribes in Chronicles, you will find many men called by this name, all of them obviously Israelites. What, then, does such a title on the psalm mean? Let us turn again to the interpretation of the name. The title runs: "Of understanding, for Ethan the Israelite." That is, a psalm that bears this inscription either concerns the understanding of the saints, who are lofty in mind and are the seed of God, or else it is for the Most High, who sowed his grace in the saints. For Ethan is interpreted "lofty," and Israelite is interpreted "seed of God." These things are therefore to be taken either of the Son of God, and from this we know that the psalm is spoken about him, or of his saints, who are lofty in mind and have been sown with his divine grace.

After this, they said that two psalms also belong to Solomon. As I said, we do not find these recorded in any of the books about him, neither in Kings nor in Chronicles. Nor are they placed together; one is in one part of the book of Psalms and the other in another. Both clearly speak about the Son of God. For Solomon is interpreted "most peaceable," and that is Jesus our Lord, who is peace by nature, which is why he has also given peace to us by his own grace. So wherever the name of Solomon is placed over a psalm, it teaches us beyond dispute that the psalm speaks about the Son of God.

They also said that the 89th psalm is Moses', as they supposed. They paid attention to the letter of the title and not to its meaning, or rather they did not even read the title itself accurately. For it does not say "A prayer of Moses the man of God" but "A prayer for Moses the man of God." That is, this title fits every man of God who runs to God's baptism. For Moses is interpreted "taken up out of water," which is what God's baptism is for each person who is baptized, since he is brought up out of the divine streams of the saving water.

They also said that some of the psalms are untitled, because they are inscribed that way, and that it follows from this that these too are not David's. But the apostle Peter and all those with him ought to carry more weight with us. In Acts they say: "You are God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, who said through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David your servant: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things? The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." By this they showed that David spoke this psalm, which is one of the untitled ones. In the same way it is clear that he also spoke the psalm before it, I mean the first psalm, for it too seems to be one of the untitled ones. David himself was the first to appoint psalm-singers, as you will find in Chronicles, where it is written: "And David appointed some of the Levites before the ark of the covenant of the Lord to minister and to cry aloud, to give thanks and to praise the Lord, the God of Israel: Asaph the chief, and second to him Zechariah, and Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom and Uzziah, with instruments, harps and lyres; and Asaph sounding aloud with cymbals; and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets, continually before the ark of the covenant of God on that day. Then David first appointed praise to the Lord by the hand of Asaph and his brothers." So if he is the one who appointed each of the psalm-singers, it is clear that no one other than David, the leader of them all, began the first psalm. The beginning of the untitled psalms and of the book of Psalms, I mean the first and second psalms, which they say are the first of the untitled ones, is thus shown to have been spoken by David. If so, the rest of the untitled psalms must also have been spoken by David. In the same way the 94th is written without a title, yet it is David's. There you will find the apostle saying to the Hebrews: "He sets a certain day, 'Today,' saying through David so long afterward, as has been said before: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion." He showed plainly that this untitled psalm too is David's and not anyone else's. So the rest of the untitled psalms are his as well.

Likewise you will find that the anonymous psalms belong to David himself. Stephen, God's first martyr, had one of the so-called anonymous psalms in mind, I mean the 131st, when he spoke to the rulers and people of the Jews. He said of David that he found favor before the God of Jacob. David himself, then, is shown to be the one speaking in the psalm: "I will not give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob." The beginning of the psalm may seem to be spoken in the person of someone else. Even so, Stephen is a faithful witness, and he teaches us too that the psalm is David's: David confesses with his own voice and teaches that he would find a dwelling for the God of Jacob.

As for the psalms that have "Alleluia" as their title, I will explain how they were spoken by David. It is written in Chronicles that David spoke the "Alleluia" about them when he brought up the ark of God with the priests and the people.

Concerning the untitled and anonymous psalms, the titles show the following. Where a psalm is untitled, it is not in the name of a single nation, or else the deed it narrates is not found among the Hebrews because of the brazenness of their unbelief. As for the anonymous psalms, which have no name in the title, this shows that the psalm is spoken about the Lord and is sung universally, for all people alike. This, then, is why some psalms are headed as untitled, or are left without a title among the Hebrews, and why others are called anonymous. As for the psalms headed "Alleluia," the word itself shows you that the psalm is spoken as a hymn and thanksgiving for certain gifts that God has given us. "Alleluia" itself is interpreted "praise and hymn to God."

There, we have given a full account of the divisions and set out plainly what is to be said about them in this prologue. The children of the Hebrews thought that not all the psalms are David's, but it has been shown in various ways that they all belong to him, to David. That is why he himself appointed Asaph and his company, all of them, to sing, and assigned to them the things they uttered in the book of Psalms. Asaph and his company were called prophets, as it says about them in Chronicles: "And Asaph and Heman and Heman and Jeduthun, of the king's prophets." Even so, we must not conclude from this that they were the authors of the psalms. They were psalm-singers and teachers appointed by the Lord through King David. Indeed, you will find that psalm-singers even now take Asaph and his company, the sons of Korah, and the Levites as their model, since in the church of the Lord they sing what David uttered, with the people singing the response. Asaph and his company may also be shown to be prophets, and leaders and teachers whom David appointed over the peoples to praise the Lord and give thanks to him.

That is what we have to say on these matters. As for the other things found in the psalms, such as the diapsalma, the obelus, the lemniscus or any other sign, I will mention them at each psalm, guided by the grace of the Lord and instructed by his power. I will also discuss the matters already mentioned more fully in what follows, by the grace of the Lord.

For piety must first be set right, and then the conduct of life can be put in order. There he commanded us not to walk, and here not even to stand. So we will take care not to share in impiety or touch it, even in passing. As for sin, even if we should happen to pass into it, we still refuse [?] to stand in it, that is, to settle in it or to remain in it. By "the pestilent" he means people who are two-faced, who keep up righteousness in outward appearance but pursue wickedness in their deeds. For these people corrupt human life. The seat of the pestilent is the seat of judges who betray justice. The seat of the pestilent is the throne of false teachers. The seat of the pestilent is the robe of hypocrites. The seat of the pestilent is the hypocrisy of priests. He commands us not to sit in it.

The Jews were cast away when the strong wind of the apostles' preaching blew against them, and like chaff they dissolved into nothing. For they had no city, no worship, nothing else of what they had possessed from the beginning, and they were scattered over the whole face of the earth, disgraced like the chaff.
He teaches how we ought to pray, how we ought to humble ourselves and call down God's mercy.

He says that his bones are troubled, and his soul as well. Perhaps, in spiritual contemplation, "bones" can be understood as the powers of the soul that are grasped by reason, which hold it up in spiritual vigor. Among these are self-control, prudence, courage according to God, temperance and justice, and, in short, every kind of virtue. If these are not present in us without confusion, that is, in their proper order, they lack their own strength. Then the soul is bound to be troubled, as the passions run riot within it.
You see that when we turn away from the workers of lawlessness, whether people or thoughts, God readily receives our petitions and our prayer.

He asks that Christ be lifted up on the cross, so that the demons may be brought to an end and destroyed. "For when I am lifted up, I will draw all people to myself." And this brought the end and overthrow of the power of the spiritual enemies.

"O Lord, our Lord": it is the Church that says this. After she came to know Christ, she turned away from the slavery of idols and began to call the one who is truly God and Lord her own Lord. The whole earth has always been truly full of the wonders of God's creation. But it has been even more so since his name, that is, the name of Christ, was made wonderful among all, Greeks and barbarians alike, through faith in him.

By “birds of the air” he means those occupied with theology, who search out lofty and sublime doctrines; by “fish of the sea,” those who swim among the affairs of this life as if among waves. Yet salvation is laid up for these too, when they walk paths no longer of the sea but “of the seas,” making their way through baptism and repentance.

For by the law of creation even the things of the senses were subject to him: cattle, oxen and sheep. But we find spiritual sheep as well, subject to Christ: the people who live in innocence. The oxen are those who carry out the commandments, of whom Moses the lawgiver said, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” This is why the Psalmist wrote not simply “oxen” but “all oxen,” for God is found by all who practise virtue, of whatever kind it may be. He calls sinners “beasts,” since they keep their eyes bent down toward the earth. But these too, if they repent and submit, will be saved, when through the life of the Gospel they take Christ upon them as their rider. For it says, “Men and beasts you will save, O Lord.”
How do we give thanks with our whole heart? When we no longer go back to the sin for which we are begging God's pardon.

Here he calls the throng of demons “nations.” For they contrived the saving cross, and through it they fell from their tyranny; “in the snare that they hid, their own foot was caught,” and “the sinner was caught in the works of his own hands.”

Many kinds of sinners are recognized, just as there are many kinds of the righteous. Here he calls the unbelievers sinners, and says that they have forgotten God. So just as those who believe in God live even if they die (for Christ says, “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live”), so unbelievers are dead even before they die, because of the denial that is in them.

He asks which sin of the ungodly God most abhors, whether the ungodly is the devil or a thoroughly ungodly man; then he himself answers the question he has posed: “For he said in his heart, He will not search it out.” He slanders God, he means, as if God let our affairs go unprovided for and unexamined; and this proves an incitement to destruction for those who are deceived. So he fittingly added:
For forgetting God is grievous, and only for a time; yet it brings a death that is total and undying.
For Satan's exaltation is the humiliation of human beings. Just as God is said to be exalted in our salvation, so the devil is said to be lifted up in our destruction.

He wants us to speak the truth first in our heart, and after that with our tongue, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” And in saying, “He did no evil to his neighbour,” he forbade here not murder alone but every other sin as well.
We should understand “those nearest” as sinners and weak like ourselves, so that we who are sinners may not reproach others with sin, but rather admonish and teach one another.

Even if they are weak, even if poor, even if barbarians, even if foreigners. For whoever holds evildoers of no account and honours those who fear the Lord turns many away from wickedness and urges them on toward godliness.

You see the Church's gratitude. She acknowledged at once both her own poverty and the wealth of the bridegroom. “I said to the Lord,” she says (that is, to Christ), “You are my Lord.” You are not a mere man, she means, but Lord, since you took a slave girl, an outcast, into the partnership of marriage.

“Of inheritance,” he says, that is, of this mystery. For in this age the Church possesses no inheritance except God alone, who makes ready for her the lot that is to come. That is why the next verse is fittingly added:
The Church blesses God, since she has received from him understanding of the mysteries and has turned away from the error of the Jews.

Do you see that the Son and the Father are equal in honour? At times the Son is said to stand or sit at the right hand, but here he assigns the place at the right to the Father, so that you may learn that the begotten and the begetter have one power, even if here, because of the flesh, he speaks in lowly terms.

Which steps does the Prophet pray may be made firm in God's paths, and which may not be shaken? Our first steps are the movements of the soul, and he prays that these may be made firm, that is, established, in God's paths, namely in the divine commands. For once these are made firm, our other steps, that is, our actions, are not shaken either, since sin cannot pry them loose.

For the demons surround our soul, and like wild beasts each one seizes hold of it, wanting to trap it. The demons' fat, their rich food, is those who sin: while such people are enjoying their pleasures, the demons shut them in so that they can no longer escape. And what arrogance is meant? Apostasy from God, unbelief in what is to come, rejection of the judgment. For these are the things that those who have resolved on sin urge upon the deceived.
He calls God's justice a sword, because like a blade it cuts down all the battle lines of the demons.

The Psalmist is not here disparaging the sons' food, as some suppose (for what goes into the mouth does not defile a person), but the sons themselves, as most ungrateful. For though they had received children from God in abundance, they handed down to them as their inheritance not virtue but the leftovers of their own wickedness.

He bowed the heavens in order to join earth to heaven and to grant those below fellowship with the things above. This could not have happened unless he had come down and sojourned on earth in the one way in which it could receive him, that is, in the flesh, which he called “darkness under his feet.”
By “mercy” he means loving-kindness, and he put it before judgment because God uses loving-kindness first, and only afterward judgment against those who have persisted in sin.

By “deeps” he means the masses of water that the Creator stored in hidden places beneath the earth, so that in this too his wisdom might be admired. Thus he founded the dry upon the wet, and made the heavy to be borne up by the lighter.

So it is in vain that we take care for the strength of the body, and to no purpose that we surround ourselves with the power that comes from relatives, friends and wealth; for nothing else can save without help from above. Take Goliath and Pharaoh as examples. The one, a mighty giant, was defeated by David, a mere boy; the other, who pursued Israel with a multitude of chariots, found his grave in the sea.

“Come,” he says to those near and to those far off, so that those far away may draw near and those near may come nearer still, offering obedience to God as to a father, and may be taught the fear of God, which brings release from the fear of demons. That is why he adds: “I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

The title of the psalm is plain; yet it refers to the spiritual David, who even takes on words of prayer. These should be understood as befitting not the dignity of his divinity but the lowliness of his humanity. For if he humbled himself by taking the form of a servant, it is fitting that at the time of his passion he prays, and at the same time teaches us to pray in our afflictions.
By “those who wrong me” he means the Jews, and by “those who fight me” the demons, who fought against Christ because of us. He wants these to be fought, that is, to be brought to nothing.

This is said of Judas the betrayer, but also of the Jewish people, and further of the devil himself. Judas fell into the snare of the noose; the Jewish people, thinking to ensnare, were themselves ensnared and caught in their own hunt. Likewise the devil, having planned the snare of the cross, fell from his own kingdom through the cross.
For as master of the house and as farmer he counted the barrenness of the Jews as his own.

He is speaking of his kindness toward Judas: how he let him carry the money box, and let him alone dip with him in the dish, as a brother and neighbour. “I was pleasing as a brother,” that is, I was agreeable to him and treated him well in every way.

Perhaps they really did gnash their teeth in savagery, all but wanting to chew Jesus up. But malice expressed in words is also called gnashing of teeth. So he wanted the Father to be a witness against those who blasphemed him. Hence he adds: “Lord, when will you look on?”

The psalm portrays not simply a lawbreaker but the hypocrite and deceiver, who has much of the mire of lawlessness in his soul and therefore says within himself that he is resolved to sin. And why does it say “within himself”? Because he ponders things that he is either afraid or ashamed to say openly.

The house of God is his body; its richness is the blood and water poured out from his side, with which all we faithful have been made drunk with a saving drunkenness. For the “torrent of delight” is the sufferings of Christ. A winter torrent, because it took place in the depth of the winter of our sin, when every virtue, and above all love for God, had grown cold and died. So the prophet Zechariah says of the day of the cross: “On that day there will be no light; there will be cold and frost; it is a great day.” And it is fittingly called a torrent “of delight,” for Christ took great delight in the sufferings he bore for us, both making sport of the devil and rejoicing over the salvation of humankind. This torrent of delight he gives us to drink in a mystery. For the Master's passion has become martyrdom for his servants.

He does well to remind us of the judgment, so that we may not look at the confusion here below and neglect virtue when we see the virtuous meeting with dishonour among men and with toil. For God “will not forsake them,” that is, he will not overlook them, but he keeps them for the age to come, where the bestowal of good things has no end.

Which sabbath? Not just any sabbath. So the psalm speaks not of the sacrifices of the sabbath under the law but of the sufferings of Christ. Thus the present prophecy is a remembrance of that sabbath of which John the Theologian said: “Then the Jews, since it was the day of Preparation, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the sabbath (for that sabbath was a great day), asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.”

We have often said that Christ, just as in his sufferings, so also in prophecy took on the person of humanity. It is in that person that he now says these things, wishing our nature to be rebuked, but not in anger, and to be disciplined, but not in wrath. What rebuke, then? The rebuke that leads to salvation. Likewise he wants discipline that brings peace. This could not have come about any other way unless Christ took upon himself the rebuke and discipline due to us, being himself both the one who rebukes and the one rebuked: rebuking as God, and rebuked for our sake as man. So, joining in himself both persons, that of the one who rebukes and that of the one rebuked, he spoke these words through the prophecy of Isaiah: “If your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow; if they are like crimson, I will make them white as wool.” And likewise of the discipline, of which the same prophet says: “The discipline that brought us peace was upon him; by his wound we have all been healed.”

So it is not in vain that Christ prays these things to his Father on behalf of the human race, but because, he says, the arrows aimed at them, that is, all the blows that fell upon our common nature because of Adam, have been fixed in me. For since I have taken up the sins of the race, I must also undergo the chastisements due for them. That is why you have also pressed upon me your chastening hand, of which Job said: “It is the hand of the Lord that has touched me.”

He shows that he is right to plead against the anger, not because it is unjust, but because it has no cure. For what remedy will be found for the anger of God? But notice the precision of the words. He did not say, “There is no healing for me,” but, “There is no healing in my flesh.” Clearly these things, the sufferings on our behalf included, are spoken in the person of humanity. And lest we think the anger of the just Judge unjust, he shows in what follows where it came from, and establishes that it is just.

Again he calls his humanity “bones.” He himself makes this clear when he says to the disciples after the resurrection, wishing to confirm the reality of his incarnation: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” So “because of my sins,” which he bore for us, he had no peace but turmoil in his bones, that is, in his humanity; for the divinity was kept free from all turmoil. You will learn this too from the Only-begotten himself when he says, “Now my soul is troubled,” for by “soul” he meant his humanity. Jesus adds the reason for the trouble within him: “And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? But it was for this that I came to this hour.” That is: in vain do I agonize in the flesh, since as God I am above death, and it was for this very purpose that I came with flesh and bore the sins of the race, that by my own death I might redeem them all.

Here he has shown clearly that the sins he has are not his own; he took on the sins of others, and for this reason a multitude of them were heaped upon the head of the Lord's flesh. For this is how heavier burdens are usually carried, which is also why his head was crowned with thorns.

And what wounds of Christ stank? For his flesh did not see corruption. And what folly did very Wisdom have? But he calls Judas his folly, taking on himself his disciple's fault as a teacher does. The wounds of his wickedness stank while the deed was still in prospect. For what could be more foul-smelling than that sin in which the creature handed the Creator over to death? And they festered when he hanged himself, for then he was utterly despaired of, just as festering wounds are given up as hopeless by physicians.

He suffered hardship not on the cross alone but also before the cross, enduring much like a farmer in order to clear our field. And he was bowed down “to the end” when he endured death for us. For he who is higher than all creation was bowed down to the very ground, wishing to raise up from there the one who had fallen.
And why the joy of the world went about gloomy, the following lines explain.

He calls the sufferings of the cross “mockeries,” since the servants of the Jews inflicted them with jeering. With these, he says, I was filled, intending through them to heal the sins of humankind. But for the Jews “there is no healing in my flesh,” that is, in the sufferings of my flesh; for they stumble at the cross, through which alone salvation is available to sinners. That is why he was rightly gloomy.

I was afflicted when I was slandered; I was humbled when I made no answer to the slanderers. And I was humbled so greatly that when the high priest put me under oath, “If you are the Christ,” I did not say “Yes,” but “You say so,” not wishing to glorify myself even in this, even though they, compelled by the truth, took the ambiguous answer as confirmation.

He says “I roared” to show how great his groaning was: just as a lion eager for prey roars when for a time it cannot find any, so he too groaned when the prey he sought, the salvation of the Jews, did not come to him. What follows confirms this interpretation.

And what was Christ's desire? To accomplish the Passover on our behalf. That is why he said to the apostles, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer”—not simply the Passover, but this one, in which the type passed away and the reality was accomplished. And why “with you”? Because the Jews do not wish to share in the mystery, and he rightly groaned over them. The Father, who knows all beforehand, knew this groaning of his. Hence Paul, imitating him as far as he could, said: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites.”

How his heart was troubled has already been said: because the Jews were not being saved. He calls Peter his “strength” because of his confession of faith: “For you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades,” he says, “will not prevail against it.” This man forsook him by denying him. And the “light” is all the apostles, to whom he said, “You are the light of the world.” These were the light of the eyes of the two covenants, the Law and the Gospel, for they illumine for us the Old and the New in the light of Jesus. Yet at the time of the cross they were not with Christ; for they fled in fear of the Jews.

By “friends and neighbours” he perhaps means the rest of the Jews: “friends” not because they loved Jesus but because they were loved by him. For as Creator he loved his own handiwork, and as shepherd he loves “the lost sheep of Israel.” He calls the same people “neighbours” because of their kinship with him according to the flesh. Nearer than these, indeed nearest of all, because of their faith in him, were the apostles. So the Jews, whom he called friends and neighbours, with great shamelessness plotted against Jesus, standing not far off but close beside him. But “those nearest,” that is, the very nearest, whom we have said to be the saints, stood far off at the time of the passion, not plotting against him themselves, but wary of those who were plotting.
What were they forcing? The opinion people held about him. For though they were plotting out of envy, they wanted to appear zealous for the law. The next verse makes this clearer.

What these were, Luke tells us: “They began to accuse him, saying, We found this man perverting our nation and forbidding us to pay taxes to Caesar”—and this although Jesus, when questioned by the Herodians and Pharisees, had said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.”

What happens to the mute, he says, whose senses are impaired by nature, he underwent by choice. When he was reviled he was not moved to anger; and it is characteristic of the deaf not to be angered when reviled, since they do not hear the insults against them. Further, when he was slandered, though he could have refuted the slanderers, he did not open his mouth, as the mute are prevented by nature from speaking. Isaiah shows that he was neither deaf nor mute, but imitated them in his humility: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth in his humiliation.” With this agrees what the Psalmist now adds in the person of the Saviour.

So he did hear, but pretended not to hear; and he had many words with which to refute them and to make his case, but he played the part of one at a loss with nothing to say. What follows shows the reason for this.

For trusting in the Father as a true and impartial witness, of whom he himself said, “The one who bears witness about me is the Father who sent me, whom you do not know,” he paid no attention to the false witnesses.

What he says is that the Father heard the prayer he offered for the apostles, so that the enemy, namely the opposing powers, should not rejoice: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are.” And again: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.” For if this prayer had not been fulfilled, and the band of apostles had not been preserved, the devil, the true enemy, and those with him would have rejoiced.

The disciples are Christ's feet, for he is their head; that is why he did not disdain even to wash their feet. So when the disciples were shaken for a little while because of the cross, the Jews boasted against Christ, as if he had been stripped of everything and could not even keep his disciples with him.
For this is why he consented to come into the world with flesh, as he himself said in prayer: “What shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? But it was for this that I came to this hour.”

Clearly this means his compassion toward us, for the sake of which he keeps the memory of his own suffering always before him. For “because he himself suffered when he was tempted,” says Paul, “he is able to help those who are tempted.”

And yet he had no iniquity; nevertheless he declares ours as his own. That is why he said in prayer: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” For even if “confession” is taken here as thanksgiving, still he gave that thanksgiving for the redemption of our sins, at the time when he was reproaching the Jews who blasphemed him as a friend of sinners and tax collectors.

He calls the sin of our race his own, since he has become the firstfruits of the human lump, and as the new Adam wishes to refashion the old Adam in himself; and he is anxious about Adam's sin, how it may be cleansed. For the words he spoke in the Gospels were those of one who was anxious: “I came to cast fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!” For he meant the fire that consumed our thorns.

He means the Jews, over whom he grieved because they lived in wickedness, and also because they had become stronger than he, that is, in their arrogance. For when he humbled himself for our sake, as Paul says, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross,” they, not knowing the reason for his humility, treated him with arrogance. And so those who hated him unjustly grew in number, as they saw the high priests' insolence spreading. And who were those who hated him unjustly?

That is, the relatives, fellow citizens or neighbours of the blind who had received their sight and the lame who had been made straight brought slanders against him instead of thanks. And why they did this, the following line makes known.
"They took my love for humanity and my goodness," he says, "as grounds for slander." They called him lawless and an enemy of God because he healed their sick on the Sabbath.

He spoke these words not on his own behalf but on behalf of the church. Or rather, on his own behalf after all, for the church is known to be one with him, as a bride is with her bridegroom. We shall see this from what follows.

He calls the church his help, wishing in this respect too to save the image of Adam. For the woman was given to Adam as a help: "Let us make," says God, "a helper for him like himself." That is why Paul also applied to Christ the words about Adam and Eve: "For this reason a man will leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh." And what did he add to these words? "This mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and the church." So he wishes the Father to attend to her and look upon her. This is not because he himself is too weak to defend the church. Rather, he wishes to show the Father how great [?] the gap is between the synagogue and the church of the nations. The Jews were not saved, although many had proclaimed him and Christ himself had come in addition, while the nations heard only the Savior's voice and were saved at once. Therefore he fittingly added: "Lord of my salvation," again calling the salvation of the nations his own salvation. For if he has made our sins his own, how much more does he count our salvation as his own?

This befits every prophet and teacher: to guard his own ways, that is, the courses and paths of his actions. Then he will not turn aside into wickedness, nor sin with his tongue by doing the opposite of what he says. For a person truly sins with the tongue when he denounces wickedness in word but approves it in deed by the very things he pursues, and when his way of life gives the lie to his own teaching.

You see that first he became deaf through disobedience, and once deaf he was humbled. For nothing humbles a person so much as insensibility, with disobedience following after it. Or else this is why he kept silent even from good things: he had ceased, that is, from studying the law, that good teacher. So it was fitting that the pain of sin was renewed, for the wound that sin inflicts on us grows heavier when we withdraw from the study of the law. [?] It is as though no remedy from the divine commandment were being applied, and putrefaction sets in. Therefore he did not persist in that silence. He came to his senses and thrust it away as destructive to the soul. To show this, he then added: "My heart grew hot."

He says "great church," meaning not only a church with a populous assembly, but much more one able to receive the lofty and magnificent doctrines of theology. The lips of the church, and its eyes, may be taken figuratively as the all-praised apostles and all the teachers who came after them. The rest of the body of the church does not hinder them from proclaiming Christ, who is righteousness itself. On the contrary, it spurs them on and gives them the cooperation that is fitting.

The Prophet often headed psalms "For the end," yet we must not think that he gives each psalm this title for no purpose. What, then, is the reason here? It is that he is speaking of things at the end, concerning the dispensation of Christ. Not only this prophet called Christ David, but another prophet did too, namely Hosea, who said: "After these things the children of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king." Yet David had died many generations before that prophet, who delivered his prophecy in the days of King Hezekiah. He means the new David, to whom those who were saved turned.

The truth of the prophetic promise has often been borne out even to this day. Many who were sick and gravely ill emptied out their wealth on the poor and needy and were immediately changed for the better. For if mercy triumphs over judgment even on the day to come, is it any wonder that here too abundant mercy overturns an expected death and turns it into health? But there is also a sickness of the soul, understood with reference to the inner person. In it the soul has slack hands, that is, slack powers of action. Its knees too are found paralyzed, and so it cannot walk the road that leads to life. At such a time the soul is held, as it were, by the grievous sickness of sloth and is therefore hastening toward the death of sin. Then almsgiving to the poor heals it and changes it. That is why he immediately added: "I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you."

He does not say this because he suffered death at their hands and wants to pay them back with punishment. After all, at the time of the cross he himself said, "Father, forgive them their sin." But he saw that the impartial and just judgment of the Father was condemning the murderers. For this reason, acting as one with God the Father, he said "and I will repay them," to show that both have one and the same working. For "the Son can do nothing of himself," he says; "whatever he sees the Father doing, the Son also does likewise." By these words he confirms that the two share the same will and the same action.

These too were psalm-singers, who borrowed from David the psalms he himself had prophesied. Perhaps the psalm is headed "For understanding" because their ancestor Korah had been a transgressor, the man who rose up against Moses with Dathan and Abiram. Yet they certainly did not imitate their ancestor, nor did their fathers. So when the whole company of Korah perished, they were saved, having presumably kept themselves apart from Korah's wickedness. At that time Moses gave this same command to the rest of the people as well, so that they would not perish. But more truly the psalm is headed "For the end, for understanding" because it foreshadows baptism, which was instituted at the end, after the Jewish purifications. And to have anticipated [?] this is truly a kind of wisdom and understanding.

He calls the cross a sword, for Christ used it like a sword and destroyed two enemies, the devil and death. By "thigh" he means the flesh, naming the whole by a part, as in the verse "nor a leader from his thighs." So he urges the one who is truly mighty in his comeliness and beauty, that is, in his divinity and his humanity, to gird the cross upon his flesh. By the one he would endure the sufferings on our behalf; by the other, being beyond suffering, he would overcome them. Or we might also take comeliness and beauty to mean his love for humanity, for nothing so befits God as saving his own creature. "Bend your bow against the enemies, prosper for the faithful, and reign over both, so that you may subdue the enemies and crown the faithful." This is the proper task of a judge and king. Moreover, for the sake of truth Christ exposed the hypocrisy of the Jews, and for the sake of meekness he patiently endured being tested. Further, the Father is the right hand of the Son, just as the Son is the right hand of the Father. So Christ is guided by the Father. This is not because he needs a guide. Rather, the dispensation on our behalf is like a road shared by Father and Son: the Son travels it, since he carries out the mystery, and the Father guides, because it was accomplished by his good pleasure.
What squall or storm is more violent than when our own conscience lashes us, and our thoughts, accusing us or else excusing us, beat on us like waves?

He calls "heaven" those whose minds are set on heavenly things. Paul spoke of them when he said: "Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly man." He calls "earth" those whose minds are set on earthly things, those who are slaves to clay and brickmaking. He promises to gather both, so that he may set his own people apart and repay each according to his works.

Here he is speaking about the Jewish people. He calls them "holy ones" because of their fathers. They define God's covenant by the sacrifices of the law, not knowing that God is pleased with one sacrifice, the rational one, and not with the many irrational ones. That is why he commanded them to gather, so that they might be taught this.

Perhaps the children of the Jews did not believe this when they heard it, and doubted whether it could ever happen at all. But now the word has been seen in fact. Their sacrifices are no longer in force, for the temple has been destroyed, the altar has fallen, and the whole order of worship tied to it has been ruined. So has the city, the only place where the sacrifices required by the law could be performed. I have no need, he says, of irrational sacrifices; otherwise, what would prevent wild beasts and cattle from being offered? Or perhaps by beasts and cattle he means the nations, and by oxen those of the Jewish people who believed. Having their offering, he no longer accepts the offerings of the Jewish people, since they are superfluous; what follows is also said about them. Understand the birds of heaven as those who practice virginity or self-control, since they fly up toward heaven, living a life of devotion equal to the angels. He calls the church itself the beauty of the field, that is, of the world, for it was made comely by the grace of baptism. So he did not say "it is beside me" but "it is with me," as a bride is with her bridegroom, for in this way the church is regarded as belonging to Christ.

Become, he says, a rival of the angels. Imitate the Seraphim in giving glory. Tell the glory of God as the heavens do. Offer the sacrifice that all creation offers as it glorifies him without ceasing. Or perhaps by "sacrifice of praise" he means the virtues, through which God is praised, that is, extolled and glorified. That is above all why he said to the apostles: "Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." Understand "affliction" as temptation, whether it comes from people or from Satan. If we call upon God at such a time, he will deliver us, as he once delivered Susanna. And when he arranges our affairs in unexpected ways, we rightly glorify him.
He is describing the day of death, when each person is called and swiftly snatched away. So we must see to the wiping away of our sins while time for repentance is still abundantly given to us.

What is this way, and what kind of way is it? It is communion in the Lord's body and blood, which he himself first instituted and showed us in Zion. Since it is given to those who receive it for the redemption of their sins, it is rightly called the salvation of God. It is rightly also called a way, for it shows those who pray as they ought how to journey to heaven.

The book of Kingdoms tells the story more clearly. From the roof David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, bathing. He desired her, summoned her, and lay with her. When she conceived, he was ashamed and arranged for Uriah to fall in battle: he had Joab the general station Uriah in the front line, and so killed him by the hands of the foreigners. God was angered at this and sent him Nathan the prophet, threatening him for the murder and the adultery. David turned toward repentance and wrote the following psalm. He was not ashamed to make his wound public, so that he might show sinners the medicine of repentance. He wants his lawlessness blotted out, so that not only is the wound healed but not even a scar remains. For this reason he also appeals to the multitude of God's compassions. A sinner cannot be saved by a single act of compassion, that is, by pardon for a single transgression. To escape the threat and the punishment we need many compassions, for many sins. He begged not simply to be washed but to be washed further, asking for a cleansing in proportion to his fall. A garment that is moderately soiled is easily washed and cleaned, but one that is badly and repeatedly soiled needs more careful and laborious washing. In the same way, a soul that has sinned once and moderately is cleansed by moderate repentance. But when it has committed many grievous sins, its repentance must not be a side matter; it must come with much toil and with good works. For it is by this that God washes away our transgressions. He rightly called his sin "lawlessness," wishing to show that even he was not permitted to break the law, king though he was. For he had offended the King who is higher than all.

It is a blessed thing when a person recognizes his own sin and keeps his transgressions always before his eyes. One who knows them, remembers them, and contemplates the wounds of his transgressions with the eyes of the soul feels ashamed. The memory pricks his soul, and shame drives him to remorse. But one who has forgotten is led on again into other sins, as though he had done nothing wrong.

This does not mean that his sin escaped the notice of everyone, as some think. The deed of adultery could not be hidden from Bathsheba herself, the woman involved in it, nor from those who had summoned her. Joab likewise knew of the murder, since he had helped the king commit it. Nor did David himself think that his kingship gave him the right to sin. That would have been unworthy of a prophet and of a king who was, as one would expect, devout. Rather, he said "Against you only have I sinned," because God alone cares that we do not sin, as a Creator who spares what he has made. And perhaps he says "and I have done what is evil in your sight" because everyone else was doing the king a favor and hiding the sin in silence, but God sent Nathan and exposed the deed as evil. Why he did this, what follows shows.

These words are not said only because of the defilement handed down from Adam. Because of him we are considered to become defiled, so that even before we reach the age that can tell good from evil, we will need cleansing as people defiled from our fathers. We find this said in Job as well: "Who," he says, "will boast of being clean from defilement? Not even an infant, though its life be but one day." Moreover, the divinely inspired Scripture usually calls desire the mother of sin, and death in turn the offspring of both. James testifies to this when he says: "Desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death." So whenever we sin, we are conceived in sins.
So too we, in the gift of baptism, are washed by the water and made radiant by the Spirit.
The bones of the soul, that is, its powers, are humbled and crushed by sin. But when they are saved by repentance they flourish again and return to their former joy.

For unless he overlooks our transgressions, we cannot be saved. And how is this achieved? When we practice good deeds and virtues, so that we may draw the Judge's eye to them instead. In this way we can turn him away from looking at our sins.

Not one, but all, for even one is enough to send a person to Gehenna. So let us not neglect any sin, whatever it may be. If our tunic is found stained with any filth at all, we cannot enter the King's bridal chamber or set foot in his court. Paul set his seal on this when he said: "Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor the effeminate, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God."

Not so that God would change his nature, for there was nothing bad in it. Rather, so that he would cleanse the reasoning of the soul and set it right, since it had become filthy through pleasures and the schemes of the devil. In divine Scripture "to create" often means "to set right."

You see that the prophet does not pray for his nature to be changed. He prays for grace to come and help a nature that is ailing and has grown old under sin. By "a right spirit" he does not mean the vital spirit within us, but the very Spirit of God, of whom he sang in another psalm: "Your good Spirit will lead me on level ground." He wants this Spirit renewed in his inward parts [?], that is, in the essential and most vital parts of the soul. Even before this the Spirit dwelt in us [?] completely, yet it did not rest upon us because of our weakness, which left us unable to receive the grace in its fullness. So he prays that the Spirit be renewed, so that it may be made fully complete in us; for the house that is being completed is the one that is dedicated. It is a bad thing for a servant to lose the sight of his master's face, and likewise for a son to lose his father's and a soldier his king's, for such a person finds himself an exile. But in God's case this brings destruction on the one who suffers it. For God is not only our Father, Master, and King; he has become everything you could name that contributes to our life and salvation. So when he turns his face away from us, we perish at once, losing the Holy Spirit, in whom lies the whole supply of our good things. Why did he write "do not take away in turn" instead of "do not take away the spirit"? Because those who keep God's commandments had already once experienced the working of the Spirit in us, [?] through Adam's disobedience, and through prophetic grace or through active virtue. So he rightly prayed that it not be taken away in turn, so that he would not suffer its removal a second time.

He had taught the ways of God before, but perhaps not to the lawless. Nor, before his sin, did he join his teaching to prayer to such an extent. He did so rather from the time he sinned and repented. A person who has been sick himself and has tried the medicine is the one people trust most when he speaks about treatment. In the same way, those who have been saved by repentance become a door of conversion and salvation for other sinners. So Paul cries out boldly: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first." If you do not believe the preaching that proclaims salvation for sinners, he says, learn from me, the preacher, that though I was a persecutor I was entrusted with becoming a minister of the gospel.

You see that David's lips had been closed because of his sin, but are opened again by repentance to tell the praise of God. [?] The sum of the hymns begins here, containing the sinner's conversion. The Spirit presents humility as a sacrifice pleasing to God, for "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." How do we crush our spirit so as to be humbled? When we do good and are not puffed up, and keep our sins continually in mind. By "good pleasure" he means the incarnation of the Only-begotten. This is clear from what Paul wrote to the Ephesians, where he says: "having made known to us the mystery of his will and his good pleasure, which he purposed in him for the dispensation of the fullness of the times." In this, then, Zion is blessed, because the mystery of the divine supper was accomplished in her, along with many other wonders that were done in her and went out from her.

The opening is that of someone astonished and perplexed, as is natural: some people have advanced so far in wickedness that they boast of the very things they ought to mourn. The historical account concerns Doeg, but the Psalmist is hinting at Judas the traitor. Judas became so mighty in wickedness that he betrayed his benefactor, the one who fed him and taught him, and was not shamed by his constant reproofs or his exhortations.

This was when Judas said to the Pharisees: "What will you give me if I hand him over to you?" They weighed out thirty pieces of silver for him, and from then on he looked for an opportunity to betray him. So he spent the whole day plotting the sin of betrayal, until night came, when he carried out the deed.

"Like a razor" means cutting without being felt. For what could be sharper than the deceit he agreed on, with his treacherous tongue, with those who arrested Jesus: "The one I kiss is the man; seize him"?

Wickedness is the devil, since he wills every evil for everyone. Goodness is Christ, for goodness belongs to God by nature. So Judas abandoned his own Christ and loved Satan. He also chose injustice over speaking righteousness. He could have taken hold of true righteousness and preached the gospel with the other apostles, but he threw himself into the injustice of betrayal. The same happens to everyone who delights in accusing and reviling his brother. He takes more pleasure in speaking injustice, that is, falsehood, and keeps silent about righteousness, that is, the virtue his neighbor possesses.

These words are said to every deceitful person, but much more to the traitor. God destroyed him utterly. He removed him from the tent, that is, from the place of discipleship, and plucked up his root, like that of a thorny plant, from the land of the living, that is, from the apostles' farm.

These words suit Peter as he recalled his own denial. He was like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, that is, he stood constantly in the faith. Even though for a little while he suffered the scorching heat of denial, he still did not wither, for he watered his root with the tears of repentance. That is why he says, "I will confess to you, because you have done it." Done what? Shown mercy, kindness, compassion. You made the one who denied you a herald of the mysteries, set up the one who was shaken as a pillar, and made the one who went astray a shepherd of the lambs. "Good," not to the Jews or to those sick with idolatry, but in the presence of the holy ones, those who have been justified through grace and gladness. For among them his name is good. What name is better than the name of Jesus? "I will wait": why? Because "the one who endures to the end will be saved."

Who else would say this but a fool? Isaiah said of him: "The fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will devise vain things." What are these? People do base and outrageous things and see that God is patient with them. They ought to give thanks and glorify him as kind and forbearing. Instead they turn aside into madness and decide that God does not watch over human affairs, which in their view are carried along at random and by chance.

Once the blasphemer's disease has spread, it leads others to be corrupted in lawlessness and to become abominable to their Creator. They grow so sick with idleness in virtue that they do no good at all. But by "the fool" he hints at the madness of the idolaters, for they said in their heart that there is no God and made idols of gods of wood and stone. And by "lawlessness," which was the transgression of the law, he hints at the Jews, whom God abhorred because they were corrupted by unbelief.

God desires truth so much that, although he knows all our affairs exactly, he still looks down, as if from a window of his condescension toward us, wishing to discern human affairs precisely. But the Psalm clearly speaks of Christ's coming. He looked down from heaven when he came to dwell among us in the flesh. Someone who leans out from a high place stays above, yet by his action he is below. In the same way Christ remained in the bosom of the Father and yet came to dwell on earth through the flesh. For what purpose? "To see if there is anyone who understands or seeks God." So he came down not so much to examine people's deeds as to see whether they had any knowledge of God at all, and whether they sought God in faith.

All who wrong the poor and seize what belongs to their neighbor are rightly said to "eat up the people of God as they eat bread," for the injustice they do to them feeds their own greed. But you will take it that the teachers of the Jews are meant above all. In their ignorance they were, as they supposed, defending the law, but by insulting the Lawgiver they were working lawlessness. These men were eating up God's people like bread: they showed partiality for the sake of a full stomach and gluttony, and broke the law in the very act of teaching it.

He is speaking of the Jews. They did not call upon Christ, the true God, and they feared with a needless fear, where there was nothing to fear, when they said to one another: "If we let this man alone, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation." Yet this would not have happened if they had kept faith in him. In the same way, all who are slack in calling upon God fail to feel the fear they ought to feel, because they do not believe in God. Instead they fear the threats of men and the power of enemies for nothing, not knowing that none of these things harm us so long as we have God's favor. He calls these people "men-pleasers," for they always want to please men rather than God. God has scattered their bones, that is, their tribes. "They were put to shame," for the one they call dead is the one who drives them out. The same happens to ordinary men-pleasers: their bones, that is, their wealth and glory, are scattered by God.

Why does the Prophet pray for salvation to come from Zion, and not from heaven, from the temple, from the ark, or from the holy place? Because it was there that Christ restored to us the original breath of life. He made this plain by adding: "When the Lord turns back." Satan took our communion with the Spirit captive by deceit, but Christ restored it in Zion when he breathed on the apostles. And why does Jacob rejoice first and Israel then become glad, when they are one and the same? Because "Jacob" means "supplanter" and "Israel" means "a mind seeing God." We must first become supplanters, that is, supplanters of the devil. Then our discerning mind rejoices in contemplating God, as far as it is able.

"Not because of my deeds," he says, "for I have none worthy enough. Not because of my fathers' noble birth, for one person cannot save another. But by your name." Salvation by his name truly stands lasting and inviolable. When people fall among robbers or barbarians and then mention the name of powerful men, they escape the danger as members of those men's households. How much more are we saved by the name of God from every plot of the demons!

He asks for judgment, not so that we may be condemned, but so that we may be freed from the one who tyrannizes us. That is why he prayed to be judged "in power": when the adversary, whether visible or spiritual, has been subdued by God's power, we will be out of reach of those who abuse us.

We have no weapon against our enemies stronger than prayer, provided only that we pray for things worthy of God. The Prophet knew this was true of himself, and so he wants God to give ear to the words of his mouth. Then God would see that he seeks nothing merely human and would accept the sacrifice of his prayer.

All who do not think the things of God are strangers, even if they are relatives, friends or brothers. That is why, though they are our kin, they are often not ashamed to plot against us as strangers against strangers. Those who have made themselves strangers to God become strangers to the law of nature as well, and how much more so! By "the mighty" he means those who are strong in wickedness. Their evil is so strong and unyielding that they plot against the soul itself, and they contrive not only our bodily death but our spiritual death too.

God does not accept an unwilling sacrifice. Such an offering is never credited to the one who offers it, but to the one who forces him. The apostle Paul knew this and said: "Not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." But you should also understand "willingly" in terms of the occasion. When we fall into affliction we often become more devout than we usually are. We ought to be found the same once the affliction has passed.

When he saw the destruction of his enemies, he called his thanksgiving a "confession," because what it achieves is good. The one who thanks a benefactor makes him more generous from then on. Being redeemed from the sins we have and from those still to come brings us close to God. It gives us hope of the good things to come and frees us from every affliction, so that for such a person life is transformed into blessedness.

The next psalm holds to the same purpose. It describes a person who is tested by temptations, and so he promises to sing with understanding to the one who is able to free him from temptations. It also contains a clear prophecy of the Lord's sufferings.

Since Christ prayed these words, let us pray them too. Let us servants imitate our Master, and let us who are poor imitate the one who is rich. He wants our prayer to be heard, and he wants this petition, made for the salvation of the human race, not to be overlooked, since he himself is the firstfruits of those for whom he intercedes. At the same time he wants to show us how we should pray, and so he says: "Give ear, and do not disregard." For often God hears our prayer and still passes over it and sets it aside as pointless and unworthy of his hearing.

"Consider," he says, "who it is that prays": the Son of the Father, a king of the same substance, yet bearing the form of a servant to save the nature he created in us. By "my musing" he means the mind's soaring in contemplation, which the Lord underwent as he thought over our condition. It troubled him that we had gone so far in folly as to trip up the one who was running the race on our behalf and to put stumbling blocks before the one who came to save us. Caiaphas, Judas and their accomplices did these things, and so he fittingly added: "From the voice of the enemy and from the affliction of the sinner." He calls Caiaphas the enemy because at the time of the trial he dared to utter such words against the Savior: "He has blasphemed. What more do you want?" And he calls Judas the sinner. How could someone who betrays his teacher not be a sinner? Deeply afflicted by him, as both disciple and betrayer, he adds what follows.

It is typical of people in temptations and afflictions to be seized not only by fear and trembling but also by darkness, as their soul gives way. But Christ, the true and genuine shepherd, was afraid and trembled for his own flock. It was not out of place for one who was distressed and grieved to fear and tremble, since he suffered everything that we suffer, without sin. So our darkness covered him too. Or rather, he means the darkness that covered the world at the time of the cross, from the sixth hour to the ninth.

He calls the apostles "wings," for on them the mystery of Christ flew over the whole world and came to rest in the churches as if in nests. He longs for these wings, like the wings of a dove, that is, wings full of what the Spirit supplies. The word "who" here is not the word of someone at a loss, but rather of someone who longs and is eager.

When Christ was judged unlawfully, his judges, namely Pilate and the Jewish high priests, contradicted one another. Pilate said, "I find no fault in this man." They said, "We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die."

"By day" refers to the time of the cross; "by night" refers to the time of the betrayal. "Upon its walls" means upon the priests, for they are the walls of the people. They are strong when they live by the law of the priesthood, but rotten and fallen when they do things foreign to their calling. By "lawlessness and toil in its midst, and injustice" he means slavery to the letter. It was lawlessness because they did not keep the law spiritually. It was injustice because, after receiving so many benefits from the Father, they handed over their physician and the one who nourished them to the cross. "And interest and deceit have not departed from its streets." Perhaps he is also attacking the greed of the Jews: the law itself forbade them to lend at interest, yet they made a profit from interest by deceit, through other devices. But the interest that deceit yields is hypocrisy. Hypocrisy, together with deceit, never left the streets of Jerusalem, for they boasted loudly of these things as if they were virtues. Let us also be on our guard. By day or by night, let us never put up with lawlessness, or any contradiction at all, on our walls, that is, our virtues. Nor let us have interest or deceit in our streets. For the broad and smooth roads are those on which offenses lead not to life but to destruction.

Attacks from open enemies are considered bearable because it is easy to guard against them. But those who seem to be friends while plotting like enemies are not bearable, for they mix their poison with honey so that no one notices, and so they bring about death. Christ reproached Judas with this through the present prophecy. To show this more clearly, the Prophet added what follows:

"Man of one soul with me": this is because of the love the Lord showed his disciples, so great that he said to the Father: "Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are." "My guide": since Judas himself carried the money-box, perhaps he had charge of managing it. "My familiar friend": for the Lord revealed everything to him as to a disciple. "You who sweetened my food together with me": for he alone dipped into the dish with Jesus. "We walked in the house of God in harmony." By the house of God he means Zion, for there Christ celebrated the Passover supper with his disciples in harmony. Yet Judas did not keep the mystery of the supper, for he went out from there and carried out the betrayal. So the Spirit of God spoke these words many generations beforehand to reproach the betrayer.

This was fulfilled in Judas, for the noose followed his betrayal. It was also fulfilled in the rest of the Jews. They had Christ, the true life, but they acted impiously toward him, and so they came under the fearful curse of death. Human life is called a "sojourning" because we cannot dwell here for long. Like temporary residents, we are thrown out at once when the master of the house gives the order. And since the Prophet spoke of many "sojournings" instead of one, he is hinting at the many different ways in which people live. Some, perhaps, follow a life of want [?]; others farm; others serve in the ministry of divine things. But in all of these the children of the Jews did evil. Not only the common people, but also their most eminent men, whether rulers or priests, practiced wickedness, holding it, as it were, in their midst.

Christ also says these words, for he cried out to God, his own Father, and the Lord heard him. You may take "the Lord" to be the Spirit (for "the Lord is the Spirit"), or the Lord himself hearing himself. Either way it is clear that Christ prays because he wants to keep the law of human nature, and yet he himself hears himself. He fulfills his own prayer: whatever he prays for as man, he accomplishes as God.

Or else he is proclaiming the mysteries that took place at the times named. In the evening: how Joseph buried him and Nicodemus prepared his body for burial; and again, how he came in a second time while the doors in Zion were shut. In the morning: how he was led away to Pilate's praetorium, and how, after rising from the dead, he showed himself to the women. At noon: how he was crucified and shook creation, wishing not to destroy it but to renew it and set it right. And why did he promise to recount these things? Because they sum up the rest of the Only-begotten's wonders as well. That is why he says the Father too will hear his voice, rejoicing as he recounts these mysteries.

He may mean the soldiers who surrounded his tomb; or the false witnesses who stood around him at the time of the trial and slandered him; or the powers in Hades. These powers surrounded him, astonished and at the same time keeping guard, so that he would not lead up the whole captive multitude of the dead.

The precision of the prophecy deserves our wonder. It was fulfilled in Judas in actual deeds, when he wanted to give the silver of the betrayal back to the high priests and so had to stretch out his hand.

The Jews, he says, spoke soft words, which seemed to surpass all kindness. With them they tested the wisdom of God, as sailors test the sea with sounding-leads. Yet they never reached the bottom. What can a sounding-lead do in a bottomless deep? And the wisdom of God is a deep. Paul said of it: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" And this same Prophet says: "Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great deep." But some copies read: "His words were softened." In that case the prophecy refers to Judas. He softened his words through [?]. At times he pretended to care for the poor so that he could steal from the money-box. At other times he mocked Christ with a kiss and a greeting.
