We believe these words were spoken to us as well. If we cast our cares upon God, we will find that he nourishes and supports us, so that we are never shaken. But it seems to me that the Prophet, having mentioned Judas, had to allude to Peter as well, in order to show the difference between an involuntary slip and a deliberate transgression. He encourages Peter after the slip of his denial and urges him to repent. He exhorts him to cast his anxiety about these things upon God. God is able to sustain the disciple by pardoning him, and he does not allow the righteous to be shaken forever. Even if the righteous man suffers it for a time, God soon turns it into calm.
Let the faithful say this, for hope in God grants freedom from evils and the presence of every good thing.

The words of the psalm seem somehow to contradict its title. David did stay in Gath when he fled from Saul. But the foreigners did not hold the prophet there. Instead they drove him away, because he pretended to be out of his mind and deranged, strumming on the doors and letting spittle run from his mouth, as 1 Samuel shows. And if we look in the historical record for a people "far removed from the holy ones," on whose behalf David wrote the psalm, we will not find one. So we must take these words spiritually, just as they were written by the Spirit. The Prophet composed the psalm on behalf of the people of the Gentiles, who were far removed from the holy ones, for they had no fellowship with patriarchs or prophets. Yet, as Paul says, those who were far off were brought near. This happened when the foreigners seized the new David in Gath, that is, in the winepress, for "Gath" means "winepress." The Church too is called a winepress, because of God, who treads out the mystery in it. We find him crying out in the prophecy of Isaiah: "I have trodden the winepress alone." And in the same prophecy the powers of heaven answer him: "Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of one who comes from a trodden winepress, full of what has been trampled?"

Our own inner person often has to endure this hard war too, attacked all day long by Satan and trampled by him. The psalm mentions a "man," but it nevertheless hints at Satan himself, who is often called this in divine Scripture, or at one of those who serve in his army. But it is also fitting for the people of the Gentiles to sing these words. Satan deceived them for a long time, and they endured his warfare through the plots of the demons, whom he hints at more clearly in what follows.

He does not mean a single day, but the whole span of time that has gone by, during which our spiritual enemies never stopped attacking and trampling us from on high. How did they trample us? Through idolatry and pleasures, among other things, they tripped us up, and then they trampled on us as we lay there. So let us not be tripped to the ground, that is, to earthly things, and no one will be able to trample us. Nor let us allow our enemies to rise above us. Instead, let us climb the ladder of the virtues and put those who plot against us beneath us.

"For if," he says, "we walk in the light, and walk decently as in the day," as Paul says, then we have good reason to fear none of those who plot against us, since we use faith and hope in God as our weapon against them.

Every word that contains the knowledge of God deserves praise and acclaim. So, he says, let us offer our praises to him as the one who supplies them. Whatever we speak in him prospers and is rightly worthy of acceptance. We will find that "flesh" often means the passions of the flesh and its pleasures, as when Paul says: "For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh." Often it also means a human being, as David said: "To you all flesh will come." So hope in God both bridles pleasure and shackles the human enemy, and in both respects it makes us fearless.

Here too he clearly hints at the Jews. They always abhorred the words of the faithful, because those words refuted their unbelief. So when Paul reasoned with them from morning until evening, they abhorred the truth of his message and were at odds with one another, as Luke says. "All their thoughts turned against me for evil." The children of the Jews think nothing good about the Gentiles (since every evil person brings forth what is evil), and they try every way they can to deceive us. Nothing, then, is clearer than this prophecy. The children of the Jews were driven out of Jerusalem and became sojourners throughout the whole earth because of their sin against Christ. When they are asked the reason, they hide it. They say nothing about their sin against Christ and put forward other sins instead, even though they are not practicing idolatry now or killing prophets. Why do they hide it? So that their admission will not confirm our faith. "They will watch my heel," he says. The Jews search out even our slightest offense. This is how you should understand what God said to the serpent: "He will watch your head, and you will watch his heel." We are commanded above all to watch his head, that is, idolatry. But we must also guard against the other sins, even if they are the least of them and seem so trivial that they count as the heel. For the enemy watches for these too, since he wants to accuse us before the judge even by means of trivial things. So it is fitting to take this verse as referring not only to the Jews but also to our real enemies, the demons, and to apply what follows in the same sense.

Blessed are those whose tears God receives, for he comforts them in their sufferings, as he pledged in his own promise. And what is that promise? "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted."

It should be noted that some of the writers have said that after the return from Babylon there was a time of plenty, with abundant rain, and that the Jordan flowed full; they said that this is what is called the river of God. Yet the returning exiles lived in the deepest poverty, as Ezra has taught; and the rest of the psalm, which calls for the calling of the nations, fits accordingly. Others say, in the manner of fables, that these things will happen after the Jews are called back in the last times, when Jerusalem is to be rebuilt.

For by the greatness of what is done on your behalf you will make those who belong to you so conspicuous that many even of your adversaries will pretend, falsely, to be your servants. This happened when many of the adversaries even submitted to circumcision, pretending to be Jews. Josephus is a witness to this in the eleventh book of the Antiquities, where he tells the story of Mordecai and speaks as follows: "The horsemen carrying the letters set out at once and completed the journey before them. Mordecai put on the royal robe, placed the golden crown and the necklace on himself, and went out. When the Jews in Susa saw him so honored by the king, they took his good fortune to be shared by them all. As the king's letters were published, joy and a light of salvation took hold of the Jews both in the cities and in the countryside, so that many even of the other nations, out of fear of the Jews, had themselves circumcised, securing their own safety by this means."
For you allowed us to suffer these things because you wished to show everyone that our piety is genuine.

He asks that the appearing of the Savior, which he foreknew, may come quickly, so that we may reap the blessing that comes from it. The face of the Creator of all, the face that fills us with blessings and mercies, shines forth when the exact imprint of his being appeared to us and showed himself to the worthy. For since he is the image of the invisible God, whoever approaches him with a pure mind sees the Father. "For whoever has seen me," he says, "has seen the Father." Then he has mercy on those he benefits, and "blesses them with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus."

For when you make your face shine, the way that leads to you, the Father, becomes known: he who said, "I am the way; no one comes to the Father except through me." And he will also be salvation among all the nations, when the saying is fulfilled, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God." You might also call his commandments a way, as in "I ran the way of your commandments"; and, correspondingly, the salvation he has come to provide, so that your salvation toward us may become plain to all.

The fall of sinners comes easily, even if they think they can rely firmly on themselves. For what dissolves more easily than smoke? Or than wax, when it is heated by a fierce fire? To these the Prophet compared sinners: for when the fire of Gehenna is fanned, all the show that surrounds them dissolves at once.

Indeed, Christ is regularly called "the Rising" in the prophets: "Behold a man whose name is the Rising, and he shall rise up from beneath him." And again: "For you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in his wings." But though he is a rising by virtue of his own light, he rode upon the west, making his chariot of the sinners who turned to him, to whom he said: "Take my yoke upon you, for it is kind, and my burden, for it is light." David commands these to prepare a way for God through repentance; for they, having not only obtained pardon before him but also been made his own, are to rejoice.

The gathering of the godly in a household is also called a church; so Paul too says, "Aquila and Prisca send you warm greetings in the Lord, together with the church in their house." He wishes the Lord and God to be glorified from the fountains of Israel, the prophets and apostles, so that we too may give glory concerning God in the way they set forth.

Christ is the God of Israel; for Isaiah says of him, "For you are our God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior." He grants strength and power to the people from the nations, so that they turn away from error and return to him; and these, as his people, are called Christians after Christ.

And how can someone who hopes in God have his eyes fail, instead of being invigorated and made stronger? But he calls the apostles his eyes, of whom he says in the Song: "Your eyes are doves, by abundant waters"—that is, at the gift of baptism, for there he granted believers a share in the Spirit. So at the time of the passion they failed and were scattered, seeing Christ hoping in God, his own Father, and saying, "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani"; for they did not know that God was holding back his own power so that there might be room for the sufferings.
He calls the faithful his hairs. For as the head takes pride in its hair, so Christ takes pride in the faithful.

He became a stranger at the time of the passion, when all his disciples deserted him and fled. By "mother" you should understand the synagogue of the Jews and all those of the circumcision who were his kin according to the flesh; and by her sons, those who denied him and said, "As for this man, we do not know where he comes from." Again they regarded him as a stranger when they said, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?" Thus he became a stranger to his mother's sons.
For he truly put on the roughness of our sin as sackcloth.
He means the Jewish rulers. For it was the custom for the council of the elders of the Jews to sit in the gate, as we shall find from the story recorded about Ruth and Boaz.

What wine? The mystical wine. For those men were not babbling but singing psalms, speaking the prophetic hymns about Christ as about God. He is still speaking of the Jews, who hated him because he exposed their hypocrisy to their faces. But they kept the water of wickedness in the depths, so that at one time they called him Rabbi, at another a truthful man and one who came from God, while hiding their malice in the depths of their hearts.

And why does the Only-begotten need to be heard, being equal to the Father and of equal honor? He himself gives the reason: "For your mercy is kind." That is: I need to be heard for this reason, because through your love for mankind I have become a man, and for the sake of all men; and so, though I am God, I fittingly take these things upon myself as well.

Why "attend"? Look at it, he says—at this soul—for it is not merely a man's, but that of God made flesh; it accepted the sufferings not for its own sake, but for the freedom of all. For "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again." Yet I pray to you on its behalf because of the subjection of the flesh. For I have endured these things not for myself but for the whole of human nature; and since I bore its sins, I necessarily bore also the shame that comes from them.
We shall find this too fulfilled at the time of the cross; for then the Jews offered him vinegar and gall.

For even if they were enrolled first, he says, because of their fathers who live with God, so that the promises were given to them as well, nevertheless, since they have dared such things, let them be blotted out; let them not be enrolled with God, he says, among the chosen righteous who are worthy of the life that is with him, since they rejected the author of salvation.

He calls "praise" the glorification offered to him by the whole of creation, which glorifies him by its natural movements. The Church, then, promises not only to offer glorification together with creation, but to glorify him with song, that is, to offer a spiritual and intellectual hymnody. For this is what singing to God properly is.
For rational praise pleases God more than the worship prescribed by the Law.

It is a blessed thing to pray to God with such boldness as even to urge him on to help us. He prayed first that God would attend, and after that that he would make haste; for if he attends at all to what help we need, or of what kind, he is moved with compassion at once; and once moved with compassion he makes haste and does not delay.

Those who seek to destroy our souls are chiefly the demons; but men also seek this, inciting us to base deeds and unseemly pleasures. Yet neither of these can do so unless they receive from us our own betrayal, unless we bind the hands of the soul and so follow them. These, then, are put to shame when they see us far above their plotting and doing what is right.

"At once," that is, immediately and without delay. And whom does he wish to be quickly put to shame? Those who say, "Well done, well done!"—that is, those who mock, who flatter, who deceive, who welcome as good things that are harmful and deadly. Note, however, that he prays that the spiritual enemies be merely put to shame and turned back, but the visible ones quickly; for these are more easily won over, being brothers by nature, of the same race and the same stock.

Christ is called the Salvation of the Father, for in him the salvation of the human race was accomplished. Hence Simeon too, receiving Christ in his arms, said: "Now, Master, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your Salvation." Those, then, who love this salvation continually magnify God, that is, glorify him; for they have abandoned idols and loved God, who truly saves and redeems.

For when we are bereft of all human help, then we shall find God in place of everything. Perhaps he also says these things in the person of the people of the Gentiles, to whom the whole psalm is fitting: Christ calling for help and hastening it, and entreating that the spiritual enemies—the demons, that is, who had long tyrannized over us—be put to shame. This people is poor and needy: poor because of sin, needy because of impiety. "Helper," as a mighty deliverer, since he gave himself as a pledge to death for us for a little while, so that our captivity might be redeemed. "Do not delay." For the sick man has been given up by all the physicians. That is why Habakkuk too said, "Yet a little while, and he who is coming will come and will not delay," hastening the Savior's arrival.

Rightly, in connection with "Let me not be put to shame," he says "in your righteousness." For even if I have sinned against you, yet [?] in your righteousness. For even if I have sinned against you, yet you will justly deliver me from these, both because they have no knowledge of your strength and because they wrong us without cause.

That is, stoop down to me as to one who is weak. "Incline your ear" as to a sinner, unable to pray with boldness; or, to put it more truly, draw near. For we cannot draw near to God unless he who is present everywhere comes near to us through his compassion.

He calls the devil "sinner," "lawless," and "unjust," and prays to be delivered from his hand (that is, from sin, which he wields through the wiles of pleasures). And if he means being delivered from sinful men, this too is a blessed thing. For if the sinner is an enemy, he does not spare; and if a friend, he is a burden even so, for the very things he advises himself he urges on his friends as well. Let us too, then, pray to be delivered from the sinner, whether enemy or friend: the one does harm through friendship, the other through domination, each of them unjust and lawless.

No one can hymn God or the things of God unless he is filled by him with wisdom and praise. And what does he wish to hymn? The glory and majesty of God; that is, the great and most glorious wonders of God, of which he said: "How magnified are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all."
He calls the Spirit "majesty," for it is in him that the great wonders and mighty deeds of God take place. And by "all the day" he means our life.

The demons watch over our souls, not for good but for evil, keeping an eye on them so as to lie in wait and ensnare them. For when, having watched us, they see that through sin we have grown weak for good works, as though we had been forsaken by God, they wish with one accord not only to pursue us but are eager also to seize us; for they think there is no one to deliver.

And how can God, who is over all and in all, be far away, except when we do things unworthy of his presence? As he said to the Jews through the prophet's tongue: "Your sins stand between you and God."

God's greatness is his condescension toward us; for being the greatest, he remains great and yet comes down to the small. And how did he increase his condescension toward us? Clearly when he became man and, turning us from error in this way, did not frighten us as slaves but exhorted us as sons.

Not so much with instruments of the senses as with a pure heart, with a tongue that is self-controlled and utters nothing foreign to holiness. For these are truly and rightly called instruments of psalmody.

He speaks of the self-emptying of the Only-begotten into the Virgin Mother of God; and he rightly called her womb a fleece, since it received the coming of God the Word quietly and without a sound, as a fleece receives the rain. You will say the same of the drops as well.

Now they do so willingly, but in the age to come even unwillingly. For, as the Apostle says, we do not yet see all things subjected to him. But then every knee shall bow to him, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And his enemies who lick the dust are those who prize the delights of the flesh.

He will persuade, then, he says, those who delight in injustice and greed to practice mercy and love of mankind. This is what the Scripture of the Gospel indicated when it said, "These twelve Jesus chose, whom he also named apostles."

What name? Christ, after whom we are called Christians. For his name has become so precious in the sight of those who were saved through him and believed that some despised wealth, others rank, and others even life itself, rather than bring themselves to deny the name of Christians.
For not only in churches, but also in marketplaces and in homes, the blessing of Christ—that is, his glorification—is continually proclaimed by those who have believed in him.

For all tribes, all tongues and lands, which formerly lived in error, have now with one voice received the blessing; and so they will also call him blessed. With what blessing, if not surely the one recorded in the Gospels: "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you"?

Why does he repeat "So be it"? Because he wishes to hasten our freedom and the hope of the righteous. For when the earth is filled with the glory of Christ, then the present world will come to its end and the kingdom of heaven will appear.

By "feet" and "steps" he means the courses of action and the movements of the mind, as he himself taught us in another part of the prophecy of the Psalms, saying, "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." And again: "Direct my steps according to your word." His feet were not shaken; that is, he did not turn his way of life toward the worse. Nor were his steps poured out; for he did not turn the impulses of his soul toward dissipation.

For there is no recovery from the death of sin, and they plainly suffer what is said in Proverbs: "When the ungodly man falls into the depths of evil, he grows contemptuous." Nor do they consent to suffer the lot of men. You see how much even a single word added to a matter can contribute to clarity. For though he could have said, "They are not in troubles," he added, "in the troubles of men." By "man" here understand one who keeps the dignity of a rational being and lives in virtue; or one who, when he stumbles, is set right through the repentance God brings upon him. In the troubles of such men sinners have no part, nor are they scourged along with men; that is, they do not toil and labor with the righteous, of whom it is said, "Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor." Nor are they scourged with those who have slipped but have hope of salvation, of whom it is written, "Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives."

They take pride in the very things they should be ashamed of, so that they use their offenses as garments and a covering. And he rightly joined these offenses together, for from pride people mostly fall into injustice and greed. But the words of heretics or blasphemers cannot prevail for long; they pass over the earth, harming only a few in passing. Understanding this, the faithful, even if they happen to have gone astray, turn back; and it is of them that the Psalmist sang what follows.

That is: So it was in vain that I purified my thoughts, in vain my deeds; I made my heart righteous, devising nothing unjust in it, and washed my hands among the innocent—that is, in good deeds, which do not carry the life [?] that comes from sin. That is: I did not reckon it a loss; for sin is truly the soul's loss, depriving it of friendship with God, the finest of all goods.

For whoever scourges himself for his offenses and sets his own reproof in the mornings—that is, in the light and not in darkness—is pure in thought and deed. He is reproved in the light who allows those who reprove him to speak freely, and who heeds that wise saying in Proverbs: "Reprove a wise man, and he will love you." But he is reproved in darkness who flees those who would shame him; to him the second line of the proverb applies: "Reprove a fool, and he will hate you all the more."

"I too," he says, "was brought to nothing"; that is, I became contemptible. Since my heart was inflamed toward greed, clearly my inmost parts were also changed—understand: toward pleasures. For when someone, beguiled by the prosperity of sinners, is roused to imitate them, he is at once brought to nothing and made worthless, having fallen from his proper dignity. And very fittingly he added, "I did not know"; for most people are unaware of the worthlessness that comes upon them from their sins, deceived by the outward guise they wear, some as priests, others as rulers.

For it is characteristic of a beast to stray, and then to be brought back from its straying, perhaps by a rod or a bridle. He opportunely added "with you" and "beside you," to safeguard his statement, since there are some who follow the devil like senseless beasts, of whom it is said, "He was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them." But how can someone who had any impulse toward the worse at all, even a passing one, be continually with God? Clearly because he did not sin by deliberate choice, but suffered this through being deceived; therefore, checked by the bridle of the law, he turned back at once.

"My heart and my flesh have failed"—that is, from worldly and human affairs. For when it fails there, that is, when it withdraws from them and ceases, then it will have God as its portion forever; and he becomes the heart's chosen possession, so that he is called its God because of this possession and his indwelling.

By "axes" you should understand the blasphemous tongues of the Jews, and the same by "hatchet" and "chisel"; nor is there anything surprising in this, for elsewhere he called them a sharp sword. These, then, he says, cut down and smashed its doors, that is, the entrances to faith in Christ. The name of the Father is the Son, since he makes the Father known and the Father is made known through him. His dwelling place (he means the incarnation) they profaned to the ground by the sufferings; for in heaven he remained glorified even at the time of the sufferings.

What feasts? Clearly those that were hoped for from the coming of the Savior: healings of diseases, release from error, entrance into the knowledge of God. For these are truly the feasts of God, which allow man to rejoice without end and to celebrate continually. These, then, they imagined they could abolish by their plot against him.

By "dragon" he means in general every hostile power: partly because it has a deadly venom, partly as a reminder of the drama that took place in paradise, when the enemy entered into the serpent and deceived the first-formed man. Christ crushed the heads of these in the water, both by being baptized himself and by handing on baptism to men. And the head of the spiritual dragons is sin.

For just as he works the gifts through the Holy Spirit, so he dries up and destroys the works of the deceiver, which he fittingly called "the rivers of Etham." For Etham means "bramble," and in divine Scripture this plant is condemned for its bad fruit.

He reminds the Creator of his own creation—not that he has forgotten it in any way, but because he wishes it to be acknowledged by all that it is his creature, possessing so great and so varied an order: day gives way to night, spring yields to summer, and the earth is measured out by boundaries, although because of its size it seems immeasurable. Each of these shows that God is the Creator, who arranged them with skill.

He calls sinners "poor": those who have no wealth of righteousness but have squandered all their father's estate. God is reasonably thought to have forgotten them, since he is patient and postpones the punishment due to them.

Note carefully that the giving of thanks belongs to many, but the telling of your wonders, O God, belonged to one out of the many who give thanks and call upon you. That is why the first statements are in the plural. Yet those of us who mean to call upon God must also offer him a twofold confession: one in words, the other in deeds. In words we offer it in prayer; in deeds, by turning away from the things for which we say we are confessing and repenting. For in this way God accepts our calling upon him as the calling of people who have been cleansed. And he also allows us to tell of his own wonders, all those recorded in the divinely inspired Scriptures.
By “the time” he means the age to come. For now is not the time for our judgment, since many sinners and many righteous people change over to the opposite side.

It comes from God’s testing and judgment, he says, for he exalts and humbles whom he wishes. “For the Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he lifts up.” Yet he does not do this without reason: he tests some through wealth and others through poverty.

Night is the best time for contemplation, because neither hearing nor sight draws one away to other things. Each of these pulls the mind toward itself and draws it away from contemplation. So it was at night that he meditated, busy with the movements of contemplation. We showed earlier that this is what “meditation” means here. “And my spirit was searching”: that is, it was troubled, because it could not yet grasp these things. The present life is night because of ignorance. In it, he says, I did not give myself over to sleep as some others do (“For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night”). Instead I stayed sober and discussed with the law what ought to be done. For once I learned that present things are temporary and will come to an end, I grasped the terrible things that surround us. Like a farmer I dug over my own spirit, so that I might sow in it and reap eternal life. “For the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.” Earlier, then, he called the soul “spirit.” Here, however, he means the spirit of man that is within him, with which the soul both searches and meditates. Surely it is not the body that does this with the soul. So the soul of man, properly speaking, meditates with the mind, and the spirit, yoked to the mind, searches. “For I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also.”
The right hand of the Father is plainly the Only-begotten, who, so to speak, changed us for the better.

God has worked many wonders in creation and in other ways. The outstanding one is that he took dust, made a rational living being from it, and established it as his own image. These are God’s wonders concerning us from the beginning, which he worked for our sake. We see him planting paradise and then shutting it again. We see him bringing on the flood, through which he both punishes and saves. We see him throwing our race into confusion by confounding the tongues of the tower-builders. We also see that for our sake he devised a written law in addition to the natural law, and prophecy in addition to that. These are God’s devices as he contrives to save our race. The prophet meditates on them, searching among them at length and reasoning about which of the things mentioned saves humanity. Then, having found something else besides these, he at once added this:

He does not say this by way of comparison, since one who is infinitely great admits no comparison. He says it in praise and wonder. For God is truly great in strength and great in condescension, great in power and great in his love for humanity, as what follows shows.

It was not for nothing that he used the image of sheep here. Shepherds guide sheep with a rod, and in the same way Christ shepherds us with the cross. That is also why he mentioned Moses and Aaron, who carried a rod as a type of the cross, a rod pregnant with the wonders in Egypt and in the wilderness. They used the rod against their enemies for Israel’s benefit, and in the same way Christ has used the cross against the demons for the sake of our conversion.

1. The heading is brief, because the psalm itself is taken up with the length of the prophecy. He gives it the title “Of Understanding” so that we may guard against the evils that came upon the Jews through their folly. The opening of what follows makes this clear: “Give heed, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth.” Do you see how great a dignity the Spirit confers on the prophet, wishing to urge us [?] … [?] of the prophecy? He calls the people of God his people, and the law of God his law. This is because the possessions of wise servants and faithful household slaves [?] … with their masters, just as God also said to Moses: “Your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have acted lawlessly.” What does “Give heed to my law” mean? Do not handle it with contempt. Search it attentively, and then incline your ear in obedience. Whoever hears God’s law casually counts it either superfluous or burdensome, and so his ear will not be able to hear. But whoever studies it attentively perceives that its yoke is easy and its burden light, and he inclines his ear to the words of the prophecy. That is, out of love for those words he gives the whole prophecy over to them [?], setting before himself the Spirit, by whom everything is worked. “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter problems from of old, all that we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.” Even though I am about to discuss parables of long-past times and ancient problems, he says, I am still trustworthy when I speak about them. For I learned them by hearing and by knowledge, which were handed down not by the fathers of the flesh but by priests and prophets. And he does well to show that he did not hear and know these things alone but together with many others, when he says, “All that we have heard and known.” For this knowledge and hearing of the prophets has become common to everyone. He speaks of parables and problems because he mixed teaching into the history, and this is characteristic of the parables and problems in the divine Scriptures. In these, he says, he opens his mouth, so that we too may imitate what is said. As we always offer God the firstfruits of every crop, so too we should offer him the firstfruits of our lips, and not move our tongue before it speaks the things in which [?] takes pleasure. Beyond this, you may say that the prophet has taken on the person of the Lord. His people is humanity, and his law is the ancient commandments. Matthew speaks about him: “So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: I will open my mouth in parables; I will pour forth things hidden since the foundation of the world.” And what did he add here? “All that we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.” These words fit his humanity. And to show that what comes from him resembles and agrees with what came through the prophets, he says: “It was not hidden from their children for another generation, as they proclaimed the praises of the Lord, his mighty deeds, and the wonders he had done.” Who [?] … about whom they said earlier, “Our fathers told us,” but on behalf of [?] … [?], assigning this to the prophecy itself.

2. "It was not hidden from their children for another generation." By "another generation" he means the Gentiles. He speaks of them elsewhere too: "The generation to come will be told of the Lord." These same people are also called children of the true Israel, as though they had inherited from them their piety toward God. That is why Paul said, "To them belong the adoption, the worship, the covenant and the giving of the law, and to them belong the fathers." These, then, announced the praises of the Lord to us as to sons. We would not even have known how we ought to praise God if the prophets had not gone before us and taught us to say, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord," and again, "Praise the Lord from the heavens," and again, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts," and all the words like these. From them we have learned the mighty deeds of God and the wonders that he did. The mighty deeds are those he displayed against Pharaoh, perhaps, or against Nebuchadnezzar, or against the giants, and others like these. The wonders are those he did with Job, with David, with Daniel, with the three youths, and with the others who were crowned in their trials. "And he raised up a testimony in Jacob." What kind, and when? When God wrestled with him at the brook of Jacob. It is clear that God wrestled in the form and shape of a man, and he shows that he was being held fast by Jacob in these words: "Let me go, for the dawn has come up." Jacob answered, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." That wonder, then, is the testimony, which Christ also established as a reminder of his own appearing as God in the flesh. "And he appointed a law in Israel, all that he commanded our fathers, to make them known to their sons." This is why, he says, God appointed a law in Israel, even though they were going to transgress it and set its ordinances aside: so that he might make known to their sons (and we have said that these are the Gentiles who turn to him) all that he commanded our fathers. So the Jewish people received the law for our sake, for we keep the law according to the spirit, as the lawgiver intended. What follows shows this more clearly: "So that another generation might know." Which one? "Sons yet to be born." Do you see that he is speaking of the Gentiles? They had not yet been born into piety, but they were going to be born through baptism. So they were rightly called "sons yet to be born." But they had also fallen through idolatry. Fittingly, then, comes the prophecy of their resurrection, which was to come through faith in Christ: "and they will rise up and declare them to their sons, so that they may set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but seek out his commandments." For this is truly the knowledge of God: to share that knowledge with others as well, and to make sons by teaching them the commandments. Those who believed in Christ have clearly done this. They begrudged no one the knowledge of God, and those who believed first do not wish to shut the road to others. Instead they urge them to set their hope in God, not to forget the works of God, and to seek out his commandments too. These things are proclaimed every day by the Church to all, both her own and outsiders. In the Church Paul cries out to all, men and women alike: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." The scribes and Pharisees did not act this way. They took the key of knowledge and allowed no one to enter, as the Lord made plain when he pronounced woe on them. The next words point to this: "So that they may not become like their fathers." The Gentiles rightly claim as fathers those who came from Israel, because Christ came from them. Some of these were good: the true prophets and priests, and all who fulfilled the law. Others were wicked: all who falsely held these offices. But since he was going to speak of the wicked and lawless, after saying "fathers" he necessarily [?] … added the words that describe them: "A crooked and embittering generation, a generation that did not set its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God." They all professed their faith with the tongue only, not with the whole heart and a pure spirit. So they were crooked and embittering, and they did not direct their heart toward God, who wishes to receive not what comes from the lips but what comes from the movements of the soul. So that we will not imitate them, the law they neglected has been given to us, to be remembered and fulfilled in the spirit. "The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows, turned back in the day of battle. They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law." Naming the greatest tribe, he means the whole people of Israel that split off from Judah, for Ephraim held first place among the ten tribes that came under Jeroboam. You will find the other prophets naming Israel this way too. Hosea shows it when he says, "What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Manasseh? What shall I do with you, Judah?" By "Judah" he means the two tribes ruled by the house of Judah, and by "Ephraim" the ten, since the tribe of Ephraim held the kingship over them. These, then, were "bending and shooting with bows," for they had the instruments of piety. Yet they turned to flight, plainly in the day of the spiritual battle, turning their backs to their enemies, the demons. What made them turn to flight and turn their backs to the enemy? Not keeping the covenant of God and not walking in his law. And when did this happen to them? When they worshiped the two molten calves. So, lamenting over them, he went on to say: "And they forgot his benefits and the wonders he had shown them in the sight of their fathers, the wonders he did in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis."

3. In a few words he recalled all the wonders done in Egypt, and he reproaches them for forgetting them. They would never have abandoned their benefactor if they had not been so ungrateful that they drove his benefits out of their memory. They also forgot the wonders to which their fathers had been witnesses, since the fathers saw the signs with their own eyes. He says these happened in the plain of Tanis, since Pharaoh no doubt lived there, as it was the more ancient and the greater city. Divine Scripture shows that Tanis is the more ancient. When it wished to testify to the great antiquity of Hebron, it compared it with Tanis, saying, "Hebron was built before Tanis in Egypt was built." Tanis, that is, was Pharaoh's royal seat. "He split the sea and led them through; he made the waters stand like a wineskin." Here he shows the great power of the wonder-worker. … the sea for the passage of the people [?] … he did make it dry land, yet, as though sparing an element that was his own, he divided it in two. That is the meaning of "he split." Then he curved each edge of the divided water like a wineskin and gave the travelers ground in the middle [?] of the sea he had laid bare. And once the people had crossed, he let the sea return to its own place. "And he led them with a cloud by day, and all night with a light of fire." Do you see how great is the providence of the wonder-worker? They needed a sign for the road, since it ran through the desert and was unknown to them. But he took care not only of their need but also of the comfort of those who received the sign. So he gave them a cloud by day to shade them from the scorching heat of the sun, and a pillar of fire by night to give them warmth as well as light, since the night is damper and colder. So we too, when we travel with God as our guide, [?] the cloud of repentance when the scorching heat of pleasures comes upon us. And when love has grown cold, we will be able to kindle it again with zeal, as with a pillar of fire [?]. "He split a rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great deep. He brought water out of a rock and made waters flow down like rivers." Some may think the prophet has described the same sign twice. That is not so. Moses brought them water out of a rock on two occasions: once in the wilderness of Horeb, and the second time at Kadesh, where Miriam died and was buried. Each time the water was abundant, which is why it says "as from a great deep." Because of its quantity, the water could be compared not to one river but to many. This proved that the wonders had really happened to them and were not mere appearances. "And they went on sinning against him still more." He makes a grave charge against the Jewish people. Though they received such great wonders, and ought to have refrained from their old sins, they added new sins to them. Nor were they simply sinning, but sinning "against him," that is, offending against the very one who provided the signs. So he went on: "They embittered the Most High in the waterless land." How did they embitter him? Not by being thirsty, nor by asking for water, but by belittling and reviling the one who provided it. That is why the places where the wonders happened were named, one "the water of contradiction" and the other "testing" and "reviling," because they tested the Lord, saying, "Is the Lord among us or not?" Moses the lawgiver recorded this in these very words. What follows plainly matches this: "And they tested God in their hearts by asking food for their souls." Do you see that they were testing God, to find out whether he could provide food in the wilderness? So their request came from malice far more than from need. That is why he does not say simply "food" but "for their souls": they wanted it to suit their own pleasures and the desires of the soul, grumbling about cucumbers, melons and onions as if they were in short supply. "And they spoke against God and said." It is a terrible thing to slander even an ordinary person, which is why David says, "Whoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I drove out." It is more terrible to slander one's master, since punishment follows the slanderer. But to slander God is most terrible of all, since God is our father and master and the one who feeds us, and he holds everything you could name of goodness or power. We must therefore refrain from reviling him, either out of fear of his power or out of love for his goodness. And what did they say against him? "Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock and waters gushed out and torrents overflowed, but can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?" Grievous indeed is the blindness of the blasphemous and lawless! The very things that should have led them to expect great things from God, and to trust that he can do all things and that nothing is impossible for him, are what lead them to give up on him. They all but say, "Even if he provided water, he cannot provide food," as though he were worn out from working wonders and had spent all his generosity on the earlier signs. Naturally he is roused by this, as what follows shows. "Therefore the Lord heard and threw back his robe," that is, "He was moved to anger." This is how Theodotion and the producers of the fifth edition render it.

4. But why did both of them take "throwing back" to refer to anger? Not without reason. People stirred by rage often throw back their robes, as though hurrying to take vengeance. And the prophets commonly attribute human gestures to God, so that by them they may show the character of each of his actions. To see that here he used "throwing back" for the swift stirring of anger, listen to what follows: "And fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger went up against Israel." For as if God were angry, fire went out to take vengeance on those who had provoked the anger. And what was the cause? "Because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation." God is provoked when he is not believed. Whoever does not believe God does not expect judgment either, and he also despises God's law. And if he despises the divine law, much more will he despise human law, and so our common life is thrown into confusion. What will those not dare to say who neither believe in God nor hope for the salvation that comes from him? At the same time he accuses them of disbelieving not only in the Father but also in the Son. That is why he says, "Nor did they hope in his salvation." He means Christ. Many of the prophets called him "salvation," and Simeon did so plainly when he took him in his arms. "And he commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven." By "the clouds above" he means those that are high up. That is why he also called them "doors of heaven," since they are set in front of heaven. Some clouds lie close to the earth, so that they are found even lower than the mountains. "And he rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them bread from heaven. Man ate the bread of angels; he sent them provisions in abundance." So that they would not think God had grown angry because he was unable to grant their request, he dealt first with their blasphemy, since they did not ask as one ought to petition God [?]. He kindled fire among them, and a large part of the people was burned there, so that the place was named "Burning." After this he gave them what they had asked for. He calls the manna "bread from heaven" and "bread of angels" because it was not prepared by human hands but came down from heaven, where the choir of angels dwells. What kind of provisions he sent them in abundance, the following words make clear: "He removed the south wind from heaven, and by his power brought on the southwest wind. And he rained down meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the seas." Good things stand ready with God, yet he keeps them for the proper time. So when he wished to fill the Jewish people, he did not produce some common (some new) creation. Instead he prevailed over the south and southwest winds [?]. These winds blow in the hotter regions, where the Creator appointed the quail to live, and so he fulfilled his purpose as if from storehouses already stocked. We should not suppose that the prophet was speaking with mere exaggeration when he said that "he rained down meat like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the seas." God's creatures are countless, and most of them are unknown to us. The birds were so many that the people used no nets, snares or other devices, but simply their hands, because the catch lay ready in front of them. What follows shows this most of all: "And they fell in the middle of their camp, all around their tents. And they ate and were filled to excess." Consider this as well: a people so great in number, and so gluttonous, was filled not for one day but for thirty, as you can learn by reading Moses' account in the book of Numbers. "And he brought them what they craved; they were not deprived of their craving. While the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God came up against them, and he killed many of them, and fettered the chosen of Israel." So it is not for nothing that God puts off many of our requests. He does it for our good, since most of our desires turn out to be harmful to us. Often he grants them to sinners in his anger. And why does he grant them? So that, as we said, they will not find fault with him as though he were weak. After granting them, he punishes those who receive them, in order to frighten us too from ever trying to force God with lawless requests. So he gave the Jews the food they craved, but while they were still eating he brought his anger upon them. He killed their fat ones, that is, the stoutest of them, and fettered the chosen. These were not the people singled out for virtue, but those singled out for vice, for some are outstanding in wickedness. "In all this they sinned still more, and did not believe in his wonders. And their days vanished in futility, and their years in haste."

5. The prophet is astonished at the disobedience and hardness of heart of the Jews. They remained unmoved not only by the good things they received but also by the punishments, and "they sinned still more," that is, they heaped sins upon sins. They did this because "they did not believe in God's wonders"; that is, they had no full assurance or faith. They thought that the miracles and signs that happened came about by chance, as the ungodly tend to do. For this reason their days vanished in haste. By "vanishing" he does not mean simply a short span of time, but barrenness in virtue. Whoever has not lived in virtue dies with his days vanished, that is, before his time, even if he happens to live a long life. He has not borne the fruit for which he entered human life. That is why Scripture calls Abraham and Job "full of days," though many others lived more years. "When he killed them, then they sought him; they turned back and rose early to seek God. And they remembered that God is their helper, and God Most High their redeemer." It is truly good to remember God at all times, so that we call on his help even when things go well. If we remember him when we prosper, then he will remember us when we are in distress. But to seek him unwillingly and under the lash, not turning back by choice but confessing under compulsion that God is their helper and redeemer, is the mark of wicked and ungrateful servants. When a master sees that such a confession is forced, he will feel no gratitude for it. How much less will God, for he knows full well the hypocrisy of deceitful and wicked men. The words that follow plainly speak of it: "And they loved him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue. But their heart was not right with him, and they were not faithful to his covenant." Isaiah also blamed the Jews in similar words: "This people loves me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." How is this exposed? For even now we find many who are pious with the tongue alone. They are exposed when, as the prophet says, they are not faithful to his covenant. When they do not trust God's commandments, they are shown to have no good disposition or conscience toward the one who gave them. Paul said of such people, "They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds." "But he is compassionate, and will forgive their sins and will not destroy them. He will often turn his wrath away and will not kindle all his anger." He will forgive—but when? By pointing to a future time he plainly foretold the incarnation of Christ, since the Father sent him as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Christ is so compassionate that the first thing he proclaimed to people was repentance. And though he found the Jewish people deserving of destruction, he did not destroy them. He did not wipe them out completely, but left them a seed and a remnant: the apostles who believed from among them. Isaiah said of them, "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." So he multiplied his mercy and therefore turned his wrath away. How did he turn it away? He did not kindle all his anger. He kindled only part of it, bringing it against the temple and the ancient city. Had he kindled all of it, the people would have perished with the temple, and the land would have been destroyed with the city, as happened at Sodom. "And he remembered that they are flesh, a breath that passes and does not return." For when does God ever forget what our nature and our weakness are like? These words are spoken rather of the Son, who became flesh for our sake. He knows our condition not only as our Maker, but also because, having become flesh, he learned our weakness by experience itself. So Paul says of him, "Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered," and again, "Because he himself suffered when he was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted" … Since, then, "the Word became flesh," he remembered that we are flesh; that is, he came to know by experience the weakness of our flesh. By "flesh" he means the whole human being. That is why he added, "a breath that passes and does not return." We do not come back again to this present life. So for this reason we ought to stay sober, since we are traveling a road from which we can never turn back. "How often they embittered him in the wilderness and provoked him in the waterless land! They turned back and tested God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel." He marvels at how much wickedness the Jews committed, and at what kind of wickedness it was. They not only embittered God many times, but did so in the wilderness, where above all they should have been contrite and looked to heaven, since nothing there deceived or enticed them as happens in cities. And they provoked him "in the waterless land," when they were thirsty and ought to have been humble, yet they showed themselves arrogant. Then, when they turned, they turned not to righteousness but to another wickedness, testing God (and it was madness to test the one who knows all things) and provoking the Holy One of Israel. By this he means Christ. Isaiah also spoke of him: "To whom have you likened me, and shall I be exalted? says the Holy One." In this he foretold the cross, for Christ too called it that.

6. Why, then, in the wilderness did they not only embitter God (he means the Father) but also provoke the Holy One of Israel, that is, the Son? Because the rock that followed them was Christ, yet they doubted whether he could bring water out of a rock and supply it to them. So Moses even said: "Hear me, you disobedient: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" Therefore God, angered with them, said: "Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel," and what follows. "They did not remember his hand, the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor; how he set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis." Again he fittingly calls Christ the hand of God, that is, of the Father, since "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." So another prophet also says: "For the hand of the Lord has made all these things." Him, then, they did not remember, who redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor (he means Pharaoh) on the day of the exodus, when he came in about midnight and struck the firstborn of Egypt. He himself set the signs in Egypt and the wonders in the plain of Tanis, where Pharaoh's palace also was. This is not because we separate the Father from the wonder-working of that time, but because whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Note, however, that he calls "signs" the things that happen according to nature, such as the locust (for it is its nature to ravage crops), and "wonders" the things above nature, such as the frog was; for it is not its nature to run about and feed outside the water. The same holds for the hail mixed with fire and the river turned into blood, for each of these was a sign contrary to nature. "And he turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink." By rainwaters he means the water of the showers, since at God's command Moses changed into blood all water, not only that in springs and rivers but also that in vessels of wood and of stone. This was so that the God worshipped by the Hebrews would not be thought to have only a limited power, but would be known as the maker and ruler of all the elements. For the sons of the Greeks assign certain limited powers to their gods. For this reason he goes through the whole of creation in turn, as what follows can testify. "He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, and the frog, and it destroyed them. And he gave their crops to the blight, and their labors to the locust. He killed their vine with hail, and their sycamores with frost. And he gave over their cattle to the hail, and their substance to the fire." The order of the signs performed in Egypt that Moses set out is different, for the prophet is not concerned with that order now. His aim is to show all the elements taking the field against Pharaoh at God's command. See how fittingly he has assigned to each plague what resulted from it. Of the dog-fly he says, "It devoured them," since it attacked not the crops but people; and of the frogs, "It destroyed them." For they did this by creeping not only into the houses but also into the ovens, and they snatched away all the food they needed; in this sense they fittingly "destroyed" them. Moreover, when they died they made the land stink, and destruction in turn naturally arose from the stench. Their labors and their crops, he says, were given to the locust and to the blight, since the damage these do touches the crops alone and nothing else. When you hear "blight," do not be surprised, as though it were not among the plagues recorded by Moses; he means the small, not yet full-grown kind of locust. That is why Aquila rendered it "young locust" instead of "blight." He rightly says the vine was killed by hail, for hail is especially destructive of its fruit and its branches; and also the sycamores by frost, since that plant cannot bear cold, so that it naturally grows only in warmer regions; and the hail produced the frost. Then there is the fire, which he mentions next. He said the cattle were killed by the hail and their substance by the fire, that is, the wealth that comes from the land, for this is what he called "substance." As the hail and fire ran through and all the shoots were consumed, it was destroyed. And for this reason the wonder was truly prodigious: fire running in water.

7. As for you, pay attention to the force, clarity and conciseness of the prophetic words, and marvel at the wisdom of the Spirit, for it alone speaks what is fitting. "He sent upon them the anger of his wrath, wrath and anger and affliction, a mission by evil angels." Not evil in nature, nor in purpose, for God does not employ such angels in his service; but he called them evil because, when ordered, they brought troubles and afflictions. Hence this same psalmist also calls the day of judgment evil, as full of distress and troubles for sinners, saying: "Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy; in the evil day the Lord will deliver him." He sets out "anger and wrath," and then again "wrath and anger and affliction" in the present verses, not to say different things, nor to repeat the same words to no purpose, but to declare how greatly God was moved. "He made a path for his anger." In what way? By long enduring and being patient with those who were going to receive it. In that sense he "made a path" for his own anger, showing that he brings it justly and in due season upon those who refuse to be corrected. What follows also testifies to this. "He did not spare their souls from death." For he states the reason why he did not spare; and the death of their souls was, clearly, sin. For "the soul that sins, it shall die"; and again, "The death of sinners is evil." For this reason, then, he did not spare: those who did not spare themselves but gave their souls over to death necessarily found no sparing. Having seen how justly he did not spare, see what he brought upon them. "And he shut up their cattle to death. And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham." God shows great kindness even toward those he chastises, beginning with lesser things so that, brought to their senses, they may gain the greater. For this reason he first shut up the Egyptians' cattle to death; but finding them insensible, he struck the firstborn. So he would not have brought the plague of the firstborn if, chastened by the death of the cattle, they had come to their senses. He rightly called their firstborn "the firstfruits of labor," wishing to recall the curse written concerning Eve: "In pain you shall bear children." And he said the plague of the firstborn took place "in the tents of Ham." For the land of the Egyptians was rightly called the house and tents of Ham, not only because Ham was the father of Mizraim, from whom the Egyptian race descended, but also because they emulated the wickedness of those men. "And he led away his people like sheep, and brought them up like a flock in the wilderness." His enemies, he says, he treated in the manner described above; but his own people he led away like sheep and brought up in the wilderness, clearly guiding them himself like a flock, showing them pastures, rescuing them from wild beasts, keeping the gathered flock together with the pipe, and turning back the strays with his staff. All this and more he indicated by mentioning flocks and sheep. "And he guided them in hope, and they were not afraid, and the sea covered their enemies." In what hope? Clearly the promise made to the fathers. For he says to Abraham: "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and afflict them and humble them four hundred years. But the nation whom they serve I will judge, and afterward they shall come out here with many possessions." Guided by this hope, then, they were not afraid to cross on foot the Red Sea, which covered their enemies; and the water rushing back became a tomb for the Egyptians. "And he brought them to the mountain of his sanctuary, this mountain which his right hand acquired." By the mountain of his sanctuary he means Jerusalem, not so much because of the sanctuary that formerly dwelt there, namely the ark, as because of the second ark, the Lord's flesh. That was truly a sanctuary, and so it is called the acquisition of his right hand, that is, of Christ's. He acquired it not with weapons but by the wonders and sufferings he underwent for us. "And he drove out nations before them, and allotted them an inheritance by the measuring line. And he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents."

8. He reproaches the Jewish people because, though they had enjoyed such great benefits—receiving a foreign land as their inheritance and dividing it with great equality, God showing that he treated Israel as a father treats his children (that is why he commanded the allotment to be made by the line, enlarging the portion for the many and reducing it for the few, so that the strong tribe [should not?] overpower the weaker)—they nevertheless remembered neither the nations driven out before them nor the God who drove them out. They should have done so in order to remain grateful to him and never to emulate the lawlessness of those who had been driven out, lest they suffer as they had. "And they tempted and embittered God Most High, and did not keep his testimonies." He sets out their twofold sin. Not only did they tempt him, he says, but they also embittered him. Those embitter who go on tempting after a first, a second and many trials. That is grievous even when done to an ordinary person, and much more so against God Most High, that is, against one who, being infinitely great, cannot be put to the test by us. On this account the Spirit is found reproaching them in similar terms through the prophecy of Isaiah: "Hear now, house of Israel: is it a small thing for you to give trouble to men? And how do you give trouble to the Lord?" Besides this, the psalmist also says that "they did not keep his testimonies." They transgressed even what he lays down as law with a threat attached and with solemn testimony, and this showed great arrogance and disobedience. "And they turned away and broke faith, just as their fathers did; they were turned into a crooked bow. And they provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they moved him to jealousy." The prophet has shifted his discourse from the generation in the wilderness to those that followed, in the way that the fathers [?]. And what did they break? Clearly the covenants with God which they made through Moses on Mount Sinai, and through Joshua son of Nun in the land of promise after receiving it by lot. Yet they did not abide by them, but were turned into a crooked bow, so that they can no longer shoot straight; just so the Jewish people, once perverted, had no upright way of life. They also provoked God to anger at their altars and moved him to jealousy with carved images—not that he feels jealousy toward dumb and lifeless idols or demons, but because he is jealous over us, as a father over his children or a bridegroom over his bride, out of concern for our salvation. "God heard, and disregarded them." When does God not hear? And what need of hearing has he who knows our thoughts? But here he says that he heard, in that he did not let it pass but was moved, and in this way showed that he had heard. And what did he do, having heard? He did not bring a plague, but disregarded them; and to be disregarded by God is harsher than any scourge, for it is by his eye alone that we are kept safe. See, then, how much they suffered when they were disregarded. "And he utterly despised Israel, and rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, the dwelling where he had dwelt among men." For had he not utterly despised Israel, he would not have rejected his own tabernacle among them, in which he dwelt in order to be a mediator for them. Perhaps you will ask: why, when men had sinned, did he reject his own tabernacle? Because he did not acquire it out of any need of his own; it was for their sake, and since they had sinned, he fittingly turned away from the place of his mediation with them. And what was this Shiloh? The Spirit did not mention it in vain, but wished to show that, just as God left Shiloh when Israel sinned and chose another place for himself, Jerusalem, so he would also turn away from this one in turn when its inhabitants acted impiously, and would give his glory to other places to be honored. "And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy." He is still speaking of the tabernacle. For this was the strength and beauty of the people, because of the service of the holy things. He delivered it into captivity—not captivity at the hands of men (for that did not happen), but captivity into the hands of the spiritual enemy. That is why he mentioned one enemy, not many, indicating by it the enemy par excellence. The other translators, wishing to make him still clearer, rendered it, some "into the hands of the adversary," others "into the hands of the oppressor." To him he handed over the tabernacle, as defiled by those who ministered in it, become profane, and bearing nothing any longer worthy of God, but only of the one to whom it was handed over. Do not be surprised at this, since Isaiah too threatened that God would hand over ancient Jerusalem to demons, sirens and onocentaurs. "And he shut up his people with the sword, and disregarded his inheritance." This too is an accusation against the Jews: though they had become God's people and inheritance because of their fathers, they nevertheless brought him to disregard them and to shut them up with the sword—not only the sword of war but also the sword of the divine word. For the word is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword; and so it is rightly called a sword.

9. How did he shut them up with it, that is, hem them in and fetter them? By commanding in the law circumcision of the flesh, but in the Gospels circumcision of the spirit; there a Sabbath perceived by the senses, here a spiritual one. Hemmed in by these things, they cannot enter the kingdom of God; and what follows shows this as well. "Fire devoured their young men." By young men he means those strong in the law, such as the scribes and the Pharisees, who trusted in the strength of the letter. These were devoured by fire, that is, by jealousy toward us, as they saw that we are justified without the yoke of the law. That is why Isaiah said to them: "Jealousy will seize an untaught people, and now fire will devour the adversaries." "And their virgins were not mourned." For there was no one to mourn them when they were dying the death of sin. So he wrote this as an accusation against the Jewish teachers: they were without compassion even for virgins who sinned, and did not imitate Jeremiah, who said: "At the breaking of the daughter of my people I was darkened with perplexity; pangs seized me like those of a woman in labor." To this he fittingly added what follows: "Who will give water to my head, and fountains of tears to my eyes?" Accordingly Paul too rebukes the Corinthians because they did not mourn over the man among them who had committed fornication. "Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows will not be wept for." This too is a charge showing how far they had gone: the priests stumbled at the word of God, for that is what falling by the sword meant. And the widows had no one to weep for them, since the order of teachers among them was without compassion not only for the virgins but also for the widows. By virgins he means souls that had only then begun to sin; by widows, those that had sinned often and had cast off the fear of God, which had brought them into fellowship with the law. "And the Lord awoke as one asleep, like a mighty man stupefied with wine." So the things mentioned before—the sword, the fire, the lack of mourning—were not punishments; they were sins, and God was roused to avenge them. He awoke as one asleep, that is, putting aside his long-suffering as though it were sleep; and it was so great that it might even be thought a drunken stupor. What sort of stupor? The kind that comes upon strong men from wine, making some of them idle and inactive for a time; but when they wake up after sleeping, they become more vehement. So too we expect God, after his long-suffering, to act more severely against those who do not perceive it. And what did he do now? "He struck his enemies in the back parts; he gave them everlasting reproach." There are those whom God has struck in front, namely those for whom the blow proved a benefit, and the scourge made them hold fast to righteousness. But he strikes in the back those who are hardened by punishment, as Pharaoh was, and to these he gives everlasting reproach. For the blows dealt to the exceedingly wicked are final, and become an example to those who are sick. Or else, by "in the back parts" he referred in decorous language to an affliction of the rear. "And he rejected the tent of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim." For pious fathers are not accustomed to benefit impious children. "And he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved." And yet Zion itself and ancient Jerusalem belonged not to the tribe of Judah but to the tribe of Benjamin. But by Judah he means the one who confesses, for that is what "Judah" means. His tribe is the Church, for through repentance and confession Mount Zion is preserved in her; and this is what they loved. For how is it that whoever watches for God is called Zion? Because Zion means "watchtower." And if you say that Zion is the place, it is not the place, he says, of which Micah and Isaiah wrote that "Zion shall be ploughed like a field," but the one among us, which God loved so much that he entrusted all the mysteries to it. To this what follows clearly applies. "And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns on the earth; he founded it forever." If these things were said of the ancient city, the prophecy would be false. For how could that city be founded forever, when not even traces of it remain? But this one he founded forever and built like a unicorn, giving it as its foundation a single horn. For it does not have various baptisms, as the Jews do, nor many distractions over new moons, purifications and Sabbaths, nor many gods, as the nations that persisted in impiety have, but "one Lord, one faith, one baptism." Hence "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it"—by which he means the mouths of heretics. "And he chose David his servant, and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the ewes in lamb he took him." You will surely say: if he was speaking of the mysteries of the Church, why did he bring David into it, who lived long before these things? Because he was the father and the image of Christ. That is why he was taken from the flocks of sheep, not from the flock. For Christ has many flocks: some of men, some of angels, some of rational and visible powers. And these are "in lamb," that is, pregnant. For he has no barren flock; all of them, through fear of him, conceive and bring forth salvation. That is why Isaiah also said: "Through fear of you, Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." From there Christ was taken. To do what? "To shepherd Jacob his servant, and Israel his inheritance"—that is, the people from the Gentiles. This people is Jacob, since by supplanting the Jews it took their birthright; and it is also Israel, for at the time of the mysteries it sees God face to face, as he did. That God shepherds, hear David saying: "The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing." Hear Christ as well: "I am the good shepherd." "And he shepherded them in the innocence of his heart, and guided them by the skill of his hands." Do you see that he is plainly speaking of Christ? For he truly had no wickedness of heart, since he committed no wickedness, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And such skill of hands did he possess that with them he gave sight to the blind, set the lame upright, cleansed lepers—in short, refashioned the whole of fallen humanity.

1. The title of the prophecy is clear, so let us turn our discussion to the interpretation of the psalm. It does not contain an accusation against the nations, as some think. It is a prophecy of what would happen to the Jewish people when the nations seized their inheritance. "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple." These things did indeed happen to the Jews when the Assyrians took Jerusalem, and after them the Macedonians, and after all of them the Romans. Since this is plain, let us also turn the prophecy toward its spiritual sense. The nations came into the inheritance of the Jews, that is, into the knowledge of God, for this was the ancient portion of the Jews. That is why Moses says to them in Deuteronomy, "But the Lord your God chose you out of all the nations under heaven." When the nations came into it, they defiled the holy temple that the Jews had possessed in ancient Jerusalem. They did not cause the defilement themselves. Rather, they uncovered the hidden defilement of the temple, the impiety that those who ministered in it committed in various ways. In the same way, a priest who examines a doubtful case of leprosy and, after diagnosing it, confirms the disease is said to defile the sufferer. He does not bring defilement on him, for that would be foreign to a priest. He makes plain the defilement that is already there. This is what happened to the Jews at the hands of the nations. The justification of the nations exposed the Jews as profane, and the obedience of the new people made the disobedience of the old people more evident. "[They have made] Jerusalem into a hut for guarding fruit." Why "a hut for guarding fruit"? Because the nations took the spirit of the law and the prophets and left the Jews only the fruit of the letter to guard. This came about not from men but from God, who willed that the proofs of our faith be preserved among our enemies. The letter is fittingly called "fruit" because it provides food that is not substantial but short-lived. "They have given the corpses of your servants as food for the birds of the sky, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth." The divinely inspired Scripture often takes the birds of the sky in a bad sense. Pharaoh's chief baker shows this. In a dream he saw the birds of the sky eating from the baskets of cakes he was carrying on his head, and the dream was interpreted to mean that his head would be taken off. To these birds the Church gave the corpses of the Jews to devour, and also the flesh of the holy ones to the beasts of the earth. These beasts too are evil powers, as Isaiah has plainly explained to us. Speaking of Babylon he says, "Wild beasts will rest there," and he adds what these are: "And sirens will rest there, and demons will dance there." It is not surprising that they are called servants. The wicked and lazy servant who hid the talent was said to bear their image. If they had been good, they would not have had corpses, that is, foul thoughts and evil deeds. And if he also called them holy ones, he means holy not in conduct but in calling. In the same way he often calls false prophets prophets, even though they do not prophesy in the name of God, and calls those anointed with sanctification holy, even if they do not keep their sanctification. That is why, when Ezekiel saw the vision of those who were destroying Jerusalem, he heard God speak to him in these words: "Do not pity old man, young man or virgin; kill infants and women to utter destruction; but do not come near anyone who has the mark; and begin from my holy ones." They were holy in appearance only, not in reality. Otherwise they would have had the mark and would not have been slain along with the others. So here too he calls them holy in name only.
