For this reason he pictured the spiritual beasts eating their flesh, that is, their earthly deeds. Those whose minds are set on earthly things are called flesh, as God made clear when he was about to bring the flood: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." "They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them."

2. "Their blood" means the sins of the soul, which are avenged by blood. These were poured out like water, so that they could never be gathered up again, just as water cannot be gathered after it is poured out. So the woman of Tekoa said to David, "We shall surely die, and are like water spilled on the ground, which will not be gathered up." Where did they pour it out? "Around Jerusalem," that is, upon the city and upon those who came from it [?]. For "their blood" was upon them and upon their children, as they themselves said when they slandered Christ. "And there was no one to bury them." Why? Because they themselves, being dead, could not bury one another, and the Church is not permitted to bury them, that is, to cover over their sins. What prevents it? God's decree, which says, "Leave the dead to their own." Why? Because those who try to cover up for sinners leave their own deeds more exposed and make them a reproach before everyone. "We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us." Poverty, ugliness, sickness and every other such thing bring less reproach on those who have them than sin does, because sin is a voluntary affliction and a wound inflicted by choice. But notice the prophet's wisdom. He says that the punishments fell on others, namely on those who had sinned, yet he shows that he himself shares in the reproaches heaped on them. Whether he was a prophet over people who disobeyed his prophecy, or a priest over people he had consecrated and initiated who then broke the law and were punished for it, he is ashamed. But to whom are the Jews a reproach as to their neighbors, and a derision and mockery as to those around them? Clearly he means the demons. Because of their wickedness the demons are neighbors of the Jews, and they are all around them, lying in wait for them every day. "How long, Lord? Will you be angry to the end? Will your jealousy burn like fire?" Moses the lawgiver also described this jealousy of God toward the Jews when he said, "They made me jealous with what is no god; they provoked me with their idols. And I will make them jealous with what is no nation; with a foolish nation I will provoke them." Then he added, "A fire has been kindled from my wrath." God's jealousy toward the Jews brought about the calling of the gentiles. Paul too says, "Just as you once disobeyed God but have now received mercy because of their disobedience," and again, "Their trespass," meaning that of the Jews, "is riches for the world, and their failure is riches for the gentiles." So the prophet must ask how long God will remain angry with the Jews, and whether he will stay angry to the end. Through Paul the Spirit answers him: "When the fullness of the gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved." "Pour out your wrath on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that have not called on your name. For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place." So he does not speak of all the nations. That is why he qualified the word, saying not simply "nations" but "those that do not know you." But we do know him, and the name of God has been called upon us. Nor have we devoured Jacob, for we do not blaspheme or revile him. Paul showed that this is what devouring means: "But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another." Nor do we lay waste his place. How could we, when each of us claims it as our common homeland in place of our own? So the prophet did not curse us. He cursed those who remained in ignorance and refused to take on the name of God's kingdom, and they had better beware of the curse. "Do not remember our former iniquities." How could we bear both old evils and new ones? Perhaps by former iniquities the prophet means those committed in the wilderness, since God made many threats of various kinds because of them. That is why he dreads having them remembered. "Let your compassion come quickly to meet us, Lord, for we have become very poor." Nothing shows a person to be as poor as sin does, and he becomes poorer still when impiety is added to sin. That is why he pleaded for God's compassion to come quickly to them, so that they would not fall into despair through their deeper poverty and perish. "Help us, O God our Savior; for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us." The prophet rightly took refuge in God's glory, since he could not put forward any righteous deeds of the people. The glory of God's name is to have compassion on sinners, since he is called compassionate, merciful and patient. Moses says, "And he called on the name of the Lord, and passed before his face and called out: The Lord, the Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient, abounding in mercy and true."

3. You see that these pleas are addressed to Christ. He is called not only God but expressly Savior as well. He is also the glory of the name of God, that is, of the Father, and so Paul called him the radiance of the Father's glory. What follows also shows clearly that these words are spoken about the Lord. "And be merciful to our sins for your name's sake, lest the nations say, 'Where is their God?'" Whose task is it to make atonement for sins for the sake of his own name, if not Christ's, who for this very reason bears the title of propitiation? He provided atonement for the sins of the Jews when, as he was being crucified, he said to the Father, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." That is why Paul too says of him: "whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness, because he had passed over the sins committed before." He is merciful to the sins of the Jews not only for their own sake, but much more for the sake of the nations. Otherwise the nations might not know of God's love for humanity, say "Where is their God?" and stumble in their ignorance. Instead, recognizing that love, they may be led by the hand by it and urged to run to him with all eagerness and be saved. What follows will prove to you what has been said. "And before our eyes let the vengeance for the poured-out blood of your servants be made known among the nations." Why does he want the vengeance to be made known to the nations? Because it was to fall on the demons who through idolatry had ruined the blood, that is, the souls, of God's servants, namely the Jews. And what was the vengeance? The overthrow of idols and the burning of the devil's temples. This takes place before the eyes of the Jews, for they see what is done and take no part in it. But it is made known among the nations, for they know by what hand and power these things are accomplished and done, and those who see it ascribe the destruction to the cross of Christ. "Let the groaning of the prisoners come before you." He means those bound not with fetters of iron but with the fetters of sin, for "each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins." He asked that this groaning come before God, so that what follows might be granted them. "According to the greatness of your arm, preserve the sons of those who have been put to death." We have often shown that Christ is called the arm of the Father. "According to his greatness" means the great mysteries of his divine manifestation, which are the cross and the resurrection. The prophet pleads with God to preserve not those who have been put to death but their sons. Those put to death were the ones who did not believe in this present life. Their sons, however, were caught in the apostles' net and grew to many tens of thousands. "Pay back sevenfold into the bosom of our neighbors the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord." Here too he does not call human beings neighbors. He would not have prayed for sevenfold punishment to fall on them, knowing that the Judge does not allow this. Otherwise, how could he sing to him, "For you will repay each according to his works"? So he is speaking of demons. They justly receive sevenfold, for their nature is higher than ours. Even after being cast out of heaven they did not truly come to their senses. Instead they trouble the earth with their schemes. They not only sin themselves but also urge us to sin, and on top of this they reproach God over his image, which had fallen. And even at the divine manifestation of Christ they did not give up idolatry but kept pressing on with it. What is their bosom? Gehenna. That place was allotted to them from the beginning, as the Lord shows: "Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." "But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture." He means all humanity. He sets us against the demons who were hurled down from above, and so he calls humankind the people of God and the sheep of his pasture. And why the sheep of his pasture? Because we the faithful feed on him when we partake of the mysteries. "We will acknowledge you in return, O God, forever; from generation to generation we will proclaim your praise." "Acknowledge in return" is said as though an earlier acknowledgment had already been made. Christ went before us and acknowledged us as sheep when he said, "My sheep hear my voice." Then, wishing to include the gentiles as well, he added, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also." We acknowledge him in return, and in the next psalm we too call him shepherd. We do this not for a season but forever, that is, continually. And from generation to generation we will proclaim his praise, offering praise and thanksgiving in all his generations. Or else it means that we praise him from both generations: not only from those still in the flesh but also from those who have already departed from the flesh, since we call patriarchs, apostles, prophets and martyrs into our midst when we pray to him.

1. By "those who will be changed" he means those who are renewed through repentance. He had good reason to add "For the end," since repentance is our last anchor, and moreover it was proclaimed at the very end of the ages through the coming of Christ. Asaph sang the present psalm as a testimony for these people, and in it he recounts what the Jewish people suffered because of their many sins. "You who shepherd Israel, give heed; you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who are seated upon the cherubim, appear." You see how well these words agree with the Lord's words recorded in the Gospels: "I am the good shepherd." But why did he pass over the others and bring forward Joseph and Jacob? Because each of them went down into a foreign land, Joseph to Egypt and Jacob to Mesopotamia, and served there as a slave. But God changed their slavery into freedom and into the good things that came with it. This is the God whom the prophet now begs to give heed. The prophet's hope was that God would see our whole race enslaved to spiritual enemies and hasten to set us free by coming to dwell in the flesh the sooner. (For the prophet did not ask God to give heed to himself in particular. He asked without limit, that is, for everyone.) We need God's coming in order to be free, and human beings could not receive the One seated upon the cherubim when he appeared in any way other than through the flesh. "Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might, and come to save us." He clearly asked for the coming of the Only-begotten in the flesh. That is why he begs him not only to come but also to stir up his might. By "might" he means the incarnation, for he called it this in another passage of the Psalms as well: "The Lord has clothed himself with might and girded himself." Christ was mighty before as well, though hidden from men, yet when he came to dwell in the flesh he revealed his power to the whole earth. Why, then, does the prophet say that this might is stirred up before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh? He names the part to mean the whole of Israel, to whom Christ came from heaven when he became flesh. That is why he says, "stir up your might before them." Or else it is because they set themselves against him and so found him to be just as they had approached him. "O God, turn us back, and show your face, and we shall be saved." As he goes on, the prophet makes his meaning clearer, showing both how Christ was to come and why. The reason for his coming was to turn us back and set us right. The manner of it was a clear manifestation, so that we might see him face to face. We would not have been saved in any other way unless he had appeared to us like this. So Jacob the patriarch said, "For I have seen God face to face, and my soul has lived." That is why Moses too asked to see him in this way. He did not ask out of idle curiosity. As a prophet he knew that salvation for humankind lay in this. He did not ask to behold the naked Godhead, for no one, as God himself says, will be able to look upon that face of his. "Lord God of powers, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servants?" He did not choose these words idly. With them he declared God's dignity and at the same time pleaded for him to come. That is why he called him not only God but also Lord of the powers, namely those in heaven. Perceiving through the Spirit that the mystery of Christ was postponed for the time being, he called this postponement anger, since his prayer was not yet being fulfilled. He asks how long the anger will last, and in keeping with this he added what follows: "You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in measure." "How long" applies to this verse as well. Until then the prophets received tears as their bread and their drink while they mourned for humanity, until Christ came to dwell among us and himself became the bread and the cup of life. He rightly added "in measure," to show that nothing with God is without measure. Everything, whether wrath or discipline, is brought upon human beings by rule and measure for their good. "You have made us an object of contention to our neighbors, and our enemies have sneered at us." Here too the text clearly hints at the same enemies and neighbors [?]. For as long as Christ postponed his coming, they held [?] men in sneering and mockery, and above all the prophets themselves, as though the prophets were not telling the truth in what they foretold about the Savior's arrival. Indeed, the prophets endured no ordinary contention from them, since the demons worked through the false prophets and uttered contrary things. So he rightly assigned "contention" to the demons, the spiritual enemies and neighbors. He shows clearly that the demons are subject to the prophets as servants are subject to their masters, yet they often grow puffed up with arrogance and talk back. "Lord God of powers, turn us back, and show your face, and we shall be saved." He holds to the same plea to show how necessary it is. At the same time he teaches us not to lose heart when a prayer is not granted, but to persevere, for we will certainly obtain what we ask. "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it."

2. Here his narrative shows how much God cared about the salvation of the Jewish people. A farmer who wants to make a vine nobler and more fruitful will move it once, and then a second time, for that purpose. In the same way God brought Israel through Abraham from the land of the Chaldeans into the land of the Canaanites. From there he brought them down through Jacob into Egypt. Finally he brought them up into the land promised from the beginning, as into a rich field. He did not simply plant it but planted it firmly, that is, he rooted it deep, so that they would never have to be moved again. But he did not do this until he had cast out the nations living there, like thorns. Because of this it flourished greatly, as what follows shows. "You cleared a way before it." How? By giving the law and by destroying the nations. "And you planted its roots, and it filled the land." The root of the Jewish vine was Moses, Joshua, Phinehas and Eleazar. These filled the land with their piety, for their virtues spread everywhere. "Its shadow covered the mountains, and its tendrils covered the cedars of God." The mountains are the righteous of God, because their way of life is lofty and exalted. The same people are also the cedars: "The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will grow like a cedar in Lebanon." These were covered by the shadow of the Jewish vine, namely the law, as Paul says: "The law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities." By tendrils you should understand the words of the prophets. Raised up by the virtues of those who practise them, as a vine is raised by the trees that support it, they display their proper fruit. These, then, covered the righteous. They did not cover them to hide them, but to keep off the frost of unbelief, or the scorching heat of any other sin whatever. "It stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the rivers." By the sea he means baptism, and by the rivers the partial purifications. The branches, from which the clusters grow, are all those whom the Jewish people had who were illustrious in their way of life. These stretched not into the sea but as far as the sea, because their virtues had brought them close to the grace of baptism. But the shoots were not branches. They imitated branches and put on a show of the righteousness of the law. These stretched as far as the rivers, the partial purifications. They were not cleansed by them but only seemed to be cleansed. "Why have you broken down its hedge, so that all who pass by along the way pluck its grapes?" The hedge of the Jewish vine is the law. If you do not believe this, listen to Isaiah: "My beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a fertile place." And again: "I put a hedge around it" (he means the law) "and fenced it with stakes" (that is, with the commandments) "and planted a choice vine, and built a tower in the middle of it" (Jerusalem) "and dug a wine vat in it" (the temple). Then he adds: "What shall I do to the vineyard? I will take away its hedge, and it will be plundered." He broke down this hedge when they sinned against Christ, who had fenced them in with the law. And they are harvested by those who pass by along the way, that is, by those who transgress the law and do not walk the royal road. Such are the present children of the Jews, who transgress while within the law. So they are said not to walk the way but to pass by along it. In the same way Wisdom in Proverbs speaks of the young man deceived by the wicked woman, "lacking sense," as "passing by in the marketplace near the corner," not as walking. "The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has fed on it." The devil is called a lion for his rapacity and a dragon for the venom of his wickedness, along with other such names given in the divinely inspired Scriptures. He is also called a boar, because he delights in the mire of wickedness and lodges in its fruitless forest. He is called solitary because he alone vaunted himself against God, and wild because he is savage and untamed. He has been ravaging the synagogue of the Jews ever since its hedge was broken down, that is, ever since Christ brought the way of life under the law to an end. For they belong to the enemy's portion, since they have neither the law, nor an altar, nor anything else that belongs to the worship of God. "O God of hosts, turn now, and look down from heaven, and see." Since neither the law nor the prophets turned Israel back, he has no choice but to call on God to turn, that is, to set things right. And how is he to turn? By looking down from heaven and seeing. When does he not see? But now he asks him to look with greater compassion, so that he may do something more for our benefit than before. What that is, the following words show. "And visit this vine. And restore what your right hand planted, and upon the Son of man whom you made strong for yourself." You see that he asked God to take on the role not only of a farmer but also of a physician. Visiting belongs to the physician, who makes the visit in person.

3. So he wants God to come and live among them as a physician, and as a farmer to restore the vine, destroying the spiritual worm and cutting away the useless branches that would keep it from bearing fruit. And for whose sake? Not for the vine's own sake, he says, since God had broken down its hedge and handed it over to the enemy, but for the sake of the Lord's branch that was to spring from it. So after saying, "Visit this vine," he added, "and upon the Son of man whom you made strong for yourself." That is: visit it for the sake of the Son who comes from the Jewish vine, "whom you made strong for yourself." And the coming of the Only-begotten truly was a visitation of the Jewish people, if only they had accepted it. That is why John said, "He came to his own, and his own did not know him." The Lord himself said, "I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." "Burned with fire and dug up; at the rebuke of your face they will perish." Since he has compared the synagogue of the Jews to a vineyard, he naturally divides his words, sometimes speaking of the image and sometimes of the people for whom he took up the image. So the vine of the Jews, that is, the synagogue, was burned with fire: the fire of which Christ said, "I came to cast fire on the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled?" The fire was cast, and the vine was dug up, so that once it had been dug up, the foundation hidden in it might be laid bare. Of this foundation Isaiah said, "Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, a cornerstone, honoured, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." David too said, "Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem," meaning the nations who said, "Empty it out, down to its foundations." For the nations dig out what the Jews have to this extent: they search it carefully and feel it over until they lay bare the foundation that the Jews keep hidden. Therefore "at the rebuke of the face of God" (by which you should understand Christ) "they will perish." For he rebuked them because they held the keys of knowledge yet neither entered themselves nor let in those who wanted to enter. "Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of man whom you made strong for yourself. And we will not turn away from you." By the man of the right hand he means Christ. He is called a man because of his humanity. He is of God's right hand, first because he sits with his flesh at the Father's right hand, and then because he established all creation. In the same way he calls him Son of man because of the flesh. But so that you may reckon him wholly consubstantial with the Father because of his Godhead, he says, "whom you made strong for yourself." The Father made him strong because he himself begot him. He made him strong for himself because he begot him equal in power and identical in every respect. He prays that the Father's hand may be upon them, that is, that signs and wonders may come forth upon us through him. These are sometimes called the hand of God and sometimes his finger. He no longer asks that the signs among us be done through a prophet or some God-bearing man, as through Moses or Elijah and the prophets, but through the Son. And he promises that if this happens, we will not turn away from him, for we have often turned away. "You will give us life, and we will call upon your name." You will give us life through the living water of baptism. For that is when we call upon his name, being called Christians after Christ. "Lord God of hosts, turn us back, and show your face, and we shall be saved." He repeats this continually. This is not the only place where the prophet makes this plea. He shows that we cannot be turned back or saved in any other way than through the appearing of the face of God, that is, of the Word made flesh.

1. Why did the prophet give the present psalm the title "For the winepresses"? Here he does not mention a winepress, or a vintage, or the firstfruits of the field at all. Instead he puts forward Joseph, who became an image and testimony of Christ. Christ trod the winepress of the sufferings on our behalf, as he himself taught through the prophecy of Isaiah: "I trod the winepress alone." Why does he call the sufferings a winepress? Because we drink the blood that flowed from them like new wine, and rejoice. "Rejoice in God our helper; shout aloud to the God of Jacob." He rightly wants us to rejoice in God, as a helper who is both powerful and true, and not in any man. In human beings neither power nor faithfulness holds firm, since their judgment and their strength are both unsteady. He also told us to shout for joy as people who have already won the victory through God's help. Which God? The God of Jacob, he says. He says nothing of Abraham and leaves out Isaac, and mentions Jacob alone as suited to his present subject. By mentioning a shout of triumph he hinted at a victory, of which shouting is the symbol. This victory came to us when Christ tripped the enemy by the heel. So he rightly brought in the God of Jacob, since the name Jacob means "one who trips by the heel." "Take up a psalm, and bring the drum, the pleasant psaltery with the lyre." The drum is a symbol of the Old Covenant, because its sound booms at random and has no clear meaning, and also because Miriam, the sister of Moses, danced with a drum before the Jewish people. The psalm-singing represents the New, for those who sing psalms utter clear, distinct and fully articulate words, just as the gospel does. He addresses these words to the Jewish people, teaching them what they ought to rejoice and shout over, and what exchange they should make with the Church of the Gentiles. So he plainly urges them to take the new things and give the old in return, since the two become more useful when combined. The one who has the truth is filled still further by receiving the image. The one who has the image gains a great deal by receiving the truth, for the sake of which he holds the image. That is why he says, "the pleasant psaltery with the lyre," meaning the new with the old. As Solomon also says in the Song: "New things with old, all that my mother gave me, my brother, I have kept for you." Why did he compare these to the psaltery and the lyre? Because the two instruments are related, but their strings are fastened differently, one from above and the other from below. In the same way the Old and the New are related, for both look to one goal, piety. But the commandments of the one are low, because what it legislates is humble. The commandments of the other are lofty and on high, because what Christ taught is so very lofty and exalted. "Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the well-marked day of your feast." The law clearly prescribes blowing the trumpet at the new moon, though not every month. That is why David mentioned a well-marked day: he wanted to refer the saying to the first day of the seventh month. This day was well-marked, that is, distinguished by the law, which says: "In the seventh month, on the first of the month, you shall have a rest, a memorial of trumpets." This is why the psalmist now added, "For it is an ordinance for Israel, and a judgment of the God of Jacob." He shows that he is not introducing anything new but is following an ancient piece of legislation. But he has mentioned it here for another reason [?]. By the new moon he surely means the time of the Saviour's coming: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new," as Paul says. By the trumpet he means the word of the gospel, and by the well-marked day the Lord's Pascha. That is why Aquila rendered it "full moon" and Symmachus "the monthly feast," both meaning the fifteenth day of the month. The law did not permit blowing the trumpet on that day, so he must be hinting at the day on which Christ suffers for us. He was handed over on the fourteenth, at the time of the Passover that was the type, and endured the cross on the next day, the fifteenth. He calls that day both new moon and full moon, since it is at once the beginning and the fullness of the time in which our salvation comes about. On that day he commands them to blow the trumpet, that is, to preach the gospel. He says this is an ordinance for Israel, and not simply an ordinance but a judgment of the God of Jacob. For the God of Jacob began his work from the cross and vindicated the preaching of the gospel. That is why he said to the apostles, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all to myself." That he gave Christ the name "God of Jacob" you can learn from what follows. "He set him as a testimony in Joseph, when he went out of the land of Egypt." Whom did he set? The God of Jacob, of whom he spoke earlier. And how is he "a testimony, when he went out of the land of Egypt"? Joseph was an image of Christ because of his brothers' envy, the sale, the slavery he suffered though free, the obeisance of the stars, and other such things that can be gathered from his story. So the psalmist wanted to show in deed that Joseph was Christ's testimony and monument, and that plots followed upon plots for Christ just as they did for Joseph. When Herod, who had tried to kill him, died, Christ came back from Egypt and hid in Galilee for fear of Archelaus, since Archelaus too would plot against him after Herod.

2. "He heard a tongue that he did not know." Which tongue? That of the slanderers, you will say. He did not know it, not because he was ignorant of it, but because he did not lend his ears to falsehood, for such a thing is foreign to God. Yet since he had become man, he was compelled to hear the slanderers when he was put on trial. This too was a testimony in Joseph, since he too heard the Egyptian woman say, "Lie with me." Yet he did not know the tongue of the woman speaking, for he did not consent. "He removed his back from burdens." He did not, he says, carry sin on his back. By burdens he means the loads of sins, whose weight David hinted at when he said, "Like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me." But Joseph kept himself from adultery, while Christ kept himself from sin altogether. "His hands served in the basket." Christ served in the present life, which is rightly called a basket, since in it we heap up all our good and evil deeds as in a basket and carry them on our shoulders when we journey from here. See, then, how exact the prophecy is, and marvel at how it says of the new Joseph, Christ, "He removed his back from burdens," since he carried no sin of his own, and yet his hands served in the basket of the present life. For he served by carrying the basket of our sins. In this psalm, however, the prophet has shifted a great deal from one person to another. Above, he addresses people who have won a victory and therefore have occasion for a feast. From there he passed to Joseph and turned his words to the image of Christ. Now he plainly addresses the people of Israel, saying: "In affliction you called on me, and I delivered you." Where and when? Surely when he said to Moses: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. For I know their pain, and I have come down to deliver them." "I heard you in the secret place of the storm." He heard them when he came down on Mount Sinai and a dark cloud covered the mountain (such a cloud is called a storm). What were they saying? "The words that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will listen." But a little later he caught them lying, as what follows clearly shows. "I tested you at the water of contradiction." There, on their journey, they reviled God. They had enjoyed many signs before, but they forgot them all and said to Moses, "Would that we had died in the destruction of our fathers before the Lord," and everything else in that passage that reveals the blasphemy of the Jews. After these verses the psalmist added a pause. He did not do this casually or for nothing. Perhaps it was to rest the prophecy for a while, but the truer reason is that he was now clearly bringing in the person of Christ. "Hear, my people, and I will testify to you." If you want to be called God's people, hear his commandment, so that you may gain this great dignity. But it is worth seeing what he testifies, and what kind of things. "Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." He set down "if you hear me" for this reason: to show that he foresaw their drunken insolence, yet did not on that account take away their ability to change. They could have changed if they had wanted to. God's foreknowledge does no harm to repentance, since he also foreknows that even sinners may change if they wish. Yet the prophet is hinting at something new and mysterious, or rather God is, through the prophet. What does he testify to the Jewish people? That if they hear him... Him, meaning whom? The one of whom Joseph was a testimony, whose hands served in the basket. Then there will be no new god among them, and they will not worship a foreign god. For Christ was not a new god, nor a foreign one. He was the one who brought them up out of the land of Egypt. He was there from the beginning, and he is there afterward as well, as he made clear through the prophecy of Isaiah, where he says, "I am God, the first, and there is no other besides me." And beyond all dispute, the one who took flesh to save our race is called Saviour. "Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." Why does he not say the ears, or the heart, but the mouth? Because the Word who came down from heaven was called the bread of life. Anyone who received him, opening wide his mouth through good will, was filled with the knowledge of God. "But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me." They could not bear to listen to him when he taught or preached the gospel, and they refused to pay heed to him when he worked wonders. They made their ears heavy so as not to hear the Lord's commandments. "They shut their eyes," as Isaiah said, so as not to see the signs. What did they suffer in return for this? "So I sent them away according to the devices of their hearts; they shall walk in their own devices." By the devices of their hearts he means the various notions and the schemes of thought the Jewish people used in plotting against the Lord, when they said: "What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." So according to this device and this counsel they were sent away and went off. For the Romans took both their city and their place, and they themselves went away as captives. "If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies in no time, and laid my hand on those who afflict them." He laments over the Jewish people because they did not listen to God when he gave them the law, and did not walk in his ways, which never lead astray and which save. Nor did they allow their enemies, the demons, to be humbled, or the hand of God to be laid on those who afflicted them. God did lay his right hand on the invisible afflicters and humbled the unseen enemies, but not for the sake of the Jews, for over them the horn of the demons is still raised high. It was for the sake of us Gentiles that the demons were humbled, for we have renounced our slavery to them and destroyed their worship. Therefore God, angry with the Jews, declares them his enemies, as what follows shows: "The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time will be forever." Who are the enemies? Those of whom Paul said: "the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction." For this reason he threatened that their time, that is, the time of the punishment against them, would last into the age to come. And how did they lie to him? He came to them as to his own, but his own, as John says, did not receive him. "He fed them with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the rock he satisfied them." He reproaches them for what they received and yet remained ungrateful, hinting at spiritual things through things of the senses. He calls the law the fat of wheat because of the spirit that dwells in the letter. That is why he says in another psalm: "He who makes your borders peace, and fills you with the fat of wheat." What this means he showed by the words that follow: "He who sends forth his word to the earth." By honey from the rock he means the prophets, since they have their prophecy from Christ, who is called the rock. God satisfied them with this prophecy, granting them not one prophet, or two, but many, over many generations.

The title of the psalm is short, and so is its subject: an exhortation to justice, and a reproach because people do not hold to it. "God has taken his stand in the congregation of gods, and in their midst he judges between gods." This too is great proof of God's generosity toward us: the Maker shared his own name with what he had fashioned. He himself is called God in the highest sense, yet by grace he has allowed certain people to bear that name too. These are all who hold the dignity of rule in imitation of God, the ruler of all, and who keep it. That is why here he calls those who are preeminent among the people "gods." Moses also spoke of them: "You shall not revile gods, nor speak evil of a ruler of your people." Some of these are true to their office and do not make it a pretense, and they keep the dignity of prophecy, or priesthood, or military command. God honors them so highly that he takes his stand in their congregation, as the psalmist says. Others act unworthily of the honor given them, and these he judges in the midst. That is, before all creation he strips them of their rank and outward show and makes an example of them, because they were appointed to rule but were instead ruled by wickedness. The prophet rebukes these people and exhorts them at the same time in the words that follow: "How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners?" He rightly puts "How long" first. It shows that they persist in injustice and do not notice God's patience. They do not understand at all that time is running out and hurrying past, and that after it judgment comes upon the unjust. So they judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners. Yet they ought to uphold the cause of God, who wants justice established everywhere and for this reason brings his own person into every judgment. Hence Moses says: "You shall not show favor to persons in judgment, for the judgment is the Lord's." But why does he say, "You show favor to the persons of sinners"? Because anyone who works to corrupt justice and to bend judgment so as to get the better of his neighbor is truly a sinner, even if he wears the guise of a just man. He adds "Pause" because he has turned the reproach into counsel. "Judge for the orphan and the poor; do justice to the lowly and the needy." He does not say, "Judge for the righteous," nor for a prophet, nor for a priest, though God gives a strong charge about these: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." Instead he says, "for the orphan and the poor and the lowly and the needy." Why? Because it is fitting for the former to suffer wrong, as Paul also said: "Why not rather be defrauded?" But it is unbearable for these to be wronged, because of the weakness that comes upon them from their age or their poverty. That is why the lawgiver defends them more vigorously. "Rescue the needy and the poor; deliver him from the hand of the sinner." He speaks of those who delight in injustice or greed as if they were wild beasts. So elsewhere he says: "He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor." Whoever saves the poor, then, carries off the rank and the reward of a shepherd: the reward, that is, of the one who gave himself for us and rescued us from spiritual beasts. But whoever seizes or ravages the poor is counted among the beasts. Wanting to strengthen our protection of those who are wronged, he adds, "deliver from the hand of the sinner." This is so that we may hurry to their defense, seeing that the wrongdoer is both weak and without compassion. The sinner is weak because he has offended God. He is without compassion because he does not spare even himself; otherwise he would not have sinned. So he spares his neighbor much less. "They have not known nor understood; they walk about in darkness." What have they not known? The rottenness of the present life and the instability of human existence. They join field to field and house to house, often storing these things up for their enemies. And what have they not understood? That by busying themselves with small things they deprive themselves of the greater. So they walk about in the darkness of wickedness, ashamed to come to the light, "for everyone who does evil hates the light," as Paul said. Perhaps he also reproaches them for this: that, walking in darkness, they have neither known nor understood what comes next. What is that? Listen: "Let all the foundations of the earth be shaken." If the foundations of the earth are shaken, how will the things on it be able to remain? And with things as they are, why do we get the better of our brother and devour the poor, when we gain no benefit from it? "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. But you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." When did he decree that all were gods and sons of the Most High? For he is no longer speaking only about rulers, but about all humanity. Surely it was when he fashioned man and set out for him such a definition of his dignity: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness; and let them rule over all the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the cattle, and all the earth, and all the creeping things." If they had kept this and remained in it, and had not betrayed God's image by disobedience, they would not have been condemned to death. For it is an outrage against God to disregard the honor he gives and to suffer the same fate as the devil. So he says, "You die like men," to show that death is a human affliction. Yet we could have avoided death if we had kept God's law from the beginning, for our nature was capable of either. "And you fall like one of the rulers," he says, hinting at the devil, who had been allotted a ruler's authority among the angels. That is why Paul says: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers." But he grew proud and desired greater things, and he fell. Man did the same. He heard the serpent say, "God knew that on the day you eat of it" (that is, of the tree) "your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil," and he gave himself over to disobedience. So he is necessarily compared with the devil because of his passion and his fall. "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations." The prophet hints, then, not at a present inheritance but at a future one. That is why he calls on God to arise and judge the earth, meaning humankind. When God arises, he assigns inheritances among all the nations. To all he gives the lot that suits them: one to the humble, another to the temperate, another to the merciful, another to fornicators, another to the proud, yet another to the greedy. For here he uses "nations" for differences not of language but of ways of life.

1. He rightly called the present composition both "song" and "psalm," since he blended a victory song over certain enemies with the prophecy, which he mostly calls a psalm. "O God, who shall be likened to you?" The prophet does not write this as a question, since that would be a foolish question. He writes it to extol God's boundless greatness and the fact that nothing in anything compares with him. No one will boast of being like God in any respect, for God is the cause of all that exists. But we should notice the exact wording. He did not say, "Who has been likened to you?" but "Who shall be likened to you?" and so he pointed to a future time. He is therefore hinting at the dispensation of the Only-begotten in the flesh, when Christ would have a reputation like that of certain prophets. That is why some thought he was Elijah, and others one of the prophets. But none of those named could be likened to him, for he alone was God and man, and he alone saved our race. "Do not keep silent, nor be still, O God"; that is, do not be patient much longer. By "silence" he means God's patience with sinners for a time. Why did he pray this? "For behold, your enemies have made an uproar, and those who hate you have lifted up their head." Sinners, he says, have grown so proud because of your patience that they have made an uproar, that is, spoken out boldly. Their shamelessness has made their wickedness as plain as a trumpet blast. They have lifted up their head, unashamed of their offenses and even boasting, as though there were no one they ought to fear. He calls sinners enemies of God because they are enemies of themselves, doing what harms them. God loves humankind and does not desire the death of the sinner, and so he counts as his enemies those who plot against themselves. "Against your people they have craftily devised a plan, and they have taken counsel against your holy ones." Here the prophet sets out another kind of enmity toward God. Those who are hostile to God's people and his saints are waging war against God himself, since these are his servants and brothers. He refers not only to the war described next, where he also names the nations that fought against the Jews. He also hints at a hidden war that sinners habitually wage against the saints. For this reason he does not simply say that they were crafty, but that they "craftily devised against" them, that is, used a varied and many-sided craftiness. Such are those who first deprive people dedicated to God of money or property or something else, in order to provoke them to ingratitude and blasphemy. When they fail at this, they put pleasures in their way: the desire for empty glory, arrogance, vain imaginings. They give an enemy's advice in the guise of friends. What follows makes this clear. "They said, Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more." Clearly these things were said and done by the enemies of Israel, whom he is about to name. But understand this also of those who counsel or compel us to evil. They want to destroy us from being a nation, so that we are counted neither with the lawless, since we sin while having a law, nor with the law-abiding, since we transgress it. They want the name of Israel handed over to oblivion. For Israel means "the one who sees God." If someone does not do what befits one who sees God and keeps the eyes of his mind fixed on him, such a person must be handed over to complete oblivion. Because of his later heedlessness, no one can even recall whether he was ever Israel, one who sees [?] spiritually, that is, whether he ever knew God at all. "For they have taken counsel together with one accord; against you they have made a covenant." Who could take counsel, or make a covenant, or even form any idea at all against God, who is beyond the reach not only of sight but even of reasoning? But God counts as his own the affairs of those who trust in him. For this reason plots against them are said to be against God himself, as the father, protector and guardian of those plotted against. And who are those devising the plots? "The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek." All of these are descended from Abraham, and so they were kin to Israel. The Ishmaelites had as their father Ishmael, the son of Abraham. The Hagrites were not descended from Abraham but from Hagar. Sarah had given her to Abraham for a time, but later grew jealous and had her driven out with Ishmael. Hagar then joined herself to another man and gave her name to her descendants, the Hagrites. Likewise Amalek was a grandson of Esau. Moab and Ammon were sons born to Lot by his daughters after the burning of Sodom. Gebal bordered on them and was perhaps also related to them, which is why it is counted among them. What, then, was the passage trying to show here? Why did it show that they were kin? So that you may know that, among one's enemies, "those of one's own household," as Christ says, that is, kinsmen, take first place. So the prophet put foreigners in a lower place, and went on: "Foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre. For Assyria also came with them." Assyria came not with the inhabitants of Tyre but with Moab and Ammon and the others, whom we have shown to be related to the Jewish people. So these foreigners did not come to that war of their own accord; their kinsmen stirred them up. That is why he added: "They became a help to the sons of Lot"; that is, they came to their aid. Beware, then, of enemies within, for they are the ones who arm those outside. And do not put your trust in kinship, since very often it turns into enmity. Consider also the curse he called down on them. "Pause": because he turned his words to prayer. "Do to them as to Midian and to Sisera, as to Jabin at the brook Kishon. They were destroyed at Endor."

2. He chose these out of all others for good reason: the war against them was turned in a wonderful way. Midian covered the land with its multitude, but Gideon came against it without weapons and overthrew and destroyed it with three hundred men. They had no swords, no shields, no helmets, nor any other instruments of war, but only torches and horn trumpets, which they used. Sisera was commander of Jabin's people and went to war with nine hundred iron chariots. God terrified him, put him to flight, and handed him over to the wife of Heber the Kenite, who killed him by driving a peg through his jaw. So he prays that the enemies he listed earlier may fall by the hand of God as these did. He mentions the brook Kishon and Endor because the battle against Sisera was fought there. "They became like dung for the earth." Their defeat brought the insolence of their arrogance down so low that they were held as cheap as dung. Dung is well said. Dung is cheap, yet it prepares the earth to bear fruit. In the same way the fall and humiliation of the proud makes our souls fertile in virtues. "Make their rulers like Oreb and Zeeb and Zebah and Zalmunna." He names men who were killed by Gideon, and asks that the rulers become like them. What follows shows more clearly which rulers he means: "All their rulers, who said, Let us take the sanctuary of God as our inheritance." He calls them rulers, then, not so much for their rank as for their wickedness. That is why they imagine that God's sanctuary will become their inheritance, so that they can use holy things for their wealth and divine things for their private gain. It is not only those who seize the sacred vessels and sell off holy things who do this. So do all who trade in divine things, selling and buying what belongs to God and striking unlawful bargains. Simon was such a man: he wanted to acquire the gifts with silver, and so Peter judged him unworthy of the gift of the Holy Spirit. "My God, make them like a wheel": tossed about in unsteady motion and constant change, for this is what a wheel does. "Like stubble before the wind": so that they may stand firm nowhere, but their substance may vanish everywhere, scattered by the force of the blast. "Like fire that burns up a forest, like a flame that consumes mountains." He prays that they may be fruitless on every side. Fire is useful when it smelts gold or silver, or bakes bread, or warms a medicine, or cooks something we need. But the fire that sets a forest ablaze or burns a mountain yields no benefit and no use. It blazes more fiercely, but when it is put out it comes to nothing but soot and ash. Such are sinners found to be after God has brought his wrath upon them. "So you will pursue them with your tempest, and in your wrath you will throw them into confusion." By "tempest" he means God's sudden and most violent movement against sinners, which wills that they be pursued and confounded. How this happens has been said in the preceding verses: they are scattered into tiny fragments as stubble is scattered, and they fall into earth and dust, their passing insolence put out like a fire. But he prays this for their benefit, not their harm. For what did he add? "Fill their faces with dishonor, and they will seek your name, O Lord." They neglected their hope in God for the sake of another hope. When they lose that hope, they necessarily suffer shame and dishonor for having trusted in vain things, because they counted fleeting things as lasting. But then they change and seek the name of God, choosing closeness to him above everything. In this present life, however, this does not happen to all sinners. Some remain prosperous to the end, while others lose their prosperity but do not turn to God. Hear what he added about them: "Let them be put to shame and confounded for ever and ever." Clearly he is speaking of the age to come. There sinners are not only put to shame but also confounded, and they perish in their shame, since there they have no time left for repentance. They cannot cover their own shame by repenting. They feel shame not only before the judge, but also before those in relation to whom they are judged: those whom they perhaps wronged and against whom they plotted in vain. They cannot help feeling shame before these, seeing them amid good things and themselves amid evils. Then, therefore, they will know God, though under compulsion, forced by both fear and judgment. But it is right that they will not be able to seek him in order to run to him, as what follows shows: "And let them know that your name is Lord; you alone are Most High over all the earth." By knowledge here he means not an acknowledgment freely chosen but a confession forced by necessity. We see that a sword is sharp, but we truly know it when we feel its edge. We admit that fire is hot, but we declare it far more when we come near it. In the same way, at the time of judgment all unbelievers will acknowledge God and will know that he alone is Most High over all the earth. Some of the ungodly now suppose that he shares his rule with the idols, and because he is patient, they think he cannot do all things or rule over all things. Then they will not say this, for he will no longer deal with them in patience, but in justice.

1. We have already shown that the sons of Korah, like Asaph, were psalm-singers who received from David the prophetic gift for the psalms. We also showed that the mysteries of Christ's sufferings are winepresses, since he fulfilled them by leaping and treading the press, as it were, when he trampled down death. This is why we find that the other translators rendered the title of this psalm "A victory song concerning the winepresses." The Seventy were also right to render it "To the end," since Christ, about whom these things were said, is the end of the law. How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts! The Lord's dwellings are not only the temples, the houses of prayer. They are also all those who, through holiness, invite God to dwell within them. This is all the more true since Christ, who dwells in us, came to live among us out of his love for humankind. This is why John the theologian also wrote: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. These dwellings, then, are dear to God, since he dwells in them. They are dear to us too, since through them we can draw near to God, who is unapproachable. My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord. It faints not from weakness but from intense love, just as ardent lovers faint from [?] when they are separated from them even for a little while. The prophet says that he feels this toward the courts of God, whether the visible courts or the spiritual ones. And he has every reason to. For there the poor man finds comfort, the wronged man patience, and the prosperous man a bridle. There all of us receive everything we need: either remedies for our passions, or what anoints and strengthens us for virtue. My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God. First the heart receives the joy of God, and after that the flesh. For if we dedicate our mind to God, the flesh is trained by it and no longer delights in drunkenness, debauchery and licentiousness. Instead it rejoices in the Living One, and through the life of philosophy it pursues whatever belongs to true life, in hope of the incorruption that will soon come. For the sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest for herself where she will lay her young: your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God. You may understand it this way: just as sparrows find a house and turtledoves a nest, so we have found the altars of God, which give us refuge and shelter. But the truer sense is that he calls the man who lives the monastic philosophy a sparrow, for he has much in common with the sparrow. He has no house on earth, takes no thought for tomorrow, practices no deceit, and eats whatever food comes his way. The turtledove is the continent virgin, because of her purity, her love of solitude and the mournful sound of her voice, which befits a virgin. It is also the widow who leads the life of philosophy and is given to tears. These have found nests and houses for themselves in the altars of God, for they want to dwell there and to nest there. They dwell there for safety. They nest there because the fruit and the children of virgins and of the continent are sanctification and the mortification of the passions, and the altars are both the image of these and the spur to them. Notice this too: he speaks of the Lord of hosts, the Lord who is in heaven, or rather everywhere, and yet he calls him his own King and God. This shows that one may hold as one's own the good that is common to all. That is why the one who can in no way be contained consents to dwell in us. Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever. The house of God is the law. He dwells there as in his own tent, and through it he reveals himself to those who carry out the commandments. Blessed, then, are those who dwell there. They are blessed, first, because they dwell together with God, and second, because they dwell in a place where no treachery can enter, a place that holds exact discernment of things present and clear foreknowledge and contemplation of things to come. This is why those who dwell there will praise God forever and ever. They already take up the life of the angels, who praise the Creator without ceasing, and they join the glorification to come with the glorification of the present. A pause interrupts the prophecy. Until now he had been speaking of those who trust in God greatly, always and without ceasing. Now he shifts his discourse to those who have come to this point and who rise toward those others through God's help and through their own progress. Blessed is the man whose help is from you. Very blessed indeed: even if he has fallen, he stands; even if he is a sinner, he is cleansed; even if he has been despaired of, he will still not see death. But hear who this man is: He has set ascents in his heart. How, and in what way? In the valley of weeping, in the place that he has appointed.

2. So God is not partial. He does not help some and not others, but gives help to all who offer themselves to him. And how do they offer themselves? In the valley of weeping, that is, in the place of repentance. There God appointed a place of conversion and salvation for sinners when he said: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. So the one who travels this road has set ascents in his heart. He has resolved to climb from earth to heaven, not by one step but by many. That is why he said "ascents" and not "ascent": we need many virtues and many different good deeds if we are to be freed from the things below and take hold of the things above. And what are these ascents? Learn: For the lawgiver will give blessings; they will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion. He means the commandments of the Gospel. In them one finds not just one blessing but many: the various beatitudes that Christ laid down as law. The one who attends to them goes from strength to strength, walking from virtue to virtue. He moves from humility to mourning for sins, from there to meekness, and after that to a constant longing for righteousness. Then he moves on to mercy, from there to purity of heart, and from that to achieving peace. The crown of all these is persecution for Christ's sake. The one who is perfected in these and reaches the goal will see God in Zion, in the watchtower of the soul, for Zion means "watchtower." The advance of blessedness, then, is to see God, not as he is by nature but as far as he grants. You may also say that everything from the point where the pause occurs is said about Peter as well. He was blessed because he received help at the time of his denial. So he did not despair, but set in his heart the ascents that come through repentance, in the valley of weeping. You see how he wept. And as he received the blessings of the new lawgiver, Christ, he went from strength to strength. He ran to the resurrection and saw the linen cloths; he also saw Christ, who later met him, as Luke made clear. Yet he was not content with these things but went on to another strength, to Zion. There the God of gods, Christ, appeared to him again, laying down blessings as law: the peace that he gave to the disciples and the gift of the Spirit. O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. Is it not enough for him to hear? "No," he says, "he must also give ear," that is, store the prayer up in his ears. Then even if he does not fulfill the prayer now, he will at least fulfill it later. As a prophet, he knew that the things he was now praying for would need a long time. Here again he fittingly added a pause, making room in the prayer so that he might pray for the same things many times, since they concerned human salvation itself. Behold, O God our protector, and look upon the face of your Christ. Behold, we need you to visit us. Behold, the wound will not heal with human remedies. Behold, the vessel is shattered: it is your body, not someone else's. Look upon us in this way, but look upon the face of your Christ, that is, in the person of Christ. Then the Father too will visit all of us in the Son, and the mystery of our salvation will be accomplished by the Father's good pleasure. But why do you ask the Father to look upon us through the Son and not through the prophets? Because one day in your courts is better than thousands. By the courts of God he means Bethlehem, the cross and the resurrection. In each of these, one day is better than thousands of seasons. What all the ages since the creation of the world could not accomplish, he accomplished for the whole human race on the day of Christ's birth, or of the cross, or of the resurrection, and also of the ascension. That is why the prophet, exalting these courts above all others, said what follows: I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. "I want," he says, "to be ranked among the lowly and the outcast in the courts I have spoken of, rather than to dwell in the synagogues of the Jews." These are no longer called dwellings of God but dwellings of sinners who break the law. So the prophet chooses to share the inheritance with the thief, who seems to be among the lowliest in the Church of God, or with the Canaanite woman, who was rejected and begged for the crumbs that fell from the table, rather than with Caiaphas and the other high priests, who held the first places in the synagogue of the Jews. Let us too pray for the same thing: to be the last of the righteous, even an untimely birth, as Paul said, rather than to dwell with sinners. Learn what follows: For the Lord God loves mercy and truth; he will give grace and glory. He shows mercy and truth to those who have repented and turned from being sinners. Because of his mercy they are ranked with the righteous, but because of his truth they do not hold an equal place with them. This is why they are said to be cast aside. So though they hold the last place among the righteous, he gives them grace and glory too: grace, because they are saved by grace; glory, because they are glorified with the righteous, even if in the last rank. What follows shows that this is true and that the righteous necessarily hold the first place. The Lord will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence. Those who have lived without wickedness and conducted their lives in righteousness, which is what innocence means, are not deprived of good things. They will receive crowns in proportion to their deeds, since each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. O Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you. The prophet has set a fine seal on the psalm: hope in God, to which it is blessed to cling. For it is an anchor to those tossed by storms, and an unbreakable wall to those under attack. The one who hopes in him is the one who trusts in nothing present, but would give up the whole world rather than his hope in God.

Fittingly this psalm too is headed "For the end," or, according to the other translators, "A song of victory." For it contains the mysteries accomplished at the end of the ages, which are truly a victory over the devil. "Lord, you have been pleased with your land; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob." What happens to man and what happens to the earth are shared. When the earth flourishes, man flourishes too; when it is chastened, he is chastened along with it, since he comes from it and is fed by it. So what the prophet now says can be taken as applying to both. As Paul says, creation, of which the earth is an element, awaits our redemption. The prophet now calls this redemption "good pleasure." It is common to the whole of humankind, and we have often shown why humankind is called "earth." But it belongs in a special way to those of the Jewish people who turned to him, whom the prophet called "the captivity of Jacob." What this good pleasure is, learn more clearly from what follows. "You forgave the iniquities of your people; you covered all their sins." For he was well pleased with us. He forgave us not one iniquity but all of them, and in his love for humankind he also covered all our sins, as a physician covers wounds with medicines. He did not mention both iniquities and sins because he wanted to repeat himself. He wanted to show that he forgave not only the Jews, whose offences are called iniquities (literally "lawlessness") because they are under the law of Moses, but also the Gentiles, whose transgressions are called sins (literally "missing the mark"). For in their offences they miss the heavenly thoughts, because their minds look toward folly. A "diapsalma" is placed in the melody here. The prophet did not pause his words for no reason. He had set forth very great things, so that the mind, wearied by the greatness of the revelations, needs to rest awhile in order to contemplate them more precisely. "You put an end to all your anger; you turned from the wrath of your fury." He put an end to his anger not in part but completely. He did not put it off for a time but abolished it altogether and left no trace of it. That is why he is also said to have "turned from the wrath of his fury": having turned from anger, he clearly inclined toward love for humankind. But since he spoke of future things as present, using the prophetic manner, notice how he turned the prophecy into a prayer. In this way he shows that these things have not yet happened but are still hoped for. "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and turn your fury away from us." So anger in God is not a passion. It is a threat made for our benefit. If we turn, he too turns from his fury and stops, because he sets great store by our salvation. He has devised many means to find many roads to it, and for this reason he is rightly called "the God of our salvation." "Will you be angry with us forever, or will you prolong your anger from generation to generation?" It is fearful enough even now for God to be angry with human beings. But since at present he mostly shows long-suffering, the anger to come is necessarily more fearful. So the prophet prays that God will not be angry with us for the whole of this present age, nor carry his anger against us over from this generation to the next, but that his love for humankind will quench it. What follows shows how this happens, and in what way, even though we are slow to turn. "O God, you will turn and give us life, and your people will rejoice in you." You may call God's turning the turning that he works through us, but properly it is the turning he made on our behalf. For he says, "O God, you, having turned, will give us life." This clearly happened when he took flesh and became man and offered himself for us. He accomplished our turning to himself, doing and suffering everything for us, and in this way he made us alive. Now he has made his people, that is, those who believe in him, rejoice and celebrate in him. "Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us your salvation." You see that the psalmist speaks as both prophet and servant. As a prophet he declared what was to come, and as a servant he prays again for what he had already announced as a prophet. What exactly does he pray for? That God's mercy and salvation may be shown to human beings, that is, God the Word appearing in the flesh. Simeon testifies that he is called "salvation." For when he took him in his arms in the temple, he gave thanks and said: "Now, Master, you are letting your servant go in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation." That he is also called "mercy," this same prophet shows a little later. Both names, however, came to him from his deeds. "I will hear what the Lord God will speak to me, for he will speak peace to his people, and to his holy ones, and to those who turn their heart to him." The prophet's faith is wonderful. As soon as he sows his prayer, he receives its fruit. Knowing to whom he had made his plea, he got ready to hear peace. This is the peace that Christ gave through the band of apostles to his people, by which you should understand those who are devout toward him. The apostles are rightly called his holy ones and those who turn their heart, because they consecrated themselves wholly to Christ and turned to him with their whole heart from all the affairs of this life. They no longer laid claim to parents, family or trade, but said boldly: "Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?" "Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land." Here he clearly testifies that, even if the synagogue of the Jews wants to be called his people, God's salvation still comes near to those who fear him, the Gentiles who have believed. For those who were once not a people are now found to be God's people, having come back to him from error, and those who were once far off have been brought near through faith. And this happened "so that glory may dwell in our land." For where was God's glory to dwell, if he turned away from the Gentiles because they were not descended from Abraham, while those descended from Abraham would not come to him? As John says: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." That is why he accepted the Gentiles: to find a place to dwell in our land, that is, among humankind. The theologian made this clear in what follows: "But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh." Here he was speaking of the Gentiles, who had no kinship with Abraham by blood or flesh but were born of God. And to this he fittingly added: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." "Mercy and truth have met; righteousness and peace have kissed. Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven." Here he speaks of divinity and humanity coming together, each running according to its own worth. This is what "they met" means, for the slow also meet the swift, and the lame the sound of foot. He indicated not only a coming together but also a union born of love. This is what "they kissed" means, since those who love and those who are loved are united to one another by a kiss. God the Word would not have come down into humanity unless the Maker had held a warm love for man. "For God so loved the world," it says, "that he sent his only-begotten Son into it." But where did this coming together and meeting take place? "Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven." Truth is the flesh. This is not only because, as the psalmist says, it sprang up from the earth, but also because he was truly made flesh, and God the Word truly became man. Righteousness is the divinity, and that is why he says it looked down from heaven. It brought about righteousness by breaking the injustice that ruled as a tyrant on earth. But after the union these two cannot be separated. Hence Christ as a whole is called truth: "For I am," he says, "the truth and the life." Again, Christ as a whole is called righteousness by Paul, who said of him: "who became for us righteousness from God." The prophet goes on explaining the mystery. "For the Lord will give goodness": the Father will give his own Word. That is why the other translators said, "He will give the Good One." For you know that Christ himself said, "No one is good but God alone." "And our land will yield its fruit": that is, the flesh that sprang from Mary. For the mystery of Christ came together from both of these. First there is righteousness, of which he said earlier, "Righteousness has looked down from heaven," for the divinity goes before the humanity. As Habakkuk also says: "A word will go before his face." Then, about the humanity, he says, "And it will go out for instruction at his feet." In this he agrees with the present psalm, which continues from what has been said: "And he will set his steps on the way." For the divinity goes before, that is, it leads its own flesh and directs its steps on the way of the dispensation, so that the flesh does not stray or stumble in any human matter.

1. Do you see the dignity of prayer? He left the other psalms for Asaph and the sons of Korah to sing, but this prayer he himself offers pure to God. He does not speak for himself alone but acts the part of the whole human race. "Incline your ear, Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy." Every human being is poor and needy, and the prophet now speaks in the person of humankind. We have become poor through sin, and we are needy because of Adam, who handed poverty down to us like an inheritance. That is why he prayed that God would incline his ear, so that he might stoop down as a rich man does to the poor, or as a physician does to the sick. Why should God stoop down? Because we often ask God for unworthy things. But like a physician, he patiently listens to the request and then gives only what is good for us. "Guard my soul, for I am holy." How can someone who is poor and needy in virtue be holy? Surely because he confessed his poverty, and by that confession he has already become holy. Or else he calls man holy because of the dignity man had in paradise before the transgression. "Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you." The prophet's words are enough to move God. A master can in no way reject his own servant when that servant hopes in him. He looks after him because of his hope in him, even if he has other faults. So the prophet points to his servitude in order to draw God toward us, since God does not want to lose what belongs to him. "Have mercy on me, Lord, for I will cry to you all day long." Do you see how we can obtain mercy? By crying to God all day long, not praying with words at one moment and provoking him with deeds at the next, nor spending time now in the church of God and now in the assembly of lawless men. David himself said of such men, "I have hated the assembly of evildoers." "Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you I have lifted up my soul." From you, he says, I ask for joy, for to you I have lifted up my soul. I raised it up lightly from the earth and carried it upward by hope in divine things, so that it would not gape after human things. So it is you who must gladden me, for I do not want the gladness that comes from men, since it is harmful and passes away. "For you, Lord, are kind and gentle, and rich in mercy to all who call upon you." It was not in vain, he says, that I lifted up my soul to you. You share our suffering because you are kind, and you bear with those who stumble because you are gentle. Besides, you do not show mercy in only one way but in many different ways: you show mercy through love of the poor, through tears, through good deeds, through faith. And you show it not to some but to all who call upon you. So those who do not call upon God cannot obtain mercy. Prayer, then, has become for us a weapon, a harbor and a door of salvation. "Give ear, Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication." "Give ear" means "judge it worthy of your hearing." "Attend to the voice" means: grant compassion to the one who offers the supplication, seeing that he is strong in intensity of soul and in longing for you. (This is what "the voice of prayer" means.) That is why he added: "In the day of my affliction I cried to you, for you heard me." Afflictions usually cut prayers short, throwing a person into neglect. But he says that this did not happen to him. Instead he cried out and raised his voice even more intensely. This was the mark of someone who had not lost heart but was confident in his request. And what is the reason? "For you heard me." Since he had already been heard, naturally he did not grow slack in prayer, and so he even raises his voice. "There is none like you among the gods, Lord, and there are no works like yours." The prophet is not speaking here about idols. (For what fellowship has light with darkness, and how can falsehood be compared with truth?) He calls "gods" those to whom the word of God came, as Christ said in the Gospels. He means the holy and God-bearing men, none of whom can be likened to the Lord. Even though Christ was their kinsman according to the flesh, he was beyond comparison because of his divinity, and indeed because of his humanity as well.
