For none of them was born of a virgin or bore our sins, and none of them overthrew death by death. So no one can be compared either to him or to the works he has done. "All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, Lord." Before you, but where? In the temple of the Jews? But the temple no longer exists, and the Gentiles, being uncircumcised, could not worship there. So he is clearly speaking of Christ, before whom all the nations worship. For those who worship at Bethlehem, at the cross and at the Resurrection worship before the face of the one who accomplished our salvation there. In the same way, those who worship at the altar worship before him, for there at every mystical sacrifice they see him seated. "And they will glorify your name." Because of what? For they used to worship wood and stone and were the subjects and slaves of demons. Then hear what follows: "For you are great and do wonders; you alone are God."

2. So they glorify Christ because they have found him to be great and the only one who has done wonders. What is his greatness, and what are his wonders? He abolished the age-old error of idols. He did not send angels to do this, or shake the earth, or rain fire from heaven. He used as his servants men who were unlettered and poor, mere fishermen. "Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth." Clearly the prophet speaks the words of the Gospel before the Gospels existed. He wants to be led by the Way to the way, and to walk in the truth of him who says, "I am the way and the life and the truth." But first we need to be led to the way of God and to learn its beginnings, that is, its first elements, and then we will walk in the truth. For the goal of the knowledge of God is to grasp the truth of the things that exist. "Let my heart rejoice in fearing your name." He asks for a fine joy and prays for a fine festival: to fear the name of God. For true joy comes to us from there. It is not a joy of the flesh but of the soul and its heart, since the soul has a close affinity and kinship with God. That is why the soul counts even the fear of him a festival, for it knows what dignity that fear has. "I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever." So he does not allow anyone to glorify God before confessing his sins. He wanted to glorify God with a pure tongue, and the tongue is cleansed when it picks out its sins from the whole heart. This is true confession: to vomit sin out of one's whole mind and never go back to it, but to turn away from it as from something vomited out once and for all. "For your mercy toward me is great, and you have rescued my soul from the lowest Hades." This is why, he says, I dared to confess my sins, when I ought to have feared and been ashamed to do so: because your mercy toward me, that is, toward man, is great. So the one who confesses his sin not only enjoys forbearance and pardon but can also expect a reward. And what is that reward? To have his soul rescued from the lowest Hades, that is, from the place of Gehenna and from the outer darkness. That place is the lot assigned to sinners, and it must be the lowest Hades, for we say that whoever goes down there cannot come back up. "O God, the lawless have risen up against me, and a gathering of the mighty has sought my soul, and they have not set you before them." Whoever wrongs his neighbor does not set God before his own eyes. If he did, he would not do wrong, because he would revere the judge, nor would he break the law, because he would consider the lawgiver's threat. Such people act this way not from ignorance but from audacity. Robbers who rob in lonely places know perfectly well that there are judges and courts, but in their folly they pay them no heed and have no fear of them. He called these people not only lawless but also "a gathering of the mighty," that is, of those who are powerful in wickedness. He rebuked them in another part of the prophecy: "Why do you boast in wickedness, O mighty one?" Why did he call those who rose up against him not only lawless but also mighty in wickedness, which we said means powerful? Because they were not after a field, a house, clothing or slaves, but after man's one and only possession, his soul. They wanted to plot against it and kill it. So these words were spoken directly about the demons, who are truly lawless and powerful in wickedness. That is why he called God to march against them. "And you, Lord my God, are compassionate and merciful, long-suffering, rich in mercy, and true. Look upon me and have mercy on me." They rose up in vain, he says. As God, you fight for the being you formed. As compassionate and merciful, you share the suffering of the one they plot against. As long-suffering, you do not hand the sinner over to his enemies. As rich in mercy, you show mercy not once but many times. As true, you drive off the wrongdoer and save the one who is wronged. Therefore, "Look upon me," for the wolf cannot seize a sheep that the shepherd is watching over. "And have mercy on me." Since I have no works with which to move your hand to come to my aid, I must appeal to your mercy, which is owed above all to those who are plotted against. "Give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid," he says. As a man he is a servant and a slave, and he asks to receive strength against the passions. As the son of God's handmaid, that is, of wisdom, he asks to be saved. Or else he calls our nature God's handmaid. For like a maidservant, our nature obeys the Creator in whatever he wishes and commands, and it [?] its own limits when it perceives that the Maker commands this. So the prophet takes pride in calling man a servant and the son of a handmaid. That is why he thought that God's strength was rightly his, as an old servant born into the household from his forefathers. Servants of this kind are trusted with their master's wealth without suspicion. Who this strength was, learn now from what follows. "Show me a sign for good, and let those who hate me see it and be ashamed, because you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me." He does not simply ask for a sign, but for one "for good," that is, one given for the benefit of the human race. Such was the sign Isaiah set forth when he spoke to Ahaz on God's behalf: "Ask for yourself a sign in the depth or in the height." After this he added: "Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel." That a virgin should give birth is plainly a sign. So too is what the Lord himself said: "This generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights." By these signs all the demons who hate us were put to shame. As Isaiah says, it was neither an envoy nor an angel but God himself who helped us. He was born of a virgin and became man for our sake, and he himself also comforted us. For when we were mourning under the sentence of death, he rose from the dead and showed that death is only sleep.

We have often said that "a psalm of a song," or else "a song of a psalm," is the title given especially to those subjects in which he blends prophecies about Christ with melody. "His foundations are on the holy mountains." The foundations of Christ are the mysteries of the sufferings and the miracles connected with him. These are found on the holy mountains: in Bethlehem, at Golgotha, at the resurrection, on Mount Tabor, the mountain of the transfiguration, and on the hill of the ascension. That is why he called the mountains holy, since they received the sanctification of the Lord's mysteries. But let the prophets too be mountains, fittingly so because of the height of their foreknowledge. They hold the foundations of God, that is, the first beginnings of the knowledge of God, for it is from them that we learn the rudiments of godliness. "The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob." The dwellings of Jacob are surely the twelve tribes, or rather Shiloh. For the ark dwelt there, as did the ancient people of the Jews itself, and there the Holy of Holies had its tent. But he loved the gates of Zion more than all of these. In those places he enacted the type, but here the truth. He also loves the gates of Zion because Zion received Christ while they were shut. So what follows fits very well: "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God. Pause." These glorious things are not only that Christ came in there when the doors were shut. They are also that, having entered without doors as God, as man he let himself be touched in you. He did not add the "Pause" for nothing. He added it because he shifted his words to the Church of the Gentiles, and at the same time the prophet set aside his own person and now brought in that of God. "I will remember Rahab and Babylon to those who know me." And why does God promise to remember Rahab? For Rahab was a harlot, and Babylon is interpreted as "confusion." The phrase that follows shows why, for he says: "to those who know me." The Church from the Gentiles is Rahab because of its fornication, and it is Babylon, interpreted as "confusion," because of its gathering of idols. Yet once it has turned and come to know God, it fittingly has a place in God's remembrance. The synagogue of the Jews, by contrast, has been forgotten because of its ignorance. But what fruit do Rahab and Babylon offer to the one who remembered them, once God has remembered them? The psalmist tells us next: "And behold, foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians: these were made there." The other translators have rendered the word "were made" more clearly, some putting "were begotten," others "were born." For the foreigners, the people of the Ethiopians, who have the blackness and darkness of idolatry, and Tyre too, which reigned in error, were all begotten to God through the Church, by the birth that comes through water and baptism. "Mother Zion will say: A man." What will she say? Clearly the mysteries foretold about the Gentiles. But she says she is not taught these things by a man, for she has Christ as her teacher. And he added how she glorifies him: "And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her." He calls Christ both man and Most High: man because of the flesh, and Most High because of the Godhead. Marvellously, then, and very clearly he has expressed the mystery that Christ accomplished in Zion when he gave himself to the disciples to be touched. For then a man was born in her, that is, was made manifest, when the Most High himself founded her, having given the grace of the Father there. Indeed, he also laid his own faith as a foundation for Zion, and of this he himself speaks through the tongue and voice of Isaiah: "Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a chosen stone, a precious cornerstone; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." "The Lord will tell in the register of peoples and of these rulers who came to be in her." Which Lord? The one who was made manifest in Zion as man but founded her as Most High. He himself tells in the register of peoples, that is, in the enrolment of the nations. He did not say one people, in case they took it to mean the people of the Jews. He said many, to hint at the nations. And he says, "and of these rulers who came to be in her," meaning the apostles, for they were appointed rulers in Zion. Take the proof of each point. John wrote that Christ said to the apostles in Zion: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you." Clearly, then, he made the apostles rulers here, for he sent them into the world with this authority. And Luke presents Christ in Zion setting out the explanation of the mystery: "Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and said to them that thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations." See, he added the register of the peoples as well, by which I mean the allotment of the nations. Fittingly, then, it is not a mere man who tells Zion the mysteries, since the man who is God and Most High himself told her each thing most clearly. The prophet added "Pause" because, after setting aside the person of God, he brought back his own, wishing to glorify Zion in his own character. And what does he say? "How the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you!" "How" here means "in what way." The prophet marvels at the way and the degree to which all who dwell in Zion rejoice as they recall the miracles done and accomplished there. And those who dwell in her are those who live by the Spirit, since Zion is the house of the Spirit.

1. You have already learned that the sons of Korah were psalm-singers. But understand also that "a song of a psalm" means the melody that is mingled with the prophecy that was to be spoken about Christ. You will ask why "For the end, on Maeleth" is written, which the others have rendered "A victory song by a chorus." So it is clear that this melody was composed not by one psalm-singer but by a chorus. It was led by Heman the Israelite, who was certainly a different psalm-singer, and the chorus answered him rhythmically and with understanding. That is why the title has: "To answer: a word of understanding, for Heman the Israelite." "O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you. Let my prayer come in before you." Each of us too, when we pray before God, that is, in a way that pleases him, ought to pray the whole day and night. We must do so if we want our prayer to come in before him and our intercessions to succeed, so that we too may hear: "Your prayers and your alms have gone up as a memorial before God." But since the whole psalm is written about Christ, he necessarily called the Father Lord and God of his own salvation. He means the common salvation, for having become the firstfruits, he counts our salvation as his own. It was by the Father's good pleasure that the Son came into the world, and so we were saved. To him he often cried out by day on the mountain, and by night at the place called Gethsemane, when Judas was about to betray him. That is, he boldly asked the Father to let his prayer come in before him. And what was that prayer? "Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done." "Incline your ear to my supplication." That is: weigh carefully the force of my prayer, or else stoop down to those for whom I offer the supplication. For I am praying not for myself but for these whose form and likeness I have taken. "For my soul is filled with evils." What evils? Human ones, for I bear the sins of all. "And my life has drawn near to Hades." For those whose bond of debt I came to pay owed death. "I was counted with those who go down into the pit." He says he is like those who go down into the pit of death. I seemed to owe death just as they did. Yet it was not so, as what follows shows: "I became like a man without help, free among the dead." As man he endured the cross and the passion without help. He did not allow an angel to stand by him, so that he could say: "I trod the winepress alone." And he rebuked Peter when Peter cut off the ear of one of those arresting him, saying to him: "Do you not think that I can appeal to my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures of the prophets be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?" By saying this he showed that he himself held back the power of his own Godhead, so that the mystery of the dispensation prophesied about him might be fulfilled. And he was free among the dead, not only as God but also as one sinless in the flesh. That is why, as Paul says when addressing the people, it was not possible for him to be held by the pangs of death. "Like the wounded sleeping in the grave, whom you remember no more, and they are thrust away from your hand." Here too we should supply "I became." He became like one wounded, since the children of the Jews tried to give him the reputation of one wounded, that is, of a sinner. That is why they even called him a deceiver when they came to Pilate. Learn from Jeremiah that Scripture calls sinners "wounded," for he says: "Who will give my head water, and my eyes a fountain of tears? And I will weep for the wounded of the daughter of my people." What the psalmist has said here also shows it. He spoke not only of the wounded but also of those cast out of God's memory and thrust from his hand, and Christ says he was counted among them. He also spoke of those sleeping in the grave, idle and inactive, and this while Christ was bringing about the resurrection of the dead. "They laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death." See how he preserves both the reality of the suffering and the dignity of the one who suffered. He was laid in the lowest pit, he says, since nothing is lower than Hades. He was also laid in dark places, so that the darkness hints at the regions of death. But by "in the shadow of death" he shows that the suffering was passing. At the same time he shows that Christ was the sun of righteousness, hidden for a short while as if by the shadow of death. "Your wrath has pressed heavily upon me." This was necessary. Since he bore the sins of the race, the wrath against sinners fell on him. That wrath was death, and a curse came upon him. Having come to rest there, it no longer falls on the human race. "And you have brought all your heights upon me." By God's "heights" he means the lofty things that belong to him, such as the kingdom, sanctification, and the privilege of servants sitting together with their Master. The Father necessarily brought upon Christ the lowly things for our sake. In the same way he brought upon him the lofty things meant for us, for it is in him that we enjoy them. Jeremiah clearly told us that "heights" means lofty things, for he says: "If the heaven be raised to the height, says the Lord," that is, if it becomes higher than it is. "Pause" is placed after these words because in the preceding verses he recalled the tomb and death, and now he carried his words back to what came before these, I mean the betrayal and the cross. "You have put my acquaintances far from me."

2. Luke expresses this in these very words where he sets out the account of the cross: "And all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things." "They made me an abomination to themselves." This too was fulfilled in Peter, in the high priest's courtyard. Some there said to him, "Truly you too are one of them, for your speech gives you away." Afraid of them, he began to curse and to swear: "I do not know the man." "I was handed over, and I did not go out." He could have gone out, that is, slipped away, since he knew when the Jews would come for him. That is why he said to the disciples: "Sleep now and take your rest; behold, the one who betrays me has drawn near." Nevertheless he willingly allowed himself to be handed over. "My eyes grew weak from poverty; I cried out to you, O Lord." He calls the passion poverty, and so Paul too says of him: "He became poor for our sake, though he was rich." His eyes, then, grew weak because of the passion, for he willingly endured what is human. And his eyes grew so weak that he even cried out: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani." "All day long I spread out my hands to you." This clearly refers to the cross. The high priest, offering sacrifice for us and stretching out his hands in the posture of prayer, accomplished the dispensation of the passion. "Will you work wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they give thanks to you?" Here he holds a dialogue with the Father, wishing to make known to us why it was necessary for him to go down to the dead. The reasons are these. He does not work wonders for the dead. He produces no lightning or thunder among them, no storm out of a clear sky, no sudden calm after a storm, and none of the other wonders of creation that he provides for the living. Nor will physicians raise the dead so that they may see these things. How then can those who died in unbelief give thanks? How can they be saved, when they have heard neither the law nor the prophets? For they had not listened to them. The prophet put "Pause" before what follows, because the Spirit had given him a rest from the melody. Yet it belongs to the same line of thought. "Will anyone tell of your mercy in the grave, and of your truth in the land of destruction?" For what prophet or lawgiver is there in the grave, or in the land of destruction? He calls the place of the dead "destruction," so naming death because it offers no hope of life. God's mercy or truth means his law and commandments, or even Christ himself. For [?] no one could tell of mercy and truth there, being subject to death because of the sentence passed on the whole race. "Will your wonders be known in the darkness, and your righteousness in the land that is forgotten?" He is still dealing with the same things. He calls Hades darkness because it is without light, and he calls the same place "the land that is forgotten." Those regions received no visitation until the Savior went down to the dead. So neither God's wonders nor his righteousness, that is, neither the signs nor the law, were expected to be made known among them. He often returns to the same words, wishing to show that the dispensation of the passion could not be dispensed with, since it benefits the dead and the living alike. "But I cried out to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer will come before you." Since he was the Son, equal in honor with the Father, his prayer necessarily came before when he prayed, as though running to meet the one to whom it was offered. And he fittingly added the time, so that from this too you might learn that what is said here agrees with the Gospels. For Luke says: "In those days he went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the whole night in prayer to God." And what follows clearly shows why he prayed with a loud cry, for these are the words of one who intercedes. "Why, O Lord, do you reject my soul [my prayer], and turn your face away from me?" He said this as one who had taken on our person. Because of the disobedience, God turned away from our person and rejected our soul, since it had transgressed and then found fault with its Maker. Christ does not ask out of ignorance. He asks to show that God should no longer turn away, now that Christ himself is offering the defense on behalf of all. "I am poor and in toils from my youth." For our sake he became poor, though he was rich, and he was in toils from his youth: he went to Egypt, then from there hid in Nazareth of Galilee, and endured many other plots. "Having been exalted, I was humbled and brought to distress." Whether you take the height to mean the signs or the cross, in both cases he was humbled and brought to distress, being scorned by the Jews. "Your wrath has passed over me." He means the wrath against humanity, that is, the punishments and threats. He received these for our sake, having offered himself through sufferings. "Your terrors have troubled me; they surrounded me like water." He means the terrors pronounced against the first-formed man. They were strong, since God's sentence sealed them and fought on their side. He was so troubled by them that he said: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death." Indeed, he was also hemmed in, surrounded by thoughts as if by water. That is why he said to the Father: "Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But it was for this that I came to this hour." "All day long they surrounded me together." Here he recalled the day of the passion, on which the chief priests, elders, Pharisees, scribes and the people of the Jews all surrounded him together. Matthew also shows this when, with everyone gathered, Pilate asked: "Whom do you want me to release to you?" "You have put friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery." He means Peter, for Peter was a friend through being his disciple. You will see this from the Lord's words: "No longer do I call you servants, but friends." Peter is also the neighbor, because his faith was so fervent and vigorous. And his acquaintances are all the apostles. They knew him better than anyone else did, as you have heard him say in the Gospels: "Righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me." Yet because of the misery of the passion they all withdrew for a time. This is counted not against them but to the Father. The mystery of the cross was beyond their strength, and this happened by the Father's counsel and good pleasure.

1. This psalmist is a different one from the one indicated by the title of the eighty-seventh psalm. That one is called Heman, but this one Ethan. They were perhaps kinsmen or fellow citizens; that is why each of them is called "the Israelite," receiving the name either from their place or from their kinship. The present psalm too is entitled "Of understanding," for what is set out in this prophecy concerns great matters, given for understanding about God. I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, unto the age. By "the age" he means the present age. Here he has pointed us not to a single kind of mercy but to many forms of loving-kindness: baptism, repentance, almsgiving. By making use of any one of these, the sinner can obtain mercy and compassion. To generation and generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth. "To generation and generation" means, of course, the present and the future, for in each we recount the truth of God. Now we learn it from the divinely inspired Scripture; later we shall receive it in the deeds themselves, and see the truth shining clearly at our judgment, when each receives the recompense for his own works. But why he assigns mercy to the present age, and truth both to the present and to the future, is shown by what follows. For you said: Unto the age mercy shall be built; in the heavens your truth shall be prepared. Each of these statements, he says, is a declaration of God. What declaration is this, and of what kind? Perhaps it is God's proclamation: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. For this was the word of one who was urging and hastening the repentance of sinners. That is why he says, "Repent": because mercy now has room, and here the architect of our salvation has built his loving-kindness toward us. Then, setting a seal on this, he added, "For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near," showing that once the kingdom of heaven arrives, repentance no longer has room, since the judge has prepared his own truth in the heavens; and the truth of a judge carries out the judgment without any partiality. How, then, is mercy built, that is, constructed, and how is truth prepared in the heavens? Evidently, as the judgment is being led on its way; but each comes about through the coming of Christ. That is why he introduces this most clearly in what follows. I have made a covenant with my chosen ones. Which covenant? The covenant of the gospel, of which the prophet Jeremiah spoke: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with your fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. And who becomes the mediator of this covenant? I swore to David my servant: I will prepare your seed unto the age, and build up your throne to generation and generation. You see that the one from the seed of David is the mediator of this covenant. He does not improvise the mystery, he says, but makes it ready on high. For the coming of the Savior was an ancient and true counsel. Hence he promised to prepare the seed of David unto the age. He means Christ, of whom Paul also wrote to the Romans: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh. This throne, that is, the kingdom, God promises to build to generation and generation. For he who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh possesses, besides the present kingdom, the future one as well. Of him Daniel also spoke thus: And to him were given honor and dominion and kingdom; all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him; his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his authority one that shall not be destroyed. The Spirit inserted a diapsalma in the middle, because he shifted the discourse to the person of the prophet. The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord, and indeed your truth in the church of the saints. Understand "heavens" as those who set their minds on heavenly things. For such a person is also called "heavenly" by Paul. That is why this same prophet says elsewhere: The heavens declare the glory of God, alluding there, as here, to the apostles. For these confess, that is, proclaim with thanksgiving, the wonders of God and his truth in the church of the saints. Which saints? Those in Jerusalem. Luke clearly recorded this about Barnabas and Paul in the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles and elders gathered to consider the question before them. For he says: All the multitude fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. For who in the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? This refers to the angels, the powers ranked on high. Who shall be likened to the Lord among the sons of God? Here he has made the comparison with respect to the saints; and yet neither angel nor saint can be compared with the Maker who is over all. He rightly used "shall be equal" of the angels, since they too are called incorporeal; yet even so they have no equality with God, for they exist in places and are circumscribed, which is also why they form a countless multitude. Of the saints, however, he used "shall be likened." For even if they preserve the likeness they received from God by guarding the image, this likeness is only partial and is given by God, so that in this respect too the comparison is unequal. For how will the one who has received be like the giver, who has the power to take away what he gave? God, glorified in the council of the saints, is great and fearsome over all who are around him.

2. Although he rejoices greatly in the assembly of the saints and counts it his own glory, he is nevertheless to be feared by them. They are round about him because they draw near to him through a life of holiness. He is to be feared by them when they sin, since he shows no favour even to the righteous. Or rather, he is to be feared even when they do not sin, so that Job says to him: "Take your hand away from me, and do not let the fear of you terrify me." Yet he makes them afraid not because he hates them but because he cares for them, for "blessed are all who fear the Lord." O God of the powers, who is like you? The prophet keeps using this phrase. He is not asking a question but expressing his amazement, and describing how incomparable God is. That is why he called him not simply Lord but also God of the powers: of angels, of archangels, and of any other powers there may be that are hidden from us. Each of these is ruled by God, so how could they be compared with their Master? You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is round about you. He has spoken of God's supremacy over created things. Now he describes the Son's equality with him, so that you do not imagine, as some of the impious do, that the Son is unlike the Father. He called the Son the Father's truth, because he comes forth from him. He also says that the Son is round about the Father, because the Son alone is able to contain the Father. "For I am in the Father," he says, "and the Father is in me." He contains him as the great contains the great, as the mighty contains the mighty. That is why, after saying to the Father, "You are mighty, O Lord," he then added, "and your truth is round about you." From this you are to learn that the Father is supremely great and mighty, and that no one can be compared with him, and yet that the Son is equal to him, so much so that he is even said to be round about him. You rule over the might of the sea, and you calm the surging of its waves. Having turned from praising God for invisible things to praising him for visible ones, he naturally mentioned the sea, since it is fearsome. God rules it so completely that he has made sand its boundary. He calms its surging and stills its waves by taking up the winds that blow on it and raise it. You have humbled the proud one like one who is wounded. He means the devil. Pride wounded him, and for this he was cast down from the regions above to the earth and humbled, so that he is trampled and crushed even by the feet of the saints. As Paul wrote to the Romans: "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." With the arm of your power you have scattered your enemies. The arm of God's power is Christ. Isaiah says as much: "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Christ scattered God's enemies, the Jews. Of them the prophet represents him as saying: "They became enemies." He scattered them by destroying the place where they carried out their worship according to the letter. The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours. This is clear from the fact that he alone uses them as he wishes. You founded the world and all that fills it. What fills the world is man. It is on his account that the world came to be inhabited by the other animals as well, which were brought in to meet our needs. This, then, is what God founded: he gave man a natural law, which is the foundation of every human good. So man is not shaken, as long as he keeps his own foundation intact. You created the north and the sea. Instead of "sea", the other translators have rendered "south" or "right". By "right" they mean the south, because it lies on the right of someone facing east. Still, it is fitting that the sea is set next to the north, since in divinely inspired Scripture this word usually stands for the western region. That is why the book of Numbers, when it sets out the tribes, some camped to the east of the tabernacle, some to the south and some to the north, uses this word for those camped to its west: "The order of the camp of Ephraim by the sea, with their host." Here, though, he has joined the west to the north because both regions are dark and wintry. Some people ascribe these parts of creation to an evil creator, dividing creation by impious and blasphemous reasoning. Wishing to do away with their error, he testifies that these too were created by the one Creator of all. Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name.

3. Why did he mention only these mountains? Surely because Tabor, the neighbour of Hermon, was where Christ was transfigured. That is why both are said to rejoice in it: the one because so great a mystery was entrusted to it, the other because it received the blessing from its neighbour. For this reason he gave Hermon the blessing in another psalm too, where he says: "Like the dew of Hermon that comes down on the mountains of Zion." Yours is the arm, with might. What might? The might of the cross. For, as Paul says, "the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." And what is this mighty deed? It is our turning back from error. The Son, the arm of the Father, accomplished this through the cross. What follows makes this clear: Let your hand be strengthened, let your right hand be lifted up. "Let it be strengthened" does not mean that it should receive strength, for it already had it. It means that its strength should be revealed when the mystery reaches its completion, as Christ himself promised when he said: "When I am lifted up, I will draw all to myself." We have already shown clearly enough that the Only-begotten is called the arm and the right hand of the Father. He is called this because the Father does all things through him, as through a hand: "For all things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being." Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Which throne? Surely the throne that is to come, which is why he spoke of preparation. For here and now, from the way we live, our judge prepares righteousness and judgment for himself, paving the way, in keeping with that conduct, for the judgment to come. Mercy and truth will go before your face. Mercy comes first, and truth fittingly follows. If he did not set mercy first, who could stand up to the judge's truth? And how is truth joined to mercy? The judge does not show mercy to everyone, but only to those who have made up for their sins through mercy, either by repenting or by showing mercy to their neighbour. Blessed is the people that knows the shout of victory. The "shout" is the cry raised by soldiers who have won a war. So all those who have defeated the devil know the shout of victory, whether they did it by achieving virtues or by repenting of their offences. Their blessedness is no ordinary one: the first will win crowns, and the second are spared punishment. You have learned not [only] "Blessed are the blameless in the way" but also "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered." What follows also applies to these people: Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and in your name they will rejoice all day long. That is, they will walk their whole life long in the light of God, which means in the law: "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." And they rejoice in his name because they take refuge in God, whose name is above every name, whose service is freedom, and whose friendship is [?] lordship over all creation. And in your righteousness they will be exalted. These are the same people. What is it that exalts them? For you are the boast of their strength, and in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted. The Jews boast in Moses and take pride in Abraham, since they are descended from him. The Greeks put their trust in wood and stones, or take pride in the wisdom of the devil. But our power is Christ, and the boast of our power is the Father. Our horn is exalted in the Father's good pleasure, and so it will never be broken, for who could overturn the glory of God? And how is it exalted? Through the Father's good pleasure, he says, by which we were called to be his adopted sons. Paul wrote this to the Ephesians, saying of the Father: "In love he predestined us for adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will." For our help is the Lord's, and comes from the Holy One of Israel, our king. See how David proclaims the same things as Paul, who says: "It is no trouble to me, and it is safe for you." Look how, through many verses in a row, he keeps coming back to the Saviour. He calls him Lord and Holy One, since he is God; he calls him Israel and our king, since he is of the seed of King David and is called Israel according to the Spirit. Then you spoke in a vision to your sons. "Then": when? In a vision to your sons, that is, in the vision concerning your sons. He calls those saved from among the Gentiles sons of God. Paul said to them: "So you are no longer slaves, but sons." He saw that the Gentiles were ready for salvation, and that by the natural law they were groping for the lawgiver without grasping him, because that law had grown weak in them through the error that had overtaken them. It was then that he spoke the words that follow: And you said: I have laid help upon one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from my people. Christ is mighty, so much so that he is even called the power of God. Upon him, that is, through him, God established help and salvation for us, the Gentiles. He did it not through a lawgiver or a prophet but through his own Son. How did he do it? The psalm itself adds the answer plainly: I have exalted one chosen from my people. It is speaking of Christ, as you see. For he was lifted up on the cross and drew to himself those who were going astray, and he was chosen from among the people of humankind. He was "chosen out of ten thousands," as the Song says. Even in the flesh he had many advantages over other men: he was born of a virgin, he had no sins, and so on. I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him.

4. Having prophesied about Christ above, here he plainly hints at the people who belong to Christ. That is why he says "I have found," as one would of someone who had strayed and gone astray. For we were the lost and wandering sheep that the shepherd left the ninety-nine to look for. He also calls this people a servant, because it no longer serves idols. He calls it David because of its kinship with Christ, and also because it is strong of hand, for the name David means "strong of hand." The people of the Gentiles is strong of hand. It alone brought the war over idols to an end, and so it has been anointed with the holy oil of baptism. John the theologian wrote of this: "And you have an anointing from the Holy One." And you all know why this people is anointed: so that it may strip boldly for the contest. For this it also needed the help that comes next: For my hand will take his part, and my arm will strengthen him. Otherwise, how could someone who was once ranked under the principalities, the powers, the world-rulers of darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness fight against them, unless God's hand and arm gave him strength? That is why he does not simply say "will help him" but "will take his part together with him," that is, will help him and take hold alongside him. This shows that he has the hand from above as his partner in the contests, sharing his toils. The enemy will gain no advantage over him. The enemy is clearly the devil, for he will not be able to draw us away from faith in Christ. And the son of lawlessness will not harm him again. He means the Antichrist, whose coming is expected. Paul wrote about him to the Thessalonians: "For that day will not come unless the apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship." He will not harm those who believe in Christ, for they have commandments telling them how to avoid him and how to escape his deception. All of these are contained in Christ's words about the end of the age. And I will cut down his enemies before him, and put to flight those who hate him. As has often been said, our enemies and those who hate us are the demons. At his first coming he cut them down and left them wounded, pierced by the cross as if by a sword. At his second coming he will rout them completely, so that they can no longer stand and make war on us. And my truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted. Everywhere he makes the believer secure, wanting him to know how he was saved, where the exaltation of his horn came from, and how he became stronger than his enemies. All of this came to us through Christ, who is mercy and truth from God, and who is also the Father's name, since in him, as the Son, the Father is made known. And I will set his hand on the sea, and his right hand on the rivers. Here he calls baptism the sea, for he says of the devil: "I will make his face vanish into the first sea." The rivers are the gifts of the Spirit, for Christ says: "Whoever believes in me, rivers of water will flow from within him." Then the Gospel writer, wanting to explain the saying, added: "He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." That, then, is where our hand and right hand are, for our strength lies in these things. He will call upon me: You are my Father. He does not dare to say this on his own account. He has been given leave by the Saviour, who made us his brothers and shaped us after himself, and therefore commanded us to say when we pray: "Our Father in heaven." My Lord, and the helper of my salvation. Though he has become our Father by grace, we will never stop calling him God, and the helper of our salvation as well. He found us wronged by the devil: being fleshly, we were overrun by the fleshless one. So he took our part, made our enemy his own enemy, and came over to our side. These, then, are the words with which we call on him. What does he promise us in return? And I will make him my firstborn. So the Jew has been cast out of the birthright. He says "I will make" to show that we were not firstborn but came into being later, like Jacob, who stole the blessing from the elder people.

5. Exalted among the kings of the earth. All the righteous, who are truly called kings of the earth, marvel at the height of our mysteries, and because of them they consider us very exalted. That is why many longed to see what we see and to hear what we hear. For ever I will keep my mercy for him, and my covenant will be faithful to him. The Jewish people cannot take pride in these words; only the people of the Gentiles can. It is for this people that God keeps his mercy for ever, since he ordained that our mystery should stand unshaken until the end of the age. And we hold God's covenant as faithful, because we come to him by faith and stand firm for it even to the shedding of blood, as the contests of the martyrs bear witness. And I will establish his seed for ever and ever. Unlike the children of the Jews, we do not expect our rewards here. Our seed will bear its fruit for us in the age to come: good things "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him." And his throne as the days of heaven. This is fitting, since "our citizenship is in heaven." And his throne as the days of heaven: take this to mean the blessed life of the angels, or time without end, since God, who is said to dwell in the heavens, has no end. If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their iniquities with the rod and their wrongdoing with scourges. People forsake the law of God when they depart even slightly from what is written in it, and when they try to carry out what the law requires for their own purpose rather than for the purpose of the lawgiver. People do not walk in God's judgments when, as judges, they defer to the rich or take pity on the poor. God is not like that; he wants the court to be the same for everyone. Again, people profane his commandments when they feign virtue and insult the commandments by not pursuing them with a pure intention. So they are said not even to keep the commandments, since they violate the purpose of the one who gave them. God punishes the iniquities of such people with the rod and their wrongdoing with scourges. So when we are scourged, let us not accuse or complain, even if we happen to be fasting or pursuing some other such virtue. For surely it is because of the way we do our good deeds that we have needed the scourge. Yet along with discipline he has promised kindness. But I will not scatter my mercy from them, nor will I do wrong in my truth. He promises to treat us with great kindness. First, he scourges those who sin: "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives." Second, he by no means judges sinners to deserve rejection, and so he does not scatter his mercy from us. How so? Because after the scourging he shows mercy to all. He also says he will not do wrong in his truth. What does his truth intend? That whoever believes in him will live even if he dies, which means that even if he sins, he will be saved by turning back. That is why the other translators rendered "faith" instead of "truth." So he disciplines the faithful so that they may turn back and be saved, and so that he is never found to break the promise he made to faith. What follows shows this more clearly. Nor will I profane my covenant, that is, I will not annul it, and what has gone out from my lips I will not set aside. He is plainly setting out what the Gospels promise about the faithful. He had mentioned a covenant, so to keep you from thinking he meant the covenant given through Moses or the other prophets, he added: What has gone out from my lips I will not set aside. This is so that you will understand him to mean the words we have just quoted, which Christ spoke with his own tongue. Once for all I have sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David. God's oath is what Scripture calls his promise, since it cannot be broken. That is why elsewhere, too, David represents God as saying: "As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest." There he calls the promise an oath. For by whom could God swear, when he is the one by whom everyone swears? And what did he promise David, so that he does not lie to him? His seed will endure for ever, and his throne will be like the sun before me, and like the moon established for ever; and the witness in heaven is faithful.

6. Who is this? Clearly it is Christ. He was in heaven, taking counsel with the Father, when these words were spoken. Isaiah also spoke of him: “Be my witnesses; and I too am a witness, says the Lord, and so is my servant whom I have chosen.” He was rightly called a faithful witness, since he backed his words with the proof of his deeds. God made this promise to David at the time when David planned to build a house for the ark. He says: “I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will prepare his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his throne for ever.” Here he calls Christ the offspring of David because of the flesh. That is why Matthew began the Gospels this way: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” Paul also says of Christ: “Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh.” His throne is like the sun, for he holds his kingdom in light. But so that you do not imagine anything small about him, he added “before me,” that is, equal to mine. Here the prophet took “before” not in the sense of something opposed, but in the sense of something of equal weight. And it is established like the day [?] for ever. By “for ever” he means the present life, as we have often said. For this life it is established no longer like the sun, but like the moon. The moon has eclipses and risings, and in the same way the glory of Christ is eclipsed for some at present, as is plain among the ungodly, while among the godly it is lifted high. At times he gives way to the persecutors and allows those who believe in him to be handed over to chains, prisons and death, and this is taken for an eclipse of his glory. At other times he suddenly casts the persecutors down and makes his glory rise so high that kings venerate those who bore witness for him as martyrs. This is why the kingdom of Christ in the present life is compared to the moon. The prophet then had good reason to add a Diapsalma, especially since he had so far set out words spoken in the person of God, and now he brings in his own address to God. “But you have cast off and scorned.” The change of speaker bewilders the more simple-minded, but it is customary with David, since a dramatic setting suits such things, and he created one through singing psalms and playing the lyre. Yet what is said now shows that the promises concerned the Gentiles and not the Jews. He says that God cast off the Jewish people and scorned them, that is, cheapened them and counted them worthy of nothing. In what way? Listen to what follows: “You have put off your Christ.” He postponed Christ's coming for a time, because they were not fit to receive him. It is not only this that shows the postponement and the contempt shown to the Jews, but also what is said next. “You have overturned the covenant of your servant.” What covenant did he overturn, and with whom, if not the covenant with the Jews? He did so by abolishing and overthrowing all the ordinances given to them. He now calls them servants, not because they served God's commandments, but because he wishes to move God to compassion. At the same time he hints at the lazy servant who hid the talent, who stands as an image of the Jewish people. “You have profaned his sanctuary to the ground.” This needs no explanation. Before the eyes of all, the sanctuary that once belonged to the Jews lies profaned, trampled not only by every kind of person but even by unclean animals. “You have torn down all his hedges.” He means the precepts of the law. They are rightly called hedges because of the curse attached to them, which plays the part of thorns. “You have turned his strongholds into terror.” The things in which they once trusted as fortifications they now fear, since their way of life has been changed. They dare not offer sacrifice or keep feasts or perform any other ordinance. “All who pass along the road plundered him.” By “road” you should understand life, for Christ says in the Gospels: “Make friends with your opponent while you are on the road with him.” Those who have believed in Christ pass along this road. They travel through life as though it were a matter of no importance, laying claim to nothing in it and hurrying to get through it quickly. It is by them that the Jewish people have been plundered of the law and the prophets, their true wealth. “He has become a reproach to his neighbors.” We are rightly called neighbors of the Jews, and we rightly regard them as deserving reproach, because salvation comes from them and yet they do not wish to be saved. “You have exalted the right hand of those who oppress him.”

7. See, he means those who hold the Roman empire. It is plain that they oppress the Jewish people. And they were indeed exalted in their right hand, that is, in their power, for they gained a wider empire once they had sacked the Jewish state. “You have made all his enemies rejoice.” If he calls the Gentiles enemies, God made them rejoice not by the harm he did to the Jews but by the gifts he gave to us. If he calls the demons enemies, God made them rejoice because he stripped the Jews of his own protecting hand and left them exposed to the plots of anyone who wished. “You have turned back the help of his sword.” The sword of the godly is surely God's command, for with it we rout the opposing powers. That is why Paul said: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword.” The sword peculiar to the Jews was the law of Moses. God turned back its help, for he annulled its use according to the letter. “And you did not support him in battle.” Which battle? The one against us. They often attack us with the law and the prophets, but God gives the support of the Scriptures to us and not to them, drawing everything written into an accusation against them and a defense for us. “You have made him cease from his purification.” In what way? By instituting the true purification, baptism. Once a complete cleansing had been proclaimed, the partial purifications of the Jews were necessarily abolished. This is why the sixth edition among the translators gives “You made him sink” instead of “You made him cease.” “You have dashed his throne to the ground.” Whether you mean the royal throne, the teacher's throne or the priestly one, all the thrones of the Jews were shattered. That is why they are said to have been dashed to the ground, for it was on the earth that their kings, priests and teachers had set their minds. “You have shortened the days of his time; you have poured shame over him.” Their polity did not last for ever, nor was it ordained to endure until the consummation of the age, as that of the Gentiles was. So they are rightly said to have had shame poured over them. It is plain that the time of their polity was [shortened] because of their lawlessness. This is shown by what God declared to Solomon about the temple: “If you and your children turn away from me and worship other gods, I will cut Israel off from the land that I gave them, and this house, which I consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight.” A Diapsalma had to follow this prophecy, since the prophet now leaves the person of the Jews and offers intercession for the whole of humanity. “How long, O Lord, will you turn away to the end?” By “turning away to the end,” that is, completely, he means the postponement of the Savior's coming. The Creator was not going to show compassion to our race in any other way than by taking up into himself the firstfruits of the lump. “Your wrath will be kindled like fire.” That is, it will consume those who heaped it up, for this is what fire does. Why does he not say “has been kindled” but “will be kindled”? Because when we sin, God is angry as a father is, but he is also patient, until we add sin to sin and kindle against ourselves a fiercer drive toward punishment at the time of Gehenna. “Remember what my substance is.” It is frail, he says, and worthless, for we come from earth and return to earth. That is why we need your providence to fashion us anew. What follows makes this clear: “Have you created all the children of men in vain?” That is, you did not make human beings as a matter of no importance, only to appear and then vanish like the other animals. You made them to stand out among all created things, and so that their appearing might show the usefulness of creation. But now things have turned out the opposite way, since man is snuffed out by death. The prophet laments this in what follows: “Who is the man who will live and not see death, who will rescue his soul from the hand of Hades?” The sentence of death, he says, holds sway over all. The souls of all, even of the righteous, are held fast in Hades, and the dignity of the image in us has been ruined by the tyranny of death. The prophet uses such words everywhere to hasten the coming of the Savior. For no one can rescue himself from death or bring his own soul up from Hades before the coming of the one who overpowers death by death. And now, see, he inserts a Diapsalma again, since he has turned the prophecy back to the Jewish people. “Where are your mercies of old, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?” That is, the mercies of your truth. He means Christ, who is the truth. What God swore to David, David himself has told in song elsewhere: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not go back on it: one of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne.”

8. So he calls on the promise to come, since he is hinting at the coming of Christ, in which every kind of mercy and every reason for loving-kindness are given to us. These mercies are ancient because God planned the mystery concerning them before the ages. That is why Paul says: “The mystery hidden before the ages and before the generations, for our glory.” Isaiah called it an ancient and true counsel. “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I bore in my bosom from many nations.” He calls the prophecy his bosom, for in it, as in a bosom, he stored up the real reproach, understood in its spiritual sense. Still more, David calls the prediction about the Lord his own bosom, since the Lord was to come forth from his loins according to the flesh. The prophecy about Christ seemed to have been postponed and was therefore thought to be false, and so they endured many reproaches from the nations. This was true not only of David but of all the prophets, whom he called servants of God. He begged God to call their reproach to mind, so that, sparing the prophets' reputation, he might make the Lord's incarnation manifest. Learn from what follows that this is so. “With which they reproached the exchange of your Christ.” Do you see that those who reproached did so because of Christ? It was not only those from the Gentiles who reproached, but the Jewish people as well. That is why Paul rightly said: “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” Above, then, he said that the prophets, whom he calls servants, were reproached by many nations. Here he says that the exchange of Christ, namely the Church, suffers reproaches from the enemies of God, that is, from the Jews. For Christ took the Church in exchange for the synagogue. It is about the Jews that this same David said: “The enemies of the Lord lied to him. And he fed them with the finest wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.” Why, then, do they reproach the Church? Because she was expected to be betrothed by faith, as Hosea says. He puts it this way: “And I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord.” He speaks to the Church as to one who did not know God, since she had received neither the law nor the prophets. But until Christ came, the preaching of faith had no place. “Blessed be the Lord for ever. So be it, so be it.” The prophet set a fine seal on his words. He doubles the blessing given to Christ, and blesses him in the same words Paul used: “From them, according to the flesh, comes Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.” This is why the other translators rendered “So be it, so be it” as “Amen, amen.” Why did he double the blessing? Because when the God who is over all came, he put an end to the reproach both of the prophets and of the Church. You should know that the third book, as the interpreters divide it, ends here and receives its seal. You will remember that we said earlier that the prophecy of the Psalms is divided into five books, and that each book is completed by a psalm that ends with a doxology followed by “Amen.”

1. The Spirit devised a fine title of honour for Moses. We have divided ourselves: some of us went over to the enemy and became the property of sin, while others, belonging to the Maker, keep what was formed unblemished for the One who formed it. So the Spirit called Moses "man of God," so that you may learn that the righteous man is God's own special possession. But why did he ascribe this psalm to Moses? Moses is not found to have written it. Or why was it not handed down together with his songs? Learn, then, the reason, which is both true and reasonable. In the opening the psalmist mentioned the Maker of the world, because he wished to devise a fitting beginning for the fourth book of the Psalms. Now it is Moses' special distinction to speak about the creation of the world, and so the psalmist allotted him this part of his own lyre. "Lord, you have been our refuge in generation and generation." The prophet shows that God's care is unceasing, for by "generation and generation" he means not two particular generations but all of them. The spiritual enemy began with the deception through the serpent, and he has gone on making war on our race in every age and in every way of life. So we had to take refuge in God. Since we could not be saved in any other way, we went to war against the one who seems to be mighty, with the One who is truly mighty on our side. "Before the mountains came into being, and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God." Here the psalmist establishes two things for us. First, that the world came into being, since some suppose it to be uncreated. So he presented the mountains as having come into being by the word of creation, and the earth likewise as being formed. Second, that God is their Maker, since he exists before all things and is therefore the beginning of all things. Having said "the earth," he did not add "the world" for no reason. By this word he calls to our attention man and the other living creatures by which the earth was allotted to be inhabited, so that we would never trace the wild beasts, or the reptiles, or any of the other animals back to another creator. And he rightly says "from age to age," that is, to the age to come. He says that God is in every way both Maker and Creator (for all this is presupposed of God's essence), and at the same time he is fighting against all the contrary opinions. For there are some who posit one God of the present life and another of the life to come, and with the words just quoted he overturned their blasphemous opinion. "Do not turn man back to humiliation." What kind of humiliation? Divinely inspired Scripture speaks of many kinds. Sometimes it means the modesty that comes from one's own disposition, as when Christ says, "Learn that I am meek and lowly in heart." Sometimes it means the humbling that comes from discipline for our correction, which is why David says, "It is good for me that you humbled me." And sometimes it means the humiliation that comes from punishment, which makes the one punished an object of reproach, as when he says of the devil, "You have humbled the proud one like one who is wounded." This is the humiliation he prays may be kept from man, so that man too may not be cast away from God as that one was cast away. That is why Symmachus rendered "condemnation" instead of "humiliation." Having prayed this, the prophet next adds God's answer: "And you said, Turn back, sons of men." For if we turn back, we are not turned away into humiliation, like the one who is sick with wickedness he never repents of. "For a thousand years in your eyes, Lord, are like yesterday that has passed, and a watch in the night." He clearly sets forth God's long-suffering. Because of it God commanded men to turn back, and he counts a thousand years as one day, the time already gone by. And not even as one day, but as a watch in the night, a time much [?] than the day, for they divide the night into four watches. So God does not grow weary of being patient through each person's whole life, since he reckons a thousand years as a very short time, and not as the present time but as time already past. "Their contemptible things shall be years." Whose? Those of sinners, for what follows is also about them. Even if their contemptible things last many years and a long time, they do not possess them forever. He gives the name "contemptible things" to the prosperity of wicked men, who boast and trust in nothing they ought to, but perhaps in beauty, or wealth, or bodily strength. Since these are temporary, they are worth nothing, and so they are called "contemptible things." That is why Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar, "The Most High rules over the kingdom of men, and he will give it to whomever he pleases, and will set over it the most contemptible of men." "In the morning may it pass by like grass; in the morning may it flower and pass by; in the evening may it fall, be hardened and wither."

2. He calls the present life "morning." He does not mean in comparison with the life to come, but that when the present life ends, the darkness of death comes on. So Jeremiah says, "Woe to us, for the day has declined, and the shadows are failing." He too calls the present life "day," and the way of life within it "shadows," since it lasts only a little while. In the present life, then, is human prosperity. One kind passes by like grass, another like a flower; that is, it passes through. The one falls like a flower, because it is so very short-lived. The other may stay green for some time, but later, heated by the sun of righteousness, it is hardened and dried up, and is shown to be grass fit for the oven and for burning. So what the prophet Isaiah, and James too, set forth for our admonition comes exactly true: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man like the flower of grass. The grass withered and its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished." But the prophet utters these words not as a wish but as a declaration, and in anger. For even though he says "may it pass by," he does not use the word as a prayer. Theodotion makes this clear, since in place of "may it pass by" he rendered "it will pass by." And when God brings punishment on sinners in due time, the splendour of the present is shown to be rotten, as the next verse shows: "For we have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we were troubled." The prophet himself usually presents wrath as milder than anger. You will see this especially when you come to this verse of his: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your anger." He assigned rebuke to wrath, and the chastening that follows rebuke, that is, punishment, to anger. So here too he says that through anger we fail, that is, are destroyed, but through wrath we are troubled. One who is troubled is not altogether destroyed. If he comes to his senses and turns back, he escapes the anger and the failing that comes from it, just as one who has been rebuked will be able to escape the chastening if he changes. "You have set our iniquities before you." First, because as one who is just he is hostile to sins and opposed to them. Second, because as judge he keeps transgressions before his eyes just as he does good deeds. "Our lifetime is in the light of your face." Nothing in it escapes God, and so it is said to be in the light before him, that is, made manifest to his face. And it is for illumination from the face of God, that is, from Christ, since he asks to be enlightened by him. "For all our days have failed." How? Learn from what follows: "In your anger we have failed." When Adam disobeyed in paradise, God was angered. Then we ourselves failed, and all our days, that is, our whole life, failed, because the judge condemned us to death. "We pondered our years as a spider." It was fitting for the prophet to ponder such things and reflect on them as a philosopher, to regard human life as a spider's web, and to keep reckoning this about himself. From this he would be able both to endure painful things and to despise the things that seem good, since their substance is rotten. "The days of our years, in them, are seventy years." "In them" means "of some," for few reach the number of years mentioned. "And if in strength, eighty years." By "strength" he means bodily vigour. Instead of "in strength," Symmachus rendered "by a marvel," showing that it is not easy even for a vigorous man to reach so great an age. "And the greater part of them is toil and trouble." So he called human life a spider for two reasons. First, because it lasts only a short time, for weakness is characteristic of the spider. Second, because it involves toil and labour to no profit. The spider too puts its webs together with much toil and effort, because they are so very fine, and yet the labour spent on them is unprofitable, for it comes to nothing useful. Why did he limit the number of human years to seventy, when many reach a hundred years and more? Surely because he did not think the years beyond the eightieth worth counting at all. They are superfluous to life, driving people into an overripe old age that makes them almost like the dead. "For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be chastened." By "gentleness" he means the sentence that went forth against us from God: "Earth you are, and to earth you will return." God wished to soften the punishments that came before it (I mean "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread" and "Thorns and thistles the earth will bring forth for you"). So he devised this death as an end for us. Through it we shall be greatly disciplined, not so much punished as benefited, for through the expectation of death we avoid many of the evils of this world. "Who knows the power of your anger, and, out of fear of you, to number your wrath?"

3. Here the prophet uses "who" not of what is impossible but of what is rare, as in "Who shall ascend the mountain of God?" and "Who is the man who desires life?" By raising the question he shows that such people are both rare and blessed. So also here. To know the might of God's anger, and out of fear of him, that is, because of fear of him, to number his wrath, that is, to examine it and reckon it up, produces abstinence from sins and the accomplishment of the virtues. "So make known to me your right hand, and those trained in heart in wisdom." He calls Christ the right hand of God. Those "trained in heart in wisdom," that is, in Christ (for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God), are the apostles. He did not say "trained in tongue" but "in heart," which is proper to the apostles as bearers of God, who also have the mind of Christ, as Paul said. So he prays that Christ and the apostles may be made known, that is, revealed, since from them salvation is secured for us sinners. But having said "So make known," he does not go on to say how. Clearly he wanted to state the manner in which he prays that Christ may be revealed, whether in exaltation or in humility, but was at a loss which of the two it was fitting to choose. Exaltation makes him inaccessible to men, while humility makes him easy to despise. Therefore Christ chose the mean between the two, healing the lowliness of his sufferings with miracles. "Turn, Lord (how long?), and be entreated concerning your servants." He prays not that God himself turn, but that he turn us, that is, correct us. Or he does want God to turn, so that, having turned, he may look upon the straying sheep like a shepherd; and he wants him to be entreated on their behalf because of their wandering. He says "how long" not as an accusation, but as one lamenting God's delay and wishing to show that our affairs need speed. "We were filled in the morning with your mercy, Lord, and we rejoiced and were glad in all our days." The prophet has not yet finished the prayer, for he continues it in the following verses. Yet he uttered these words as though he had already been heard. In them he glories in having been filled with God's mercy, that is, in having enjoyed it abundantly. He says we were filled "in the morning." By this he means either the time of the Saviour's resurrection, which took place "very early in the morning," as Mark says, or the present life, in which Christ, the mercy of God, came to dwell among men. With his good things, which are many, we have been filled, and over them we rejoiced and were glad all our days, the kind of days that once came to the Jewish people when they held power for a time and then again fell under their enemies and served them. You will find this recounted again and again in the book of Judges. "We were glad in return for the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we saw evils." What days is he hinting at, if not the days we spent enslaved to idols, when he humbled us by allowing us to serve the things we ourselves had made? Then we saw many and various evils. We not only blasphemed against the Maker, but were also ignorant of what nature itself requires, for we sacrificed our sons and daughters to demons. "And look upon your servants and upon your works, and guide their sons." Do you see again how he has taken up the prayer once more? And what exactly is he praying for? That God would look upon us and upon our works. He will look upon us and hold us as his own servants when we obey his law, for this is the mark of servants. Then he will consent to watch over our works too, as good works. And he will guide us and our sons, both those of the flesh and indeed those of the spirit, since they are taught good things by good people and he has seen that they are fit for guidance from God. "And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands upon us." Suppose we share in the brightness of God, that is, the illumination of the Spirit. The saints who share in it possess a brightness of their own, for it says, "In the brightness of your saints; from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you." Then you will say that "the works of our hands," our deeds, are directed by God "upon us," that is, for our benefit. They are done according to the law he gives, so that what was said to the apostles is said to us as well: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." "And direct the work of our hands." Here the psalmist is hinting at almsgiving, for this is the outstanding work of our hands. That is why he set it apart from the many works he mentioned in the earlier verses, wishing to confer, as it were, a special honour on almsgiving. When almsgiving directs us, we gain no ordinary reward, but mercy and compassion from God, for "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy."

1. The other translators have this psalm without a title. Yet that is no reason to reject the title; rather, we should accept it. It comes from the Seventy, who showed by their agreement with one another that they had been supplied with the Spirit. Under the Spirit's guidance they had good reason to give the present psalm the title "A Praise of a Song, of David," that is, the praise of a song. Among his melodies this one above all should be held in high honour, since it contains great and wonderful things. "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the shelter of the God of heaven." The help of the Most High is the law he gave, for it has been given to us as an ally against our invisible enemies. So the one who lives according to its aim dwells in it. This man "will abide in the shelter of the God of heaven," clearly in the age to come. He will live together with God and inhabit the same dwellings as the Maker of heaven. Or else he will be sheltered by God himself and not by any created thing. "He will say to the Lord, You are my helper and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him." Rightly so. The one who lives according to God's commandments speaks boldly, as one who hopes in him. He will have God as his helper as he stands spiritually against the spiritual wars. And if he is weak, not because God's help has been defeated but because he himself has grown weaker through slackness, he will say to God, "You are my refuge." Nor will you do wrong in saying it, if you speak boldly on the strength of the life you have already lived. "For he will rescue me from the snare of the hunters and from a troubling word." The snare of the hunters, and the troubling word too, is every counsel that urges toward base things, muddies the souls of the deceived with pleasures, and trains them in that way. God rescues us from this when we take refuge in him. We can no longer be snared by pleasures, because we find everything in the world worth nothing in comparison with God. "With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope." Why did the prophet speak the preceding words in his own person, but now speaks as though addressing someone else? Surely because what is said now is directed to the people from the Gentiles. He is instructing them in how they will be able to overcome the demons who tyrannize them. And what kind of alliance does God promise them? He says the first comes from the Law and the Prophets. These are God's shoulders, since he laid up his knowledge in them as on shoulders. With them he overshadows the one who comes to him, not allowing him to be scorched by the devil's burning heat. That is why Paul too declared that the law has a shadow.
