The wings are the Gospel, since one who lives according to it is lifted lightly from earth to heaven as if he had grown wings. Under these, then, we must hope, that is, have the kind of hope in God that the command of the Gospel enjoins, so as not to hope in God and mammon, but in God alone. In this way we can never be harmed by enemies, whether visible or spiritual. "His truth will surround you with a shield." Truth is a strong weapon for one who does not lie. But indeed Christ is truly the truth of God, as we have often said. His weapon is the cross. Surrounded by it, we face every war with confidence and rout every enemy, as what follows shows. "You will not be afraid of the terror by night, of the arrow that flies by day." The terror by night is that of the pleasures of the flesh, for it attacks above all in darkness. The arrow that flies by day is greed, for that is the right time for it to fly, that is, to be at work. Yet understand both of these as the assault of demons. They usually frighten us at night, since darkness helps them with their terrors. By day they fly, for they are creatures of the air. They are never still, but like arrows they attack those who are unguarded and stripped of the weapons of the flesh. "From the thing that walks about in darkness, from mishap and the noonday demon." Do you see that what came before was also said about demons? Since they come in many kinds (for deceit runs in many divisions), he says, "From the thing that walks about in darkness," that is, from anything at all whose activity and course lie in darkness. By saying this in general terms, he called to mind the opposing powers, which delight in darkness and, because of their wickedness, have no fellowship with the light. That is why they will also be led away into the outer darkness. But they also haunt the noonday part of the day, for at that time most people are accustomed to rest. Being thieves and robbers, they dread people's constant gaze, shrinking from the authority of the image we bear. That is why they mostly busy themselves around tombs and mires and other places empty of people. For this reason they also dare to fall upon us and meet us in the middle of the day. "A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you." The apostle Paul taught us about the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left: glory and dishonour, ill repute and good repute, and what follows. With these the opposing powers are fought and fall. Fewer fall by the weapons on the left, more by those on the right. Therefore he says that thousands of enemies will fall "at your side" (by which the prophet here meant the left side, as is clear from his distinguishing it from the right), but tens of thousands at the right. And do not be surprised. The fall of the demons begins with the sufferings of the godly, that is, of the martyrs and of all who have emulated the martyrs' contests. Sufferings are counted among the weapons of the left hand, and so he counted first those who fall on the left.

2. Even so, most of the powers of the idols were brought down by the honours later paid to those who were devoted to Christ. He says that the victory over the enemies and their overthrow are achieved so effortlessly that they do not even come near us, because they are wary of fighting at close quarters. Only with your eyes will you look on, and you will see the recompense of sinners. Even if they make war from far off and unseen, he says, as invisible beings, you will still see with your own eyes the trophies raised against them, and the recompense paid back to them by those they had deceived. For those who once fashioned idols now pull idols down; those who once built temples now burn temples; those who once made gods of the works of their own hands now throw them down with their own hands. Hear how this was accomplished. The prophet gave the part of humanity, which answers: For you, Lord, are my hope. These words show both gratitude and truth. For it was by hope in God that we won the war against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of darkness. Otherwise we who are flesh could never have overcome beings without flesh. You have made the Most High your refuge. No evils will come to you, and no scourge will draw near your dwelling. The prophet has brought in a fine personification. He approved that the man who had conquered gave God the credit for the victory, and so he took care to anoint him, like an athlete, with these further words too. He says that evils will not merely fail to overpower him, but will not come near him at all, for fear of God, who dwells in him and shields him. This is the God he has made his Refuge, or his Dwelling, as the other translators have rendered it. So great a good is it to take refuge in God. That is why Jeremiah also said: Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope. How could he not be blessed, when evils do not come to him at all, and no scourge draws near his tent, that is, his body? For Paul too called it this: For we who are in this tent groan under our burden, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. And why will no scourge draw near? Because being scourged belongs to sinners. Whoever has taken refuge in God will not be among the sinners, and so it is only right that he is not scourged. For he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up on their hands, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone. So the one who takes refuge in God is found to be a son of God, so great is the dignity of these words. The Adversary applied them to Christ when, tempting him, he urged him to throw himself down from on high. You see too how he says that God gives command concerning the one who has taken refuge in him not to one angel but to many, so that they guard all his ways and bear him on their hands, that is, carry him along. So angels do not only guard the devout; they also lead them by the hand, so that they may not strike their feet. And he ordained that the one below should be served by the powers above, in honour of the image that the one below bears. But you should also understand here God-bearing angels, that is, messengers: those who have the knowledge of God and guard and guide us in all our ways, that is, in our ways of life, so that we may not strike against the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence. That God has appointed for us angels who teach and proclaim his knowledge, hear from Malachi, who says: The priest's lips will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty. You will tread on the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon. By these words he hints at the evil powers, in which the venom of wickedness is stored up as it is in reptiles. That is why the Lord also said: See, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. So whoever tramples down anger tramples a lion, for that animal is full of rage. That is why Solomon too says: A king's threat is like the rage of a lion. In the same way, whoever tramples down pleasures and every other vice tramples asp and basilisk and dragon. For the pleasures of the flesh, and all the wickedness of this life, are fittingly likened to reptiles that crawl along the ground. And perhaps it is in the proper sense the basilisk that is trampled by whoever tramples down envy, since envy reigns as king among the vices. At the same time, the basilisk is said to carry its venom in its eye, just as the envious are said to cast the evil eye. Because he hoped in me, I will rescue him; I will shelter him, because he has known my name. The psalmist had said great things, almost incredible things: that powers so wicked and so strong that they are compared to the lion, the dragon, the asp and the basilisk, the most dangerous of all beasts, are trampled by us. So, see, he brought in God himself to confirm what was said, and to show us that hope in him is an armour that cannot be pierced. By it we are rescued from our enemies, if we first place ourselves under him, and we are sheltered, so that they can no longer plot against us. We have only to know God's name, that is, to worship him gratefully in deed and word, with tongue and mind, in thought and action. For the one who knows a king is not someone who has merely heard of him, but someone who conducts himself toward him as one ought toward a good king. He will cry to me, and I will hear him. What could be more blessed than this, to have God ready to help, prepared to stand against our enemies? I am with him in affliction; I will deliver him and glorify him. So affliction is no longer affliction. It becomes joy and glory because of the One who dwells with him and shares it, and the purpose of those who afflict him turns into its opposite. So it was with Nebuchadnezzar, when he threw the youths into the fiery furnace to destroy them. They were not only rescued from the destruction he had threatened, but were even worshipped by the tyrant who had threatened them. With length of days I will fill him: clearly this means the enjoyment of the age to come. For however long human life here may be, it is very small compared with that. And I will show him my salvation. You may say that 'salvation' means the salvation by which those who have believed in God are saved at that judgment. But above all you will say that it means Christ, who is the Father's salvation, for in him the Father saved our race. This, then, is the one he promised to show us. For the hope of the devout is to see him face to face, as Paul also explained to the Corinthians.

1. The psalm is anonymous, but not untitled. It has a title that shows its subject, but it hides the name of the one who sang it. The title itself shows the reason. This psalm had been assigned to the Sabbath day, as one sung by all the psalmists, so it is fittingly ascribed neither to David, nor to Asaph, nor to the sons of Korah, nor to anyone else, since it was common to all. Still, it is clear that the prophecy belonged to David, as with the rest of the psalms. It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing to your name, O Most High. How could it not be good to confess to the One who is good, who is kind to those who confess and never punishes them? Although he knows our affairs, he gladly learns them from those who confess. He wants to cut short the enemies' accusation against us, and to justify us through our confession. For the righteous man is his own accuser at the very start. But he rightly commanded us to confess first and then to sing, because God must be praised from a pure heart. How else is anyone cleansed of sins except by being freed of them through confession? And what does it mean that singing is good? That it is beneficial and useful: To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth by night. He commands us to meditate on God day and night, for by saying 'morning' he meant the day. But he assigned meditation on truth to the night, to stir fear and compunction in us at that hour. Most people spend the night mostly on pleasures and schemes. He wants them to remember that God's truth is terrible to sinners, and so to stop every improper deed and lawless thought. And if they do commit some offence, he wants them, when morning comes, that is, when day has arrived, not to despair at all, but to meditate on God's mercy and look toward repentance, which alone can obtain mercy for sinners. Then how ought we to sing and proclaim? On a ten-stringed psaltery, with song on the lyre. He wants the one who sings to meditate on mercy and truth from both Testaments, that of the gospel and that of the law. That is why he mentioned psaltery and lyre. By calling the psaltery here ten-stringed, he hinted at the Testament of the law, for the law has ten commandments. And he assigned the song to the lyre. This is surely the new song, of which this same psalmist said in another part of his prophecy: O God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will play to you. So he is hinting at the Testament of the gospel. And why does he use two instruments for his melody? For you have gladdened me, Lord, by what you have made, and I will exult in the works of your hands. I have twofold blessings, he says; that is why I have eagerly taken up twofold instruments of praise. For we rejoice in what God has made: in the beauty of the sky, the variety of the stars, the good things of the earth, the working of the sea. Divine Scripture regularly uses this word to describe the whole of this visible world. Solomon shows this in Ecclesiastes when he says: I gave my heart to every work that has been made under the sun. The works of God's hands are ourselves. Your hands made me and fashioned me, he himself says in another psalm. And Isaiah says: And now, Lord, you are our father; we are clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hands. So we rejoice in creation, because we enjoy it. But we exult over ourselves, and exulting is greater than rejoicing. This is quite reasonable: we are made of clay, yet we have so great a possession to enjoy, and besides that we are called sons of the Maker. How great are your works, Lord! Your thoughts are exceedingly deep.

2. God's works were magnified. They did not themselves grow in size; rather, we grew in knowledge of them and became able to grasp their greatness, as far as that is possible. Or rather, we became able to know this about them: that they are beyond comprehension. His thoughts too, that is, his counsels concerning us, which he plans and arranges for us, are so deep that Paul says: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways! The righteous glorify God for these things and marvel at him beyond measure on their own account. Sinners, by contrast, stumble over them because of their folly, and indeed because of the [?] that comes from folly. What follows shows this: A senseless man will not know, and a fool will not understand these things. For it is the mark of the senseless not to yield to God's wisdom, and not to know that he steers all things with justice, governs them with equity and arranges them for our good, even if for a time we do not know the causes of what happens. Where, then, does the stumbling of the foolish come from? He made this known in what follows. When sinners sprang up like grass, and all who work lawlessness peered out, it was so that they might be destroyed for ever and ever. The springing up of sinners has only a passing comeliness. He called it a springing up, a rising, not because of its brightness, but so that you may learn that misfortunes come after it. It deceives the senseless and foolish, and leads them to think of God as having left the world without providence. They do not notice that even if sinners spring up, it is like grass, which withers as soon as it has bloomed. Yet when sinners prosper, all who work impiety peer out. They show themselves boldly, but that boldness turns out to be the cause of their eternal ruin, for to be bold about evil deeds is worse than doing them. But you, Lord, are Most High for ever. It has often been said that this prophet especially calls the present life 'the age'. In it, he says, God is Most High, that is, incomprehensible, for that is what he hints at by 'height'. God is always so, but now even more so. For in the age to come we shall grasp, if not everything, still a great deal of God's judgments compared with what we know now. That is why Paul says: We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, then what is partial will be done away. Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known. For see, your enemies, Lord, for see, your enemies will perish, and all who work lawlessness will be scattered. This is why, he says, we cannot now grasp God's judgments: his enemies, that is, the sinners, perish only in the age to come, and only then are all who work lawlessness scattered. So now, while they are gathered together and still standing, and have not yet received the destruction owed to sinners, some deceive them and lead them astray into thinking they will not pay the penalty. Yet even here they have penalty enough, in being called enemies of God. And the gravest threat is that they will not only perish but also be scattered. So it is in vain that they [gather] for themselves kinships and friendships forged in wickedness. They do not know that none of these can stand for long, since God scatters every gathering of the lawless. And my horn will be exalted like a unicorn's, and my old age in rich mercy. The righteous are unicorns, but Christ is so above all, for he used one horn, the cross, against the opposing powers. He has given us faith in him as a horn against our adversaries, and that faith is exalted in the same way as the Lord's horn, that is, the cross. For just as the cross was glorified through sufferings, so the faith of the devout is exalted through persecutions and glorified through sufferings. And our old age too, that is, the last times, is exalted in rich mercy. For in the last times the One who shows us abundant mercy came to meet us so generously that he invited sinners and tax collectors into his kingdom. And my eye has looked upon my enemies, and my ear will hear about the evildoers who rise up against me. Scripture has often declared that the demons are our enemies. Our eye has looked upon them as it watched the fall of the idols, the burning of the temples and the overthrow of the altars, by which they had netted us for death. Our ear too has heard what Jesus threatened would come upon them in the future, and we have seen those things just as surely. What are they? That the eternal fire has been prepared for the devil and his angels. He did well to call them those who 'rise up', showing that we are as far above them as masters are above servants. But if we grow slack, they rise up when they see us weak or fast asleep, just as servants rise up against masters who are sick or asleep. The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; like a cedar in Lebanon he will be multiplied.

3. It is not for nothing that he likens the righteous man to the palm tree. Only a small part of the palm is in the ground, and all the rest is above it. Its fruit, too, cannot be gathered by wild animals, because the tree is tall and hard to climb. Besides this, nothing in the palm is useless; everything about it is serviceable. If you apply each of these points to the righteous man, you will marvel at how exact and true the image is. Palm branches are also given to athletes and runners as a symbol of victory. So we can be crowned in the age to come in no other way than through righteousness. That is why Paul said: From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day. And why, you will ask, does he say, Like a cedar in Lebanon he will be multiplied? Because Lebanon, on account of the barrenness of its cedars, is a figure and symbol of the Gentiles; and yet God's righteousness is multiplied among the Gentiles too. Many prophets, many patriarchs, and other God-bearing and righteous men came from Israel. But the martyrs who arose from the Gentiles outnumbered them, and in these God's righteousness grew into a multitude. Learn from what follows how it increased. Or else the point is this: the palm has a white flower, and keeps its fruit hidden while it is unripe; but when it means to bring the fruit to maturity, it shows it outwardly. So too the righteous man is eager at first to keep his virtues hidden, but when he reaches perfection, they reveal themselves. Planted in the house of the Lord, they will blossom in the courts of our God. Instead of 'planted', other translators have rendered 'transplanted'. This makes clear that he means not simply cedars, but those transplanted from error into the house of God, of which Paul wrote to Timothy: So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God. Or else: Lebanon is a mountain of idolatry, and as long as the cedars are there, Scripture disparages them; but when they are moved to build the holy temple, it praises them. For Solomon took some of these for the temple of the Lord. They will blossom in the courts of our God: that is, in the local churches. For by 'the house of God' he meant, in a comprehensive sense, the universal Church. Or else the house of God is the law. Into it those from the Gentiles were transplanted from the lawlessness that prevailed among them, and they were granted to blossom and bear fruit in the courts of God, that is, in the commandments. They will still be multiplied in a rich old age. Their prosperity, he says, is not temporary. Because of the word 'blossom', someone might suppose that it was temporary for the Gentiles. But they multiply and advance in a sleek old age, for as time goes on the piety of the Gentiles increases. And they will be faring well, to proclaim that the Lord our God is upright, and there is no unrighteousness in him. You see that from faring well, that is, from being vigorous and in their prime, they advance to zeal. Or 'faring well' (eupathein) may properly be said of the faithful in the sense of suffering (pathein) readily for the One in whom they have believed. So by faring well they proclaim God's uprightness, and that there is no unrighteousness in him. For since he is upright and just, he crowns those who suffer for him and grants them exceptional prizes. And we too, knowing God's uprightness, should become upright both toward him and toward our neighbour. We should not pursue the virtues in hypocrisy, nor work deceit against our brother. For there is no unrighteousness in our judge himself; he renders judgment to each according to his deeds.

Among the Hebrews this psalm has no title. In the Septuagint, however, it has one, because those translators wished it to be understood of the true David, the one strong of hand, that is, Christ (for this is what “David” means). This is because the prophecy that follows was composed in praise of Christ, and also as a song. The opening words of the title are not found in the more accurate copies, so we did not think it necessary to add an interpretation of them. “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty. The Lord has clothed himself with power and girded himself.” And when, you will ask, did God, the King before the ages, begin to reign? And what beauty could he put on at all, when he himself is beauty? If the heaven is so beautiful that one can never have enough of it, and the same is true of the stars and the other elements of creation, how could he who made so much beauty not be beautiful beyond measure and in his very essence? But the psalmist is plainly prophesying the Lord's incarnation. His flesh is rightly called beauty: first, because it bears his image; then, because it is sinless; and besides, because the mystery wrought for us was fitting for him, since he is good and loves humankind. That is why the Spirit in another psalm called him “fair in beauty beyond the sons of men.” This flesh he calls not only beauty but also power. This is not because the Mighty One gained power from it, but because through it he displayed to the world his own power, which had been unknown. And to “clothing himself” he had to add “girding himself.” He shows by this that the Lord not only took the form of a servant, but in an ineffable way so girded himself, that is, so united humanity to himself and bound it so tightly, that the Word and the flesh are one. This is why he is also said to have become flesh. And why did he plan this mystery? “For he established the world, which shall not be shaken.” Here, he says, is the reason for the Word's incarnation. The world was being shaken by error, and by coming to dwell in it he made it firm, so that no further shaking need be expected. You may also call the Church the “world,” the inhabited world, for it is inhabited by the angels and by God himself, which is why it is also called his house. It shall not be shaken. Many plot against it, yet it is built on the rock, “and the gates of Hades,” that is, the mouths of the heretics, “shall not prevail against it.” “Your throne has been prepared from of old; you are from everlasting.” He calls Christ's humanity not only beauty and power but also a throne. Another prophet also spoke of it: “And a throne shall be set right with mercy, and a righteous king shall sit in the tent of David, judging.” The psalmist, prophesying of Christ, says this: “His throne is like the sun before me.” So the mystery of the Lord's incarnation has been prepared from of old. “From of old, from everlasting,” he says, that is, from the beginning of the creation of the visible world. For then, when he created man, he fashioned him after his own image and gave him a royal stamp, since he knew that he was going to take that nature upon himself. That is why he added “You are,” as if to say: you who have now become flesh, you are the one who from everlasting created man as seemed good to you. “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices.” Understand the rivers as the workings of the Spirit, for Christ says: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” The evangelist explains this, adding: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” These gifts of the Spirit, then, lifted up their voices, that is, raised them high, for they were made manifest everywhere on earth, as if borne down from the height of heaven. And clearly they lifted them up through the tongues of the prophets who prophesied beforehand. “The rivers will lift up their crashing waves.” What instruments did they use? Clearly the apostles. He has now mentioned a time still to come, when the gifts of the Spirit were exalted through the apostles and raised their crashing waves especially high, that is, their swells. Or you may take “crashing waves” as “the depths,” as Symmachus rendered it, or as “lowliness,” for this is how the fifth and sixth editions have handed it down. If it means the depths of the spiritual rivers, these are the hidden mysteries of the gifts of the Spirit. If it means lowliness, that is because most people think little of the glory of the Spirit. Either way, these things escape the notice of most, but through the apostles they are exalted and made manifest.

1. The fleeting nature of prosperity. He spoke these words as though complaining about the wicked, indignant that time is being spent on them while God is long-suffering, so that they even boast of things for which they ought to feel fear and shame. And what is their boast? “They will utter and speak unrighteousness; all who work lawlessness will speak.” Those who did not hold back from wicked deeds, how will they hold back their words? So they are always talking and urging others to fall. At one moment they say, “Let us do evil, that good may come”; at another, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”; and again, “The Lord does not look upon the earth”; and all such sayings for which the prophets are found to denounce them. “They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your inheritance.” They do both by deeds and by words. The one who humbles God's people and afflicts his inheritance, that is, humanity, is not only the one who robs, beats, reviles and judges unjustly. It is also the one who gives bad counsel and recommends lawlessness as if it were profitable. Of such people it is said: “Bad company corrupts good morals.” Did not the spies sent out from the desert humble God's people when they advised a return to Egypt? “They have slain the widow and the orphan, and murdered the stranger.” This does not mean that they always used the sword or other weapons of war against them. Whoever takes the only field they own does away with the stranger and the widow. So does whoever robs them of their daily bread, or seizes the house that is their only shelter, or corrupts the court that hears their case. Many people do such things to them even now. Learn from what follows how great this sin is. “And they said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.” Robbers and lawbreakers may not say this with their tongues, but they say it in their minds. Moses the lawgiver wrote that God is the father of orphans, the judge of widows and the lover of strangers. These men would never have dared to rob or murder such people unless they had fallen into such arrogance as to agree in their own reasoning that they can escape the Creator's notice, that he set up the world without providence, and that the Judge does not watch over human affairs. Mocking them, he added what follows: “Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last.” This prophet's custom is to call “senseless” those who think blasphemous thoughts about God. Of them he says: “The fool said in his heart, There is no God.” Such are those who sin against widows, orphans and strangers, or commit any other lawlessness. Rebuking them, he urges them in the first line to understand. In the second he says, “Become wise at last,” showing that if they do not repent and become wise now, they will not be able to do so later: “For in Hades who will confess you?” That is why he also called them fools, because they idly waste the time for turning back. This is the mark of fools: not knowing how to make proper use of times and circumstances, and not even understanding what everyone agrees on. That is what comes next: “He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?” By the organs he also points to the senses that reside in them, hearing and sight. We have these and our other senses because God made them for us. How then, he says, can they claim that God is insensible to our affairs, when he gave us perception itself? He would not have given it if he had not known that what he gave was good. And whatever is good holds first place with God, the cause of all good things. “He who disciplines nations, shall he not reprove, he who teaches man knowledge?” He asks these questions too, not as doubtful matters but as things everyone agrees on, and the questions bring shame on those who argue otherwise. If he disciplines many nations, that is, humanity, how will he not reprove those who sin one by one? And how does he discipline the nations? “By teaching knowledge,” he says. What knowledge? Clearly the ability to tell good from evil, and the harmful from the beneficial. He taught us these not through any studies [?] or teachers, but through our natural notions. So for this reason too he will reprove sinners, that is, judge them. We cannot plead ignorance of what is unjust or just, since God has taught us the difference between them through the natural law. “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain.” The psalmist did not put this here in vain. He wants to keep us from thinking that God puts up with people because he does not know how badly they stumble in their thoughts, or how many vain things they devise that border on blasphemy against Christ. So he is not ignorant. He knows, and he reserves his judgment on them for the time to come. Not on all of them, however, for some he chastens already. The next words speak of these: “Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O Lord, and teach out of your law.”

2. The one disciplined by God is blessed in many ways. First, he becomes better and more self-controlled, so that he no longer lives the life of a beast and, having been made rational, is no longer counted among the irrational creatures. Second, when he is disciplined by God he is struck as by a father. That is why he is not said to be punished, but disciplined: punishing belongs to judges, disciplining to teachers. So the psalmist added, “You will teach him out of your law,” to show that God does not discipline in anger, but makes the one he disciplines learned in the law. And what is the gain? “To give him relief from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.” This prophet regards deliverance from the punishment to come as a great blessing. So in another psalm he says: “Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day.” It is fitting, then, that here too he calls blessed the one disciplined by God. Through discipline in this life such a person escapes the terrors to come and enjoys relief in the evil days. These are the times when those being punished undergo their pains. In those times a pit is also dug for the true sinner, namely the devil, of whom Paul said, “that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.” The punishments to come are being prepared for him. The psalmist had good reason to call them a pit, since the devil will never be able to climb out of them, but stays in them like someone buried in a pit. Still, one point deserves attention. David did not mean the same thing by “the evil day” and by “evil days.” The first is the day on which the judgment takes place, the day from which God delivers the merciful man and grants him complete freedom. The second are the times of torment. That is why he spoke of them in the plural and wrote “days,” not “day.” In those days God gives relief to the one who was disciplined, that is, he lightens the torments in proportion to the discipline, or to the conversion and amendment that came from it. “For the Lord will not cast off his people, nor will he forsake his inheritance.” Here the psalmist added the reason why God disciplines in this life those whom he calls blessed. Because he spares his own people and his own inheritance, he disciplines some of them. In this way they themselves may turn back and be saved, and may become an occasion and an example of turning back for others. If he had wanted to cast off his own people when they sinned, or to abandon his inheritance to its spiritual enemies, he would not discipline us. He would leave us to advance from injustice to something worse. You will hear from God himself that abandonment is a sign of great wrath, when he says to the Jews: “I will not punish your brides when they commit adultery, nor your daughters when they play the harlot.” And again: “I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest.” “Until righteousness returns to judgment, and all the upright in heart hold to it.” This does not mean that when righteousness returns to judgment God will cast off his own people or his inheritance. He gave his disciplines as proof that he does not neglect his inheritance, and by these words he wants to teach you how long they are needed. Christ, the true righteousness, will return to judgment and turn from long-suffering to judging. And “all the upright in heart,” that is, the righteous, will come to be “holding to it.” They will not be in it as people being judged, but will stand around it as a guard escorting the judge (which is why the other translators rendered “after him” instead of “holding to it”). Then the disciplines given one by one will cease, for God's tribunal is a place not of admonition but of recompense. He added “Pause” at this point because he was turning from general discourse to his own person. “Who will rise up for me against the evildoers, or who will stand with me against those who work lawlessness?” Here the prophet hints at the evil powers and the strong and fierce war they wage against us. He all but says the words of Paul: “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness.” Against these he asks and looks for an ally. Who can rise up to help us against them and fight at our side? So do not take pleasure in evildoers or delight in those who work lawlessness. The prophet is not only ready to fight them but also seeks someone to fight alongside him, and he names that ally next: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would very nearly have sojourned in Hades.” We need the alliance of God alone, he says, for he alone can defend us against such an army. Did he perhaps sing these words remembering his sin with Bathsheba? Had God not helped David then by sending Nathan and rousing him to repentance through the prophet's words, David's soul would have been in danger of sojourning in Hades, that is, in the death of sin.

3. If the righteous man who grows careless sojourns in death, the ungodly man lives there and makes it his home. “For he has no recovery in death,” since, as Solomon says, “when he has fallen into the depth of evils, he scorns.” “If I said, My foot has slipped, your mercy, O Lord, helped me.” Someone may recognize and confess his own sin, and when he is shaken may neither grow careless nor despair, but come to his senses. Such a person at once feels God's favor and mercy coming to help him. “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.” This too is the mark of a skilled physician: to apply remedies in proportion to the wounds. “Sorrows in the heart” may mean grief over one's own sins, born of conversion and compunction. It may mean grief at the prosperity of sinners, or at the troubles unjustly brought upon us. For all of them God provides a consolation that matches. Those who are unjustly plotted against have a new consolation, this beatitude of Christ: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Those who groan over their own sins are also greatly blessed: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” And those who groan at the prosperity of the lawless become aware of their own glory when ruin overtakes the lawless: “For the righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” You may also call sins the sorrows of the soul, as if they were toils and wounds. For these too Christ gives great consolation: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” And again: “I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world.” “Let not the throne of lawlessness be joined with you, which makes toil out of the commandment.” The devil is fittingly called the throne of lawlessness. You may take “throne” to mean kingship, or rest, or a seat; in every sense lawlessness both reigns and rests in the devil. He is also called the judge of injustice, not because he condemns injustice, but because he judges unjustly. He makes toil out of the commandment, that is, God's commandment. He makes the divine law seem laborious to us by suggesting pleasure and ease instead. God puts up with this because he wants to increase the reward of those who keep his law, since “each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.” The devil will not be joined with God. That is, he will never stand beside him at that time, namely the time of judgment. The angels will stand beside God as he judges, but the devil will not, for although he still exists, he has fallen from his rank. Why will he not stand beside him? Because God judges with love for humanity, while the devil is extremely hostile to humanity, as what follows shows. Of him and of those who sit with him and fight in his ranks it is said: “They will hunt after the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood.” He has clearly stated why the devil will not stand by at the coming judgment. Such beings will not hesitate to hunt the soul of the righteous, using as a pretext even a fault committed in ignorance or against one's will. They will also condemn innocent blood if they are given any power to condemn. That is why, when our failings are judged, God does not allow them to accuse us or bear witness against us. Instead he calls our own thoughts as accusers and our conscience as witness. For Paul says: “Their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else defending them.” This is how our hidden things are judged before God. “And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.” Who became this? The other translators rendered it “will be” [?], so the saying should be understood of the coming of the Only-begotten. For he became our refuge when we were pursued by real enemies. He also became the helper of a hope that was already in danger, since we were in despair because of the great mass of ungodliness. But he put an end to that despair when he said: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.” “And the Lord will repay them their lawlessness, and according to their wickedness the Lord God will make them vanish.” This is the mark of a just judge: to repay lawlessness to those who caused it. When you hear “lawlessness,” understand the punishment prepared for it. That is why the fifth and sixth editions read “their pains.” The wicked suffer their greatest punishment when they themselves and their works are taken out of the way, and when they no longer feed on human quarrels and stumbling. He will make them vanish, then, but not by destroying their being. He wants them to remain under punishment forever, which is why the fire prepared for them is called eternal. Rather, he makes them vanish by taking them out of the way, abolishing their dominion and no longer allowing them to be among us. For now, while we contend in order to be crowned, the devil holds the place of an opponent, and so he is allowed to act. But the age to come is not a time of contest but of reward, not of wrestling but of the crown. That is why Paul says of the present life: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” And of the life to come he says: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day.” So it is fitting that the enemies vanish once the deception connected with them has come to an end.

1. Although among the Hebrews this psalm has no title, since its subject is a general one, the Seventy nevertheless give it a fitting title, heading it "A Praise of a Song," because praise is mingled with prophecy, and it is customary for psalms of this kind to be titled in this way. "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout aloud to God our Savior." To whom does he say "Come"? You see that he has not added this. By issuing the call to no one in particular, he allows everyone to come forward as one who has been called. What this call is, and on what grounds he taught it, the following words make clear: "Let us come before his face with confession, and shout aloud to him with psalms." Do you see that he is announcing the good news of redemption from sins? For the confession clearly indicates this. So he rightly urges us to rejoice over this and to shout aloud, that is, to raise a cry of victory, since our spiritual enemies have been defeated. We are to shout aloud and rejoice to God, for the defeat of the enemies and the forgiveness of our offenses are his work. Hence he also bids us come before his face, that is, go out to meet Christ. For he is the face of the Father, [?] through confession. For we sinners can come into the Judge's sight in no other way than by anticipating him and confessing our offenses first. For he says, "State your sins first, so that you may be justified." And when we have confessed, then we are able to shout aloud with psalms as well. For a song of victory, which is what a shout is, is not fittingly offered from a defiled heart and a profane tongue; but when both have been cleansed by confession, the song becomes a sacrifice, and the psalm proves to be our shout of victory. "For the Lord is a great God, and a great King over all the earth." Do not credit the victory to yourself, he says, and when you shout aloud do not boast of the rout of your enemies as though you had achieved it yourself. For how could you, who are below, have conquered those who make war on you from on high? Or how could you, who are flesh, have conquered beings without flesh? Yet you did conquer, because God, who came to our aid, is a great Lord and a great King: as a great Lord, he not only sets free those who have served him well but also calls them to adoption as sons; as a great King, he does not merely make rulers of those who have campaigned with good zeal, but makes them sharers in his own kingdom. Over whom is he great? "Over all the gods," that is, the righteous. For the greatness of God is unknown to the ungodly but known to the godly. Just as the glory of the sun is not diminished because the blind do not know the light, so, because the ungodly misjudge the power of God, it does not follow that the godly should think meanly of his might. These he even called gods, because the righteous have been appointed by God as gods over the ungodly. Hence he says to Moses, "I have made you a god to Pharaoh." "For in his hand are the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his." Having called God great, he fittingly describes his greatness, not as great as it is, but as far as we are able to grasp it from the visible creation, and he sets out things in harmony with the prophecy of Isaiah. For Isaiah says, "He who holds the circle of the earth in his hand," and again, "Who set the mountains on scales, and the valleys in a balance?" "For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land." In naming the elements, he necessarily indicated what is in the elements as well. So whether we travel by sea or farm the land, knowing whose creatures and possessions these are, let us give thanks that he has brought such great things into being for our use, offering him praise not in words only but in deeds. And what praise is this? "Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and weep before the Lord who made us." Let us worship as servants; let us fall down as those who need his help; let us weep as sinners, who would obtain our petition in no other way than through his compassion. Nor is it fitting for us to be ashamed of any of these things, for they are done before him who made us, that is, who brought us into being out of nothing; and he who brought us into being out of nothing is the cause of every benefit.

2. Who, then, would be ashamed to bow down before someone who has done him even a small kindness, let alone so many, or even to weep as he entreats him? So he very fittingly adds what follows: "For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." Although God is our maker, yet because of the care and providence he has for us, "we are the people of his pasture," that is, we feed on him and have him as our food. And we are also "the sheep of his hand," since God is also the shepherd of the human race. And how does he shepherd us? With his own hand, that is, with his humanity. For in it he showed what is proper to a shepherd, laying down his life for the flock. That is why Isaiah also says, "Like a shepherd he will tend his flock, and gather the lambs with his arm." "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness, when your fathers tested me." Paul, writing to the Hebrews, taught us that "today" does not signify a single day, but the present age. For he says, "Exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin." If, then, we hear his voice in the present age (for we have heard, "My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me"), let us not harden our hearts, nor imitate the Jewish people, who are called in the prophets a rebellious house and a hard-hearted people. Many times they tested God in the wilderness and provoked him, but especially when, having conquered the Canaanite, instead of giving thanks as they ought, they spoke against God, blaming him for their departure from Egypt; it was then that he sent serpents to kill them. So Paul too says, "Let us not put the Lord to the test, as some of them tested him and were destroyed by the serpents." He urges us, therefore, that when the spiritual enemy has been routed and God's voice has become audible through the coming of the Only-begotten (for then the prophet was no mere prophet, nor a mediator of the law, but God himself was speaking), we should not speak against him for things for which we ought to give thanks, as the children of the Jews did when they called him a deceiver and a transgressor of the law; for which reason those who speak against him are destroyed by the spiritual serpents. "They tried me and saw my works for forty years." Put a stop at this point, and after that chant what follows: "I was angry with that generation"; for Paul too punctuated it this way when he cited this testimony from the psalm. He said, "They tried me and saw my works for forty years," and then added, "Therefore I was angry with that generation," making a necessary and reasonable break, since it was for forty years in the wilderness that God was tried by them. He was tried by being made to display signs, when they said, "Since he struck the rock and waters flowed, can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?" And he "rained down manna on them to eat, and rained flesh on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the seas." For these things were sung by the Spirit in the seventy-seventh psalm. Because of this he was angry with that generation, which remained ungrateful and unbelieving after so many signs, and not for a time but perpetually. That is why he did not add any length of time. But instead of "I was angry," the other translators have "I was displeased," that is, "I was ill pleased, and not pleased at all." "And I said, 'They always go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways.'" God rightly remained displeased with the Jewish people, since their straying is perpetual, not temporary. And when will one who strays perpetually turn back? Besides, they go astray not with the tongue but with the heart, which is the worst of all; for when the heart is deceived, the disease is incurable. Hence he rebuked them through the prophecy of Isaiah: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." And what caused the straying of their heart? Ignorance of the ways of God, that is, of the commandments, which those who study them do not know as well as those who carry them out. So here he has called idleness ignorance. For true knowledge comes through deeds. We all know the sea from hearsay, or from seeing it at a distance, but those who work on it have the true knowledge of it. "As I swore in my anger, they shall not enter my rest." Here "as" is not a comparison but a confirmation of the statement, meaning "I truly swore," as when he says, "How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart," and again, "How great are your works, O Lord; in wisdom you have made them all." Understand God's oath as his irrevocable threat. For since we are not permitted to go back on what we have sworn, whatever God has promised or threatened and no longer changes, he says he has sworn. What, then, did he swear? That the Jewish people would not enter his rest. This was fulfilled in those who provoked him in the wilderness: they fell in the wilderness and did not receive their inheritance in the promised land. That the prophet was also referring to the true rest of the age to come [is clear]. For he would not have taken up again a saying about that rest which had already been fulfilled, unless, as Paul says, he had in mind another rest remaining for those who would obey, in which God rested from all his present works.

1. This psalm too has no title among the Hebrews, but only in the Seventy. The Jew has naturally rejected their title, for it refutes him by showing that the psalm was clearly written about the people. For David, whose song the psalm is, lived long before the captivity after which, according to the title, the house was built. So the captivity meant is the one Paul describes this way: "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts among men." And by the building of the house he means the incarnation of God. For he himself says of his own flesh, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The building of this house, then, took place after our captivity, that is, the captivity brought about by the devil. For it was because Christ wished to set this captivity free that he became incarnate. Of it David himself said in another part of his prophecy, "You ascended on high; you led captivity captive." "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name." Why did he command the whole earth, and not Judea alone, to sing a new song, if not surely because of new wonders? David all but anticipates Paul in proclaiming the good news: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." What, then, is the "new song," and from whom shall we learn it? The prophet has set out many songs for us, but in now saying "a new song" he hints at something novel besides these. Isaiah too sang a song: "I will sing," he says, "to the beloved a song of my beloved concerning my vineyard. The beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a fertile place," and so on. But it does not suit the whole earth to sing this, only Judea, to which the song is addressed. So it refers to the song of the angels recorded by Luke, for that was new. And the prophet extended it to the whole earth, since this evangelist records that the angels sang: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men." When was this said? When the house was built, that is, when Christ became incarnate. For at his birth the angels leapt for joy in Bethlehem and sang these words. And having commanded them three times to sing, he names the Lord three times, wishing the Trinity to be glorified in Christ. For through him we have come to know both the Spirit and the Father. Hence he fittingly added, "Bless his name," whether you take it as the name of the Father, of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit; for the name of the Trinity is God. This name the angels blessed who revealed the new song, offering up glory to God in the highest at its very opening. "Proclaim the good news of our God's salvation from day to day." For as time advances, the gospel advances too, and as time extends, the knowledge of Christ extends with it, as what follows shows: "Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all the peoples." Can the Jewish people claim these words for themselves? How could someone declare God's glory among the nations who is not even permitted to read the law outside his own borders? For the prophet Amos rebuked them for this: "And they read the law outside, and called out professions. Declare that the children of Israel have loved all these things, says the Lord God." And what is the punishment? "I will set your teeth on edge in all your cities." So David clearly accepted the covenant of the gospel, first saying, "Proclaim the good news," and then commanding, "Declare the wonders of God to the nations and to all the peoples." What wonders are these? That we, who were born through blood and flesh to death, are born again through water and baptism to life. For these are the wonders that God commanded the disciples to hand on to the nations: "Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you." Concerning this name, that is, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, see what the prophet adds next: "For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods." It is superfluous to say how great God is, for this is acknowledged in everyone's mind. He calls him greatly to be praised for this reason: that though he is exceedingly great, he comes down to the lowly, and though he is righteous, he bears with sinners for their salvation. And to us he is kind, but to the demons he is fearsome. For it is these that he has called "gods" here, not because they are gods, but because some people call them so. Paul bears witness, saying, "We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one. For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth..." By whom they are so called, learn from what follows: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." It is the custom of divine Scripture to call evil spirits demons, as the Gospels show by using the word constantly. And although the children of the Greeks speak of the name in lofty terms, saying that demons (daimones) are so called as being daēmones, that is, fiery and knowing, in the very thing they praise them for they unwittingly disparage them. For since they are knowers of wickedness, they bear a shameful name. Symmachus, however, has rendered "demons" as "nonexistent ones," since they devote themselves to wickedness, which has no real existence; and Aquila has "fabricated ones," for they acquired the name of gods falsely and by fabrication.

2. All the gods of the nations, then, are demons. They may consider some gods lesser and others greater, but all of them belong to the hostile and wicked power. How is this clear? "But the Lord made the heavens." That is, the demons would not have been cast down from the heavens if they had not, through wickedness, rebelled against the one who made the heavens. But see whom heaven received in their place, and on what grounds: "Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and majesty are in his sanctuary." By "confession" he points to those who confess, and by "holiness" to the saints. These are the ones God has taken up into the heavens in place of the demons who were cast down. He joined beauty to confession, because whoever declares his own sin before God becomes comely instead of unsightly, and comes to stand before him, where he did not stand before. For God turns his face away from sinners until they repent and confess, so that this same psalmist cries out to him, "Do not turn your face away from me," at the time when he became aware of his sin. And to holiness he joined majesty. For nothing is more majestic than a saint — not a prophet, not a priest, not a king — since God, being holy, rests among the holy. That is why he does not keep them before him, as he does those who confess, but has taken them into his own sanctuary and made them sharers of his dwelling and partners in his glory and kingdom. Understand that the words that follow are addressed to them: "Bring to the Lord, you families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory to his name." It was not for nothing that at the opening of the psalm he commanded us to sing a new song. Because the calling announced in this psalm is something new, the preaching about it is new as well. For the nations, as you see, are summoned here, and what is required of them is a spiritual offering — not calves or rams or any other sacrifices of that kind, but glory and honor. Glory, as to God, for to be glorified belongs to him alone. That is why the cherubim also offer him this hymn: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place." Honor, as to a Father; for the law declares, "Honor your father and your mother." And the nations have received God as Father through adoption by the Spirit. That is why we were taught by the Savior to say to him, "Our Father, who art in heaven." Now, having said "glory and honor," he mentioned another glory again, saying, "Bring to the Lord glory to his name." So by this second glory he is hinting at the cross, which he wants offered to Christ, since it is his glory. That is why the other translators rendered it "the glory of his name." How, then, do we offer him the cross? By crucifying ourselves in the way we live. For he says, "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." And notice how he wants God to be glorified as Trinity: that is why he commands the offering to be brought three times, and three times he names the Lord. "Take up sacrifices and enter his courts." What courts? Clearly the churches throughout the whole world. And so that we would not think them divided from one another because of their number, he called the many one. For what did he add? "Worship the Lord in his holy court." They are many, then, in number, and one in power, and this one court is called holy because it is the body of the Holy One who dwells among the holy. For he commands us to offer sacrifices not of blood but of praise, and he made this plain by saying, "Worship the Lord." "Let all the earth be shaken before his face." Why? So that it may exchange its old position and become firmer, founded and established by Christ.

3. The earth was indeed shaken at the time of the cross and the resurrection, each of which is the face of the Only-begotten. For in the cross and the resurrection we behold his power, as in a single face, even to this day. "Say among the nations that the Lord has become king." Why among the nations? Because the children of the Jews will not bear to hear it. That is why Paul and Barnabas said to them, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, see, we are turning to the nations." And what is the sign of the Lord's kingship? "For he has set the world right, and it shall not be shaken." By the kingdom of God, then, he would mean our submission, for it is through this that he set the world right, bringing disobedient and unruly humanity into subjection to the knowledge of God. And why will it no longer be shaken? Surely because by his coming he put out of the way those who were shaking it, namely the demons. "He will judge the peoples with uprightness," that is, with justice. For it is impossible to plead ignorance, and we cannot find fault with God's judgment on the grounds that we did not know his law, since the Gospel of Christ has reached every part of the earth. Still, this applies far more to the people of the Jews. He will judge them with uprightness, since "he came to his own, and his own did not receive him," as John says. "Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice." And what is the reason for this gladness? The coming of the Savior, as what follows will show more clearly. The mystery accomplished on earth thus became something shared by heaven and earth. For he who bowed the heavens and came down is himself said, in turn, to have sprung up from the earth, because of the flesh. "Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it" — not with a turbulent tossing, but with one of joy and leaping. By "all that fills it" you will understand the rivers and the lakes, since every gathering of waters has been given the name of sea by God the Creator: "God called the gatherings of the waters seas," Scripture says. And what do the waters contribute to the mystery of the Only-begotten? Baptism, surely. "The plains shall rejoice, and all that is in them." Having spoken of the sea and mentioned all that fills it, he now necessarily added the plains, that is, the fields, and what goes with them, wishing to present through these all that fills the earth. And why did he command them to rejoice? "Then all the trees of the forest shall exult." When, and why? "Before the face of the Lord, for he is coming." The prophet proclaimed a special joy for the trees at Christ's coming because of the cross — and not for trees in general, but for the trees of the forest, that is, the fruitless ones. For it is clear that it was not a fruit-bearing tree but a fruitless one that was cut down to make the cross. Yet everything that springs from the earth shared in the joy, as the preceding verse already set out. You, however, may understand the trees of the forest, on account of their fruitlessness, as sinners, about whom Isaiah said, "Let not the eunuch say, 'I am a dry tree,'" that is, barren. But the Lord's coming made even these rejoice. "For he is coming, for he is coming to judge the earth; he will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his truth." It is not for nothing that he doubles "he is coming." He wanted to point to each of his comings. Above, he clearly proclaimed Christ's first coming, which is why he wrote of it without mention of judgment; for he did not come then to judge the world but to save the world. Here, however, he proclaims the second, in which he will judge the earth and the world — that is, the human being: fittingly called earth, since he comes from the earth, and called the world [oikoumene, "the inhabited"], since he has become God's dwelling place. "For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." And he called him not only earth and world but also "peoples," not "a people," because of the differences of languages, of ways of life, of beliefs about God, and of the many other things that cut human beings off from fellowship with one another in essential matters. Now if it is said that he will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in truth, then just as the world is nothing other than the peoples — for if there were no peoples, whose world would it be? — so righteousness is nothing other than truth. Each contains the other: there is neither righteousness without truth nor truth without righteousness. That is why Christ is called by both names.

1. Among the Hebrews this psalm too is counted among those without a title, but the Seventy devised for it a title suited to its prophecy. Since what the prophet sings here concerns the kingdom of Christ and what it accomplished, he fittingly dedicates it to the spiritual David. And he says, "When the earth was being established for him," that is, when humanity came to be in a settled state; for before, it had lost its sound reason. "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice, let the many islands be glad." God has always been king, as Creator and Lord of the whole world. But because for a time he turned away and allowed the human race to be tyrannized by its spiritual enemies, and now has subdued them and set humanity free, he rightly says, "The Lord has become king." He calls the kingdom of God the destruction of error and the overthrow of idols, at which the earth rejoices, seeing the freedom of those for whom it used to groan together with the rest of creation. And the many islands are glad too — the churches of the nations — for the destruction of error has opened the way in for them. But why does he call the churches islands? Surely because, just as islands are inhabited in the midst of the waters, so too are the churches, in baptism. And he wrote well that many islands are glad, not all of them, showing that there are other islands — the churches of the heretics — which also boast of the water of baptism. Yet it is not fitting for them to be glad, since by their impiety concerning the Godhead they make the grace of baptism void. "Cloud and darkness are round about him," that is, round about the one who has become king. He means Christ, whose body is a cloud; for because of its fineness it is called undefiled. But with the cloud darkness is joined, which Symmachus rendered "mist." For the flesh, like a mist, turned the eyes of most people away from recognizing the dignity of the Godhead of the Only-begotten, so that elsewhere this psalmist says, "He made darkness his hiding place; round about him is his tent." "Righteousness and judgment are the establishment of his throne." For these are what the kingdom of God has established. This is clear from the fact that we were set free from those who had unjustly enslaved us, while they were condemned. But we too must accomplish righteousness and judgment, if we wish to reign with him. "Fire shall go before him and burn up his enemies round about." Here he plainly recalls the judgment to come. That is why he does not say of the fire "goes before" but "shall go before"; it is the fire that will burn up his enemies, namely the sinners. They are God's enemies because when he called they did not listen, when he appealed to them they were not persuaded, and when he offered reconciliation they did not want it. Paul bears witness, saying, "We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us. We implore you on Christ's behalf: be reconciled to God." "And burn up his enemies round about," that is, all of them. For it will not stop circling and running until it has seized all who are guilty. Daniel too mentioned this fire, as running ahead of the Judge: "I watched," he says, "until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels burning fire. A river of fire issued and flowed out before him." "His lightnings lit up the world." By his lightnings we shall understand his radiance, which does not wait for the age to come but already lights up the world here and now. You see, then, the difference between fires. The fire that is his own gives light; the fire that is not his own but runs before him burns, for that is what it has been appointed to do. By his lightnings, then, he means the apostles, since having shared in the true light they are rightly called light themselves. That is why the Lord said to them, "You are the light of the world." "The earth saw, and was shaken." For it is good for what stands badly to be shaken, so that it may gain a firmer footing; builders, too, shake whatever walls they find rotten, wishing to rebuild them better. So the earth — that is, humanity — was shaken at the sight of the apostles, so that the people in Thessalonica said of Paul and Silas, "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too" — and this so that it might become firmer than it was. "The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord of all the earth." Just as the mountains are higher than the earth, so the prophets are higher than other people, and for this reason they are called mountains. Fittingly, then, at the coming of the Only-begotten — who is Lord, that is, of humanity, having become Lord of the whole lump by taking its firstfruits — the prophets melted like wax. For their prophecy had previously been hardened by the letter, so that it was unintelligible to those who read it. When the Only-begotten came, it melted, that is, it became soft and pliable, so that all could use it for the colors of the mystery of the Only-begotten, and through it, as through wax warmed by fire, could fashion images of the Lord. For it melted, he says, "before the face of the Lord," that is, by the working of the Spirit. Since he names the face of the Lord twice here, it is clear that he calls the Son the face of the Father, and the Spirit the face of the Son. So the prophetic wax was melted not only by the coming of the Only-begotten but also by the gift of the Spirit. For even after Christ had come, they could not understand the prophecies about him unless he gave them the gift of the Spirit. The Lord shows this when he says to them, "O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!" "The heavens proclaimed his righteousness, and all the peoples saw his glory." It is true that the heavens often proclaimed the righteousness of God, that is, Christ; for a voice was borne from them: "This is my beloved Son" — not only at the baptism but also on Mount Tabor. And again, when Christ cried out to the Father, "Father, glorify your Son," a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." Nevertheless, the heavens that proclaim God's righteousness are, properly speaking, the apostles; for they were not of the dust but heavenly, which is why they are called heavens.

2. As they proclaimed, all the peoples beheld the glory of Christ, seeing unlettered men speaking eloquently and demons driven out by the shadows of the apostles. "Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who boast in their idols." Not only those who received the written law deserve to be ashamed of idols made by hands, but also those who have the natural law. For to whom is it not obvious that making belongs to God? How, then, can something made by another be called God? So whether someone worships, or does not worship but boasts as the maker of the things others worship, he too deserves to be put to shame, for he has put a grievous stumbling block in the way of our life. "Worship him, all you his angels." He necessarily brought in the angels' worship here, so that we would not be ashamed to worship God, whom the angels worship, and at the same time would know that we who worship God rise to the rank of angels; and further, that it belongs to angels to worship, not to be worshiped. So the demons, who have even fallen from the dignity of angels, can certainly not be worshiped. "Zion heard and was glad, and the daughters of Judea rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord." By the daughters of Judea he meant the churches throughout the whole earth, since confession dwells in them; for that is what "Judea" means. But he placed Zion first, as the firstborn Church. She, he says, heard and was glad: she heard of the shame of the idolaters, and also of the worship that the angels offer to God; and she was rightly glad, since she reveres the one God, the Father of creation, who is worshiped. Her daughters, the daughters of Judea — we say they are the churches — sharing in the joy, rightly rejoiced. And these are the judgments of God, on account of which joy is rightly proclaimed. Since, then, those who worship carved images and boast in idols have been condemned by God and are put to shame, learn from what follows how this was brought about. "For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods." Since he is alluding to the judgment carried out through the cross, and the cross is the exaltation of the Only-begotten — for he says, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all people to myself" — he declared that Christ is not only high but Most High over all the earth, so that no one would think he was not high before. In saying "the earth," he named the whole creation from a part of it. Yet through the cross he was exalted above all gods, that is, the falsely so-called ones; for when they were cast down by the cross they learned by experience how high God is, so that through what was thought to be weakness he overcame those who were thought to be mighty. "You who love the Lord, hate evil" — so that, finding your love pure, he may receive you as true and genuine lovers. For whoever says he loves God but is attached to wickedness of any kind, or is in love with any of the things of this life, deceives himself. "For friendship with this world is enmity toward God," says James. "The Lord guards the souls of his holy ones; he will deliver them from the hand of the sinner." See how much we gain from pure love toward God. We become holy, and we have God as the guardian of our greatest possession, our soul, so that it does not fall into the hand of the enemy. And if we do fall into it, he does not stand by and watch, but delivers us, shackling the real sinner and root of sin, the devil, while giving us his hand so that we may escape the one who has unjustly risen up against us. "Light has dawned for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart." The law of God has become a lamp and a light for the righteous. That is why David says elsewhere, "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." The same law is also gladness to the upright in heart, that is, to those who walk straight; for it shows them the way they pray for, and anoints them for the virtues they strive for of their own accord. But you may also understand the light that has dawned as the Only-begotten, of whom John the Theologian wrote, "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings." That is why Malachi called him the sun, and declared, as David does, that he rises for the righteous; for he says, "For you who fear the Lord the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings." "Be glad in the Lord, you righteous." The righteous are rightly blessed in their joy. For they are not glad over any of the passing goods of this life, but over God, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present from above, as you have learned from the Epistle of James. "And give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness." You may take "confession" either as thanksgiving or as the acknowledgment of faults — for the latter also befits the righteous, since there is no one who will live and not sin. Either way it is fittingly offered at the remembrance of God's holiness, that is, when we call it to mind. We ought to give him thanks because he has given human beings a share in his holiness, and we ought also to confess ourselves sinners. For however righteous a person may be, when compared with the holiness of God he is found to be a sinner, so that Isaiah says, "All our righteousness is like a soiled rag before you."

1. It is not without reason that the psalm is inscribed "To David." Since it prophesies the mysteries concerning Christ, it bears his name, for the prophet Ezekiel, or rather the Spirit that was upon him, taught us to understand Christ as David. He says: "And I will raise up for you a shepherd, my servant David." Yet David had died many generations before. He calls Christ David, not only because he was descended from David, but also because he is king; and he calls him servant because he took the form of a servant. For this reason the psalm here too is inscribed not "Of David" but "To David." Sing to the Lord a new song. For what reason? Because he has done marvellous things. This, then, is the theme of the new song: that God has done marvellous things, or "wonders," as Symmachus rendered it. And what are these? His right hand and his holy arm have saved him. And what is so marvellous about this? Surely that man had been given up as lost through the excess of his wickedness. So Isaiah says: "Every head is in pain, and every heart in grief. From the feet to the head there is no soundness in him; wound, bruise, festering sore: there is no salve to apply, nor oil, nor bandages." And David says this: "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one." For this reason God's right hand and arm were needed, that is, his Only-begotten. Each of these terms signifies him, and Isaiah too says of him: "Like a shepherd he will tend his people, and with his arm he will gather the lambs." It is not without reason that the psalmist called him holy: he wished to show him in his own distinct hypostasis. He saved, then, the very creature that was lost: "For he did not come to judge the world, but to save the world."
