Isaiah makes clear that the prophet is alluding to the coming of the Only-begotten (for that coming alone saves the human race) when he says: "Not an ambassador nor an angel, but the Lord himself will come and save us." What follows also makes it clear. The Lord has made known his salvation; before the nations he has revealed his righteousness. Our discourse has often shown in what came before that Christ is called salvation and righteousness. Here the psalmist displays the precision of the prophetic wording, saying that he was first made known and afterwards revealed. He first made him known to the prophets, who were entrusted with the knowledge of him through the contemplation granted by the Spirit, so that the Lord says: "Abraham our father rejoiced to see my day; and he saw it and was glad." Afterwards he was revealed through the flesh, and further through the miracles of the apostles, which laid bare the power of the Only-begotten. Before the nations. For they believed and received the manifestation of Christ. Besides, since the overthrow of idols is clear proof of his coming in the flesh, it follows that the Only-begotten could be revealed before the nations. He has remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel. Why was he not content to say Jacob, but added the house of Israel as well? Surely to show that the one who accomplished what is now being prophesied was the same one who named Jacob Israel. That is why he also wrestled with him, wishing to prefigure the mystery of the incarnation, for wrestling and grappling belong to flesh. He remembered, then, what he had promised to Jacob and Israel, and fulfilled the mystery by the grace he showed to him. How so? Clearly in that he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, bestowing his mercy not on them (for they were not worthy) but on Jacob, from whom the race descended. He also remembered the truth of the house of Israel. He brought into effect and made true the blessing which Israel, prophesying, allotted as an inheritance among his sons to the tribe of Judah. It was this: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he is the expectation of the nations." So what follows fits very well: All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. He came to the Jews as to his own. But they shut their eyes ("For they have closed their eyes," says Isaiah, "lest they should see"), and so in their place the ends of the earth, that is, the nations, beheld the salvation of God, though before they had not seen.

2. This is what the prophet is now astonished at, and what the Lord too marvelled at when he said: "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." Shout to the Lord, all the earth. Rightly so, since the good things are shared by all. The mystery that has been accomplished no longer belongs to one country, such as Judea, or to one nation, but to all humanity. For this reason he wants them to shout like people who have won a war together. By "earth" he meant humanity as a whole, as is said more clearly in what follows. Sing, and rejoice, and sing psalms. So he means to speak not about the element of dry land but about human beings. That is why he addresses them as a multitude. He bids them first to sing, then to rejoice, and then he added singing psalms, so that our joy in God may have its glorifying of him as both beginning and end. Sing psalms to the Lord with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of a psalm, with beaten trumpets and the sound of the horn trumpet. Shout before the King, the Lord. Even if there was a time when people used these instruments to glorify God, we should understand the lyre as the harmony of the virtues. This harmony is achieved only when we put the flesh to death, so that the sound of the virtues is produced in it as on strings, and the sound of a psalm pleasing to God is sent up to heaven. But since he mentioned the trumpet after the lyre, he must be calling the Old Testament a lyre, on which he commanded us to sing psalms (for psalmody comes from it). The trumpets are the Gospels, on which we are rightly bidden to shout before the King, the Lord, that is, Christ, as people who have conquered their enemies through the way of life of the gospel. He mentioned many trumpets and also one for this reason: the Gospel, though one in power, became four because of the evangelists who set it down. Notice the precision of the prophetic wording. The trumpets, spoken of in the plural and taken to refer to the persons of the writers, he calls "beaten," that is, forged, for the tongues of the evangelists were forged by the supply of the Spirit. The single trumpet he calls "of horn." This is the gospel message and the mystery it contains, which is fittingly called a horn because it has Christ as its head, for in him we have received the power to gore our enemies. To this Gospel, then, he fittingly assigned the sound, saying "with the sound of the horn trumpet," since, though several set out the story, the voice of one Gospel is heard through them all, because they wrote the mystery in harmony. Let the sea be moved, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it. We said earlier that the sea and its fullness (he means the living creatures in it) are moved to dance. But you may also understand that it is moved out of fear at the miracles the Lord performed in it. For it bore not only the Lord walking on it but Peter as well; and at Jesus' command it brought up a fish holding a stater. You may say the same of the world and those who dwell in it. The miracles performed by Christ and the prophets were enough to astonish it and shake it, so that when they prayed, as Luke relates, many things were shaken. Rivers will clap their hands together. You may take these as the operations of the Spirit, which are said to clap their hands because they were gathered into one at the time of Christ's coming. Of them he said: "He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." You may also say that the visible rivers clapped their hands and danced when the Jordan received Christ at his baptism, for this was a joy shared by the rivers and the waters. The mountains will rejoice before the face of the Lord, for he is coming. We have said that we take the mountains to be the prophets, because of the height of their contemplation. They will rightly rejoice at Christ's coming, since their prophecy is coming to fulfilment. And even if you take it of the visible mountains, they too rightly rejoice, since the Jewish people used to sacrifice to idols on the high places, as is said in the book of Kings, and this was abolished by Christ's coming. For he has come to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in uprightness. How can he say that the same one "has come"? Clearly because, being a prophet, he saw as present what he was foretelling as future. Alternatively, the first statement concerns the coming in the flesh, which took place first; the second concerns the second coming, in which he comes as judge. Of the first he says "he is coming," because he was looking forward to the good things it would bring; the second he regarded as already present, out of fear of the judgment. It is very profitable to keep fearful things before our eyes and to see them as close at hand, so that we may be held back from sinning. What is the order of the judgment? Righteousness and uprightness. Let us then flee injustice and turn away from crooked ways; let us not put our confidence in deceit, nor pursue greed. For these things are contrary to God's judgment and lead those who pursue them to condemnation.

1. All the other translators gave out this psalm without a title, but the Seventy assigned it to David, since it too prophesies about the spiritual David, Christ. The Lord has become king; let the peoples be angry. He means the peoples of the Jews, for Christ's kingship roused them to anger and fury, so that they said to Pilate: "Do not say that he is King of the Jews"; and again: "We have no king but Caesar." He who sits upon the cherubim: let the earth be shaken. Again he is alluding to Judea. When the magi came from the east saying, "Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east and have come to worship him," Herod heard it and was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. What follows shows what the one who sits upon the cherubim did. The Lord is great in Zion, and high above all the peoples. In Zion he entered while the doors were shut, displaying his own greatness, and through that miracle he showed clearly that he is the one who sits upon the cherubim. And for this reason the works of the maker of all creation surpass our nature. Then too he was shown to be high above all the peoples, when he gave the apostles the gift of the Holy Spirit, and they proclaimed his loftiness not to one people but to all, and everywhere. Let them give praise to your great name, for it is fearful and holy. Every name of God is great, since his names are to be understood in proportion to his glory. Even if he is called Master, it is not in the same sense as we are; and if he is called King, the dignity of kingship is understood of him in a far higher sense. Nevertheless, the great name of God is the one he gave himself, when Moses said: "Behold, I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them, 'The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me to you'; and if they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?" He answered him: "You shall say to the children of Israel, 'He Who Is has sent me to you.'" It is to this fearful and holy name that the prophet commanded us to give praise. A ruler who lasts only for a time, even if he is powerful, is not greatly to be feared, since once some time has passed his power comes to an end. But he who always is and is eternal is rightly to be feared, for there is no hope that he will change or cease. Since he says that this name is holy and fearful, you should understand it as fearful to his enemies, that is, to the demons, which is why they flee when it is invoked; and as holy to the faithful, for they receive sanctification in no other way than through the name of Christ. And the honour of the king loves judgment. For what is the work of judgment? To acquit the innocent and expose the guilty. That is why the king's honour, that is, his rule and authority, loves judgment. Hence the other translators rendered "honour" as "strength" in some cases and "might" in others. You have prepared uprightness. How did he prepare it? By sending the law ahead, in which he laid down the commandments as upright ways. For those who walk by them can cut a straight road through life. You have done judgment and righteousness in Jacob. In what way? Clearly in the way just described. The law given in Jacob (he means the race of Israel) brought judgment, that is, condemnation, on sinners, and showed those who live good lives the righteousness by which one must conduct oneself. Why has he set these things out now? Because he wishes to secure our hearing and to bear clear witness that the one who accomplished these things is the one who endured the cross for us. What follows shows this: Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet, for he is holy. Why does he bid us worship not at God's throne but at his footstool? And what footstool does he mean at all? The earth? "For heaven," he says, "is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet."

2. Yet we are not permitted to worship the elements. Rather, he means the place which he described more plainly in another psalm, saying, "Let us worship at the place where his feet stood." He means Golgotha. For that place truly came to be under the feet of his flesh at the time of the cross. That is why he was not content to say "footstool," but says "the footstool of his feet." Yet it is plain to everyone that a footstool is a footstool for feet. But here by "feet" he means Christ's humanity, just as by "head" he means his divinity. Golgotha, then, came to be under the feet of his humanity, and whoever worships there exalts Christ. For he regards his sufferings as his exaltation, since it was through them that he accomplished our salvation. That is why he said to Nicodemus: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." He is rightly called holy, since the holiness present in him is so great that he makes even sinners holy by their sharing in him. Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name. They called upon the Lord, and he heard them. Since the priests and the prophets were also called holy, and yet it is not right to worship at the footstool of these holy men, he named them because he wished to show how great a difference there was between Christ and the other saints. For he was the Holy One of the holy ones. For this reason he mentioned Moses as lawgiver, Aaron as high priest, and Samuel as leader of the prophets, men who were indeed holy. Even so, they called upon the name of God, and what they did, they did not by their own power but by the power of the one they called upon, as he shows more clearly in what follows. In a pillar of cloud he spoke to them. For they kept his testimonies and his ordinances, which he gave them. These men, he says, made progress through virtue, by keeping God's law and carrying out the ordinances he had given. And when they were counted worthy to see God, they beheld him in a pillar, since they could not bear to see his essence. But it is not so with Christ: he has the Father in himself, and he himself is in the Father; nor did he rise to his dignity by making progress. See what he said in answer when Pilate asked him, "Are you a king?": "You say that I am a king; for this I was born." That is: I possess my kingship without beginning in time, just as I do my birth. It is to him, beyond all doubt, that the psalmist addressed what follows. O Lord our God, you heard them. "Our God": whose? The God of those who have enlisted in his service through faith and, through the adoption of baptism, have made the God who is over all their own. Thomas teaches that he is called God in a special sense by those who have believed in him: "My Lord and my God." Calling him his own Lord and God, he cried out to the God who is over all. This God, then, in whom we have believed, was not unknown even to the righteous of earlier times, and so he heard them when they prayed. What follows bears witness to this. O God, you were gracious to them, and avenged all their undertakings. You see that he is speaking about Christ, for it belongs to him to make atonement for our sins, not only now but in times past as well. Paul too speaks of him: "Whom God put forward as an atonement through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness." He avenges all the undertakings of the righteous. They undertook many things to save the human race, but the spiritual enemy opposed them; so the cross avenged them, at once establishing the undertakings of the righteous and overthrowing the one who made their labours seem useless. It was over this that Jeremiah cried out: "Woe is me, mother! What kind of man did you bear me, a man judged and disputed with throughout all the earth? I have neither profited anyone, nor has anyone profited me; my strength has failed among those who curse me." Exalt the Lord our God. But what need has the Exalted One to be exalted? And how will he who is in heaven be exalted by human beings? He means: think lofty thoughts about him. In what way? And worship at his holy mountain. The exaltation of God the Word, then, is worship at the holy place. Just as trophies won in war are a king's glory, so Christ's glory is the victory he won through his sufferings, which took place on the holy mountain that received the cross. He calls the mountain holy not on its own account but because the Crucified One came to it. That is why he added: For the Lord our God is holy. And if he is holy, whatever he comes to is made holy.

The psalm has no name in its title, but that does not make it foreign to David's prophecy. Perhaps he simply did not get the chance to play it on the lyre in the temple, nor did he hand it over to other psalm-singers. That is why prophecy set it down without a name. Even so, we must understand "confession" here as thanksgiving, for this is what the aim of the prophecy that follows requires. That is why Aquila says "For thanksgiving" and Symmachus "A blessing," while the fifth version gives "For praise." "Shout to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness." Here too those who examine the prophecy closely will find that its order is carefully arranged. He wants all the earth to shout as people who have defeated our common enemy, and, knowing that God is the cause of the victory, to serve him with gladness. As Paul said: "Let us all rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything." We should know whom we serve and on what terms, what slavery we were rescued from and what we were called to, and what kind of yoke we took in exchange for what kind: we traded the heaviest yoke for one that is exceedingly light. "Enter before him with exultation"—that is, with joy. But he does not mean this passing joy. Grown men laugh at the joy of children, because children rejoice and pride themselves on things of no value. In the same way the righteous find the joy of sinners shameful. Sinners rejoice in blind wealth and in riches gained by robbery, and in other such things that will give no cause for joy when we are about to stand before the fearsome Judge. It is in the opposite things, when we are robbed and when we are slandered, that we will be able to enter before God with exultation. The Lord's words make this plain: "Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and falsely say every evil word against you on my account. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven." "Know that the Lord himself is our God; it is he who made us, and not we ourselves." You see that the Spirit takes the field against every heretical tongue. Some people want to cut the Trinity apart and belittle the dignity of the Only-begotten. They say that the divinely inspired Scripture calls him Lord but calls the Father God, and so they introduce a difference between Lord and God that does not exist. To their own harm they drag into blasphemy the Apostle's saying: "One God the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." They make the Son lesser than the Father on the ground that he is Lord, for they say he is never called God. So the Apostle's words apply to them as well: "But not everyone has this knowledge." The prophet wants to demolish their clever talk, and so he says, "Know that the Lord himself is our God," so that we will no longer try to separate Lord from God, or the Son from the Father. "It is he who made us, and not we ourselves." We did not come into existence by ourselves, as some imagine. Rather, "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works," as Paul wrote. We must acknowledge someone as our Maker. "We are his people and the sheep of his pasture. Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns." Learn whose sheep we are from the Only-begotten, who says: "My sheep hear my voice." We are also the people of the one who told us through the prophet's tongue: "And you shall be my people, and I will be your God." So the Lord himself is God, for the Son is called both, just as the Father is. He commanded us to enter this one's gates with confession and his courts with hymns. So we must first confess and only then sing hymns. Gates stand in front of courts, and no one can get inside a court without coming through the gate. In the same way we will not be able to sing hymns before we have confessed. We need a pure heart, and a tongue that has put off the filth of sins, if God is to be pleased with the sacrifice of our hymns. "Confess to him, praise his name." Once again he puts confession before praise, because he wants to make what he said in the earlier verses clearer to us. He commands us to confess to him as God, and to praise his name, which is Savior, for that name has become the source of our salvation. Peter, speaking to the Jews together with John, will testify to this: "For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." So the psalmist went on quite fittingly: "And his truth endures to generation and generation, for Christ is Lord; his mercy endures forever." His truth begins in the present generation and will be revealed in the generation to come, when he repays each person according to his deeds. This is the unassailable and unerring truth: that Christ is Lord, and his mercy endures forever. As Christ, that is, as one who is compassionate and loves humankind, he has given his mercy in the present age, so that even if we go astray through carelessness, we may still turn back to him through his love for humankind.
